trap: Not kutsu o kiru: anything on the feet or legs takes haku.
freqNote: Rank is for 履く #3474. Kana はく is mostly 吐く 'throw up' (#1739), so the kana count was not used. Pairing commonness is judged.
why: Said at every doorway (kutsu haite, hayaku). The haku/kiru split is the core of the wearing system.

trap: kiru only covers tops and whole-body clothes (shirt, coat, dress, kimono). English 'wear' also covers shoes, trousers, hats and glasses, which each take a different verb.
freqNote: Rank is for 着る #754. Kana きる is mostly 切る 'cut' (#546), the same sound. Pairing commonness is judged.
why: The base wearing verb (nani kiteku? / kore kite mite) that every other wear verb is learned against. shatsu, kooto, seetaa and kimono take it too.

trap: Not kutsu o toru: shoes and clothes come off with nugu, and toru sounds like picking them up.
freqNote: Ranks are for 靴 #1818 and 脱ぐ #2074. Pairing commonness is judged; kutsu o nuide kudasai is heard at Japanese entrances every day.
why: Heard or said at every Japanese doorway, and the model take-off verb for anything worn with kiru or haku.

trap: Not zubon o kiru: trousers, skirts, socks and tights take haku, like shoes (anything you step into).
freqNote: Ranks are for ズボン #6081 and 履く #3474. sukaato (#6710) and kutsushita (#5748) take the same verb.
why: A worse trap than shoes, because trousers count as clothes, so learners reach for kiru. sukaato o haku and kutsushita o haku go in its notes.

trap: Not megane o kiru or tsukeru: glasses 'hang' on the face, so the verb is kakeru.
freqNote: Ranks are for 眼鏡 #4549 (the katakana spelling メガネ is listed separately at #6067) and the kanji 掛ける #2742. Kana かける (#244) also counts the call, sit and spend senses.
why: Used for routines and for describing people (megane kaketeru hito). Builds on the 'put on' sense of versatility kakeru.

trap: Not boushi o kiru: anything pulled over the head (hat, cap, helmet, hood) takes kaburu.
freqNote: Rank is for kana かぶる #1926, the usual spelling; the kanji 被る is #7902. The kana count also includes the casual 'clash/overlap' sense (yotei ga kaburu), so it overstates the wearing sense.
why: Hats, caps and helmets are everyday, and the partner verb can't be guessed.

trap: Not masuku o kiru: small worn items (mask, watch, scarf, tie) just take suru, as in masuku shiteru. masuku o tsukeru is the announcement register.
freqNote: Ranks are for マスク #5039 and する #15. The drama corpus is partly older than 2020, so マスク may rank lower than it is used today. That is a judgement; the rank was not adjusted.
why: Masks are routine in Japan (colds, pollen). masuku shiteru and masuku hazushite ii? are everyday phrases.

trap: Not megane o nugu: nugu is only for clothes and shoes. Glasses, watches, masks, rings and earrings come off with hazusu.
freqNote: Rank is for 外す #1043, which also counts 'miss' and 'step away (seki o hazusu)'. Pairing commonness is judged.
why: One take-off verb covers every accessory (masuku, tokei, yubiwa o hazusu). It undoes kakeru, suru, hameru and tsukeru.

trap: Not tokei o kiru: a watch takes suru (tokei shiteru). tsukeru also works but sounds stiffer.
freqNote: 時計 #3262 also counts clocks; 腕時計 'wristwatch' is #10342. Pairing commonness is judged.
why: Comes up in everyday talk ('no watch on today'). The clearest example of the suru-for-accessories rule.

trap: English 'fit' has no one-word verb: say saizu ga au / awanai. This au means 'match' and sounds the same as au 'meet'.
freqNote: Rank is for 合う #563. Kana あう is mostly 会う 'meet' (#110). Pairing commonness is judged.
why: The phrase for trying clothes on in a shop (saizu awanai, chotto ookii). The learner has to say it, not just hear it.

trap: Not fuku o toru: every garment comes off with nugu, whichever verb put it on.
freqNote: Ranks are for 服 #1051 and 脱ぐ #2074. Pairing commonness is judged.
why: Covers uwagi nuide ii? and atsui kara nuida. It is the clothes half of nugu, a reserve if kutsu o nugu already carries the verb.

trap: Not keshou o tsukeru or kiru: makeup takes suru. Many speakers say okeshou suru, and younger ones meiku suru.
freqNote: Ranks are for 化粧 #4597 and する #15. The younger alternative メイク is #5468.
why: Part of the daily routine. 'Put on' leads English speakers to a wear verb, but makeup is something you do.

trap: Not yubiwa o kiru: things you push a finger or hand into (rings, gloves) take hameru. yubiwa shiteru is also common for wearing one.
freqNote: Rank is for kana はめる #2952, which also counts the drama-heavy 'set someone up' sense. 手袋 'gloves' is #6640.
why: Covers rings and gloves; tebukuro o hamete is the everyday winter use and goes in the notes.

ja: アクセサリーを付ける
kana: アクセサリーをつける
trap: Not akusesarii o kiru: earrings, necklaces and badges take tsukeru, or just suru (piasu shiteru).
freqNote: Rank is for 付ける #1452. The 'wear' spelling 着ける is #3726, and kana つける (#393) also counts the turn-on and attach senses. ピアス 'earrings' is #13111.
why: Completes the wear verbs (kiru/haku/kaburu/kakeru/suru/hameru/tsukeru). It is less frequent than the others.

trap: Not keshou o nugu or toru: makeup is 'dropped' with otosu, the same verb used for dirt and stains.
freqNote: Rank is for 落とす #923, which is mostly the 'drop' sense. Pairing commonness is judged.
why: The take-off half of keshou o suru, done daily by people who wear makeup. The partner verb can't be guessed.

trap: Not nekutai o kiru: a tie is 'tightened' with shimeru, which sounds like shimeru 'close'. Wearing one is just nekutai shiteru.
freqNote: Rank is for 締める #4630. Kana しめる is mostly 閉める 'close' (#1764).
why: For talk about work clothes. beruto o shimeru (belt) uses the same verb and goes in the notes.

trap: Not kontakuto o kakeru like glasses: lenses go in with ireru and come out with hazusu or toru.
freqNote: コンタクト #8030 also counts 'contact (get in touch)'. コンタクトレンズ is #34753. Rank is for 入れる #222.
why: Daily for lens wearers, and it builds on versatility ireru. Narrow outside that group.

trap: Not mafuraa o kiru: a scarf takes suru (mafuraa shiteru), or maku 'wrap' for the act of putting it on.
freqNote: Ranks are for マフラー #11291 and する #15. 巻く 'wrap' is #3104.
why: A winter item. It repeats the suru rule already taught by masuku and tokei, so it is a reserve.

trap: English 'put your hair up' doesn't carry over; the verb is musubu 'tie' (casually kami shibaru or matomeru).
freqNote: Rank is for 髪 #1752. Kana かみ is also 紙 'paper' (#2672) and 神 'god' (#1988). Hair kami was left out of the 180 nouns as a homophone of 10-list-nouns #14 (kami 'paper'). 結ぶ #2173.
why: Everyday for long hair (kami musunde iku?), but mostly guessable, so a reserve. Cutting and washing hair belong to body/home.

trap: Not boushi o hazusu: hats come off with toru (boushi o nugu also works), not with the accessory verb hazusu.
freqNote: Rank is for 取る #228, the broad 'take' sense. Pairing commonness is judged.
why: Completes the kaburu pair. Low trap risk because English 'take off' leads to toru, which is correct.

trap: Not densha o noru or densha o toru: you ride on a vehicle with ni noru, and 'take' is never toru here.
freqNote: Phrase not counted, so noun and verb are ranked separately. The same frame covers basu (#2466), takushii (#1987), hikouki (#3222) and jitensha (#2927) ni noru.
why: One frame for every vehicle; English 'take' and the habit of using o both push learners wrong.

trap: Not densha o tsukamaeru or densha o toru: making a train in time is ni maniau ('be in time for').
freqNote: Phrase not counted. maniau ranks high because it covers any deadline.
why: Said daily (maniau? / maniawanai! / maniatta), and English 'catch' has no matching Japanese verb.

trap: Not michi o nakusu or michi o ushinau: getting lost is michi ni mayou ('stray on the road'), or casually just mayotta.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. mayou alone also means 'can't decide', which raises its rank.
why: The core travel-trouble phrase; English 'lose' leads to nakusu (lose an object).

trap: Not densha ga osoi: osoi means slow, and a train running late is okureteru. Switching ga to ni flips it to 'I missed the train'.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. okureru's rank also covers people being late.
why: The standard excuse (densha okurete...); learned with densha ni okureru, where the subject changes.

trap: Not densha kara deru or densha ni oriru: getting off is oriru, with the vehicle marked by o (or kara).
freqNote: Phrase not counted. In speech the noun usually drops: tsugi de oriru.
why: The partner of ni noru; the particle switch (ni to get on, o to get off) is the classic slip.

trap: Not jiko o shita or jiko o motta: being in an accident is jiko ni au, the same sound as meeting someone. A driver who causes one jiko o okosu.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. 遭う is ranked apart from 会う (#110), though they sound the same.
why: English 'have' or 'get in' gives no clue. The same ni au frame gives ame ni au (get caught in the rain).

trap: Not densha o misu shita or densha o nakushita: missing a train is ni okureru (casually also nogashita or noriokureta).
freqNote: Phrase not counted. Alternatives natives use: nogasu (#2510) and the single verb noriokureru (#13876).
why: English 'miss' has no direct verb. Must be kept apart from densha ga okureru (the train is late).

trap: Not seki ga furii or seki ga hima: a free seat is aiteru ('open'), as in koko aitemasu ka?
freqNote: Phrase not counted. 空く (aku) is ranked separately from 開く (#14086, a door opening).
why: Asked whenever you sit next to a stranger. Kept apart from suku (empty), though both are written 空く.

trap: Not kado ni magaru: the corner takes o and the direction takes ni (tsugi no kado o migi ni magaru). 'Turn' is not mawaru (spin).
freqNote: Phrase not counted. Both words rank mid-list because drama dialogue rarely gives directions.
why: The backbone of giving and following directions, with two particles in one phrase.

trap: Not michi ga isogashii (busy is for people) or kuruma ga ooi: crowded roads, trains and shops are konderu.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. komu is written 混む or 込む, and the list splits them (#5984 / #10624).
why: One verb for crowded roads, trains and shops (densha konderu, mise ga konderu); English 'busy' leads to isogashii.

trap: Not hoteru ni iru or sutei suru: staying the night is tomaru, the same sound as a car stopping.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. 泊まる is ranked apart from 止まる (#776).
why: Used for every trip and sleepover (doko ni tomaru?, tomodachi no ie ni tomaru). The transitive tomeru means to put someone up (tomete!).

trap: Not kuruma o paaku suru: parking is just 'stopping' the car, tomeru (chuusha suru is the word on signs). Not yameru, which means quitting.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. 止める covers stopping anything, so its rank overstates the parking sense; the parking spelling 停める is #22793.
why: The transitive half of the tomaru/tomeru pair. doko ni tomeru? is the parking question.

trap: Not densha ga yameru: yameru is quitting. A train stopping (at a station, or halted) is tomaru.
freqNote: Phrase not counted.
why: Two daily uses: kono densha Shibuya ni tomaru? and densha tomatteru (service halted). The intransitive half of kuruma o tomeru.

trap: Not takushii o toru or takushii o tsukamu: hailing one in the street is hirou ('pick up'). tsukamaeru also works; phoning for one is yobu.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. hirou's rank mostly counts picking things up.
why: A verb nobody could guess; part of a set with takushii o yobu and takushii ni noru.

kana: しゅうでんがなくなる
trap: Not shuuden o misu suru: Japanese says the last train 'is gone', as in shuuden nakunatchau!
freqNote: Phrase not counted. 397 is the kana spelling なくなる (無くなる #8961), and its rank covers running out of anything.
why: The everyday excuse for leaving a night out; the train is the subject, not the speaker. Alternatives: shuuden ni maniawanai, shuuden nogashita.

trap: Not kuruma de byouki ni naru: motion sickness uses you, the verb for getting drunk (kuruma yoi, fune ni you).
freqNote: Phrase not counted. you's rank is mostly about drunkenness.
why: Common on bus and car trips and impossible to guess; the noun form kuruma yoi (suru) is just as frequent.

trap: Not nimotsu o oku or nimotsu o nokosu: handing bags over to be kept (hotel, locker, airport check-in) is azukeru. Leaving them behind by mistake is wasureru.
freqNote: Phrase not counted.
why: A hotel and airport staple where both 'leave' and 'check' mislead.

trap: Not michi ga karappo or michi ga hima: an uncrowded road or train is suiteru, the same suku as in onaka ga suku.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. The list files nearly all 空く under the aku reading (#1498), so suku's #47898 comes from how the list splits words, not real rarity.
why: The opposite of michi ga komu, learned with it; densha suiteta is just as common.

trap: Not michi o iu or michi o hanasu: telling someone the way is oshieru ('teach'), as in eki made no michi oshiete kuremasen ka?
freqNote: Phrase not counted.
why: How the learner asks for directions; the partner of michi o kiku.

trap: Not eki o tsuku or eki ni kita for 'I'm here': arriving is tsuku with ni, as in ima eki tsuita.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. 着く is ranked apart from the kana spelling つく (#355).
why: The most-said travel update on the phone. Low trap because tsuku is already on the versatility list; only the ni is new.

trap: Not densha ga hanareru or densha ga saru: a train or bus leaving is just deru, as in tsugi no densha nanji ni deru?
freqNote: Phrase not counted. deru's rank covers every sense of going out or appearing.
why: The everyday way to ask about timetables (shuppatsu suru is the announcement word); built on H-deru.

trap: Not michi o tanomu or michi o shitsumon suru: asking the way is kiku, the verb for listening.
freqNote: Phrase not counted.
why: For telling the story of a trip (michi kiitara...); the other half of michi o oshieru.

trap: Not seki o ageru: offering your seat to someone is yuzuru ('hand over').
freqNote: Phrase not counted.
why: A verb nobody could guess and a common train situation, though it's more often heard or told about than said.

trap: Not michi ni wataru or kurosu suru: what you cross takes o (michi, hashi, shingou o wataru).
freqNote: Phrase not counted.
why: Used in directions and warnings to children; the o for the path crossed is the only trap.

trap: Not takushii o kakeru: kakeru goes with denwa (the phone call), while the taxi you summon is yobu.
freqNote: Phrase not counted.
why: The easy half of the taxi set (hirou to hail one, yobu to call one); a reserve.

trap: Not jikan o toru: the time a task takes is kakaru (jikan o toru means setting time aside).
freqNote: かかる #385 is the kana spelling across all senses; 掛かる #5316.
why: The everyday way to say how long anything takes (dore gurai kakaru?), and English 'take' points straight at toru.

trap: Not ikura kakaru for a price tag: what an item costs takes suru (kore ikura shita? = how much was this?); kakaru is for running costs of a trip or service.
freqNote: いくら #553 counts all uses, including 'no matter how'. The shape is price + suru, so it takes amounts in place of ikura.
why: People ask and give prices all the time (sore ikura shita?), and nothing in English suggests suru for 'cost'.

trap: English 'it costs a lot' has no verb to copy: money kakaru, the same verb as time (kekkou kakatta).
freqNote: お金 #422. The casual 金 (kane, #670) sounds rougher. かかる #385 is the kana form across all senses.
why: The usual way to talk about overall costs (a trip, a car), and it uses the same verb as jikan ga kakaru.

trap: Not jiyuu: being free is aku, 'to open up' (ashita aiteru? = are you free tomorrow?).
freqNote: 空く (あく) #1498. The kana あく #3508 mixes senses, and 開く (a door opens) is ranked separately.
why: The everyday way to ask about and offer availability, usually said as aiteru with jikan dropped.

trap: Not yotei o motsu: having plans is aru (yotei aru kara = I've got plans).
why: The standard reason for turning down an invitation, and the opener for asking about one (konshuumatsu yotei aru?).

trap: Not jikan ni tsuku or dekiru: making it in time is maniau, with ni on the deadline or train (densha ni maniatta).
freqNote: 間に合う #904 counts the whole verb, which also means 'be enough' (mou maniatteru = I'm fine, thanks).
why: Said constantly when running late. Its opposite, jikan ni okureru, is H-okureru, and ni marks what you catch.

trap: Not okane o toru: cash from the bank or ATM is orosu, 'bring down' (dasu also works casually).
freqNote: 下ろす #2775 covers all senses, including lowering things. 降ろす #4786 is letting people off.
why: A weekly errand phrase (chotto okane oroshite kuru), and no English verb leads to orosu.

trap: Not jikan ga tooru: time passing is tatsu (jikan tatsu no hayai ne), a different tatsu from 'stand'.
freqNote: 経つ #3603 is the time sense. The kana たつ is dominated by 立つ #610.
why: A common remark (mou ichinen tatta), and English 'pass' leads to tooru. sugiru is possible but more formal.

trap: Not benri: a time that suits someone is tsugou ga ii (benri is for tools and places). The opposite is tsugou ga warui, 'can't make it'.
freqNote: いい #24 is the spoken form; 良い #1474.
why: The tactful way to ask when someone is free (itsu ga tsugou ii?) and to decline (sono hi wa chotto tsugou ga warukute). tsugou ga warui is folded in here.

trap: Not okane o tasukeru or setsuyaku suru: saving up is tameru, 'pile up' (setsuyaku means cutting back).
freqNote: 貯める #10930 is the money spelling. The kana ためる #3410 covers every sense.
why: How people talk about saving for a trip or a purchase, and English 'save' leads to the wrong verb. It pairs with okane ga tamaru.

trap: Not yotei ga kuru or deru: a plan that gets booked 'enters' (sono hi yotei haitteru = I've got something that day).
why: The standard way to say a day is taken or that something came up. It pairs with yotei o ireru.

trap: Learners swap kariru (borrow) and kasu (lend). The lender takes ni or kara (tomodachi ni karita).
why: Comes up every day (karite ii?), and mixing up which way kasu and kariru go is a classic learner error.

trap: Not yakusoku o motsu or tamotsu: keeping a promise is mamoru, 'protect' (jikan o mamoru = be on time).
freqNote: 守る #303 is likely inflated by its 'protect' sense in drama plots.
why: A common reminder and reproach (yakusoku mamotte yo), and English 'keep' gives no route to mamoru. jikan o mamoru is folded in here.

trap: Not okane o sugosu: money is spent with tsukau, 'use'; sugosu is only for spending time.
why: A common phrase (okane tsukaisugita), and 'spend' sends learners to sugosu.

trap: Not jikan o korosu: killing time is tsubusu, 'crush' (kafe de jikan tsubushiteta).
freqNote: 潰す #2027 also covers 'crush' and 'ruin'. The kana つぶす is #4184.
why: The natural phrase when you're early for a meeting; a literal translation of 'kill' gives the wrong verb. The noun hima tsubushi is also common.

trap: yakusoku isn't only 'promise': it means any arrangement to meet, so kyou wa yakusoku ga aru = I'm meeting someone today.
why: Goes beside yotei ga aru: yakusoku is plans with a person, yotei is anything scheduled. Learners only know yakusoku as 'promise'.

trap: Not keikaku o tsukuru: plans are tateru, 'stand up'. yotei o tateru works the same way.
freqNote: The rank is for 計画; yotei (予定 #843) also takes tateru.
why: How people talk about planning a trip or a budget, where English 'make' leads to tsukuru. yotei o tateru is folded in here.

trap: Not yoyaku o tsukuru: you 'take' a booking (yoyaku toreta? = did you get one?). Plain yoyaku suru also works.
freqNote: 取る #228. The potential 取れる (#631) is the form heard most (toreta, torenakatta).
why: Used for restaurants, salons and doctors, and toreta / torenakatta is how people say whether they got in.

trap: Not jikan o tsukau or sugosu: putting time into something is kakeru (jikan kakete tsukutta), the transitive of kakaru.
freqNote: かける #244 is the kana form across every sense (call, sit, wear glasses); 掛ける #2742.
why: The transitive partner of jikan ga kakaru. okane o kakeru works the same way and is folded in here.

trap: Not kokoro o kaeru: changing your mind is ki ga kawaru, with ki as the subject (ki ga kawattara itte).
why: The plain, literal way to say you changed your mind about a plan (so not an idiom). Keep it apart from ki ga suru and ki ni naru.

trap: When the money is the subject the verb is tamaru (okane tamattara = once I've saved up), not transitive tameru.
freqNote: 貯まる #24870 is the money spelling. The kana たまる #1650 is mostly other senses (tamaranai).
why: The intransitive half of okane o tameru, the form heard when people talk about plans (okane tamattara ikitai).

trap: Swapped with kariru: kashite = lend me; karite ii? = can I borrow?
why: Completes the kasu / kariru / kaesu set. The verb is already H-kasu, so this mostly adds the money pairing.

trap: Not okane o harau: paying back a loan is kaesu, 'give back' (ashita kaesu ne).
why: The third verb of the lending set, where 'pay back' tempts learners toward harau. Keep it apart from kaeru (go home).

trap: Not yotei o tsukuru or oku: you 'put in' a plan (raishuu ni ireta = I put it in for next week).
why: The transitive half of yotei ga hairu, used when booking things into a calendar.

trap: Not yakusoku o kowasu: breaking a promise is yaburu, 'tear'.
why: The opposite of yakusoku o mamoru, mostly heard as a complaint (yakusoku yabutta jan).

trap: Not jikan o jiyuu ni suru: clearing time for someone is akeru (ashita akete oku ne).
freqNote: 空ける #3596. The kana あける is dominated by 開ける #480 (open a door).
why: The transitive half of jikan ga aku. Less frequent, but the natural way to promise to keep a slot free.

trap: Not shawaa o toru: you abiru (pour over yourself) a shower.
freqNote: Both parts ranked; abiru is almost only used for showers, sunlight and criticism, so this phrase is where learners meet it.
why: A daily-routine staple ('shawaa abite kuru'), and the verb is impossible to guess from English 'take'.

trap: Not ofuro o toru: you 'enter' the bath, so it's ofuro ni hairu.
freqNote: お風呂 #1921 (plain 風呂 #2586); 入る #115 counts every sense of hairu.
why: The nightly routine in Japanese homes ('ofuro haitta?'), and its particle and verb both differ from English.

trap: Not denki o mawasu or akeru: lights are tsukeru'd, and denki here means the light itself.
freqNote: つける #393 is the kana spelling across all senses (付ける #1452, 点ける #52228); 電気 also counts 'electricity'.
why: Said every evening ('denki tsukete'). It sets up tsukeru for the TV and air conditioner, and starts a four-way transitive/intransitive set.

trap: Not denki o tomeru or shimeru: lights, TVs and heaters go off with kesu (put out).
freqNote: 消す #964 also covers erase and delete.
why: The other half of tsukeru, used just as often. terebi o kesu and eakon o kesu use the same verb, so they don't need their own entries.

trap: English 'lock' gives no verb: you kakeru the key, and 'it's locked' is kagi ga kakatteru (kagi o shimeru is also heard).
freqNote: かける #244 is the kana spelling across all senses (掛ける #2742); カギ #9849 is a variant spelling of the noun.
why: Comes up every time someone leaves the house ('kagi kaketa?'). Unlocking is kagi o akeru, which can sit in this entry's notes.

trap: Not yume o motsu (that's a life ambition): dreaming in your sleep is yume o miru, 'seeing' a dream.
freqNote: 夢 #351 covers both night dreams and ambitions; 夢見る #4121 is the one-word 'dream of' verb.
why: Common morning small talk ('hen na yume mita'), and English 'have' sends learners to motsu. Could also sit under senses.

trap: Not mezamashi o oku or setto suru: alarms are kakeru'd, like locks and vacuum cleaners.
freqNote: 目覚まし #15035 is the everyday short form; アラーム #12854 competes (araamu o kakeru / setto suru). かける #244 counts every sense.
why: Needed for every 'I set it for six' exchange. The noun is rare on its own, so the phrase is the useful unit.

trap: Not only okiru: waking from sleep is me ga sameru ('eyes wake'); okiru is getting up.
freqNote: 覚める #6527; 目覚める #3028 is the one-word narrative/written form.
why: Plain, literal way to say 'I woke at 4' or 'I'm wide awake now' (me ga sameta), which okiru can't express. Not a figurative idiom.

trap: Not uchi o hanareru or nokosu: leaving home for the day is deru, and the place you leave takes o.
freqNote: うち #113 also counts 内 'among/while'; 家 read いえ is #152.
why: Every 'what time do you leave?' exchange uses it ('nanji ni uchi deru?'). The trap is the o particle and the many senses of English 'leave'. Overlaps the travel domain.

trap: Not gomi o toru or motte iku: taking out the trash is gomi o dasu (put it out).
freqNote: ゴミ #2709 (ごみ #8915); ゴミ出し #17427 is the noun form.
why: The chore everyone has to mention, and English 'take' points to toru.

trap: Not ha o burashi suru or haku: teeth are migaku'd (polished).
freqNote: 歯磨き #16183 (hamigaki suru) is the competing noun form, worth noting as a partner.
why: Core routine phrase, and English 'brush' gives no route to migaku.

trap: Not toire o tsukau: asking to use someone's toilet is 'borrowing' it (toire karite mo ii?).
why: A learner needs it at friends' homes, cafes and shops, and the natural verb can't be guessed from 'use'.

trap: Not terebi o akeru or on ni suru: screens, like lights, are tsukeru'd, and off is kesu.
freqNote: つける #393 is the kana spelling across all senses.
why: Very common at home ('terebi tsukete'). It uses the same verb as denki o tsukeru, so the selector may fold it in. Overlaps media.

trap: Not denki o tsukeru when nobody's doing it: 'the light is on' is denki ga tsuiteru.
freqNote: つく #355 is the kana spelling across senses (付く #1570, 点く #45903); 着く 'arrive' is ranked separately at #957.
why: Intransitive half of the pair, and how you say 'you left the light on' (denki tsuitteru yo). It sounds the same as tsuku 'arrive'.

trap: English 'vacuum' is a verb, but Japanese says soujiki o kakeru, not soujiki suru or soujiki o tsukau.
freqNote: かける #244 counts every sense of kakeru.
why: A routine chore with a verb no one would guess. It belongs to the kakeru family with kagi, mezamashi and airon.

trap: Same tsukeru as lights, and eakon o kakeru (run it) is equally natural; not on ni suru or mawasu.
freqNote: 暖房 #15369 and 冷房 #25132 take the same verbs (also ireru); つける #393 counts every sense.
why: Said all summer and winter ('eakon tsukete ii?'). Notes can cover the kakeru variant and danbou o ireru.

trap: Not mizu o niru: you boil 'hot water' (oyu), and the verb is wakasu; niru is for cooking food.
freqNote: 沸く #6780 is the intransitive (oyu ga waku = the water's boiled).
why: Needed for kettle, tea and instant noodles. The trap is double: both the noun and the verb differ from English. It sits on the food boundary.

trap: Not kakeru or tsurusu: laundry put out to dry is hosu, and the noun is sentakumono (the clothes), not sentaku.
why: Everyday in Japan because laundry is line-dried ('sentakumono hoshita?'). Both the noun and the verb are traps.

trap: Not denki ga kesu: the intransitive is kieru, and 'the light is off' is denki kieteru.
why: Completes the four-way tsukeru/kesu/tsuku/kieru set, and covers power cuts and lights that are off.

trap: English uses one verb; Japanese needs ibiki + kaku, the same kaku as ase o kaku (sweat).
freqNote: かく #11889 is the kana form this phrase uses (掻く #51963); 書く 'write' #233 is a different word.
why: Common family and travel-room talk, and the verb is unguessable. It shares kaku with the body domain's ase o kaku.

trap: No English verb leads here: bed hair 'sticks on' (neguse ga tsuku), as in neguse tsuiteru yo.
freqNote: つく #355 is the kana spelling across senses (付く #1570).
why: A frequent, friendly morning remark, and both the noun and the verb are unguessable.

trap: Not sentakuki o hashiraseru or ugokasu: you 'spin' (mawasu) the washer.
freqNote: 回す #1242 counts every sense of mawasu.
why: Everyday household talk ('sentakuki mawashite oite'), and the verb is a pure trap. Plain sentaku suru is the guessable alternative.

trap: Not doa ga akeru: when it opens by itself or is open, use aku (doa aiteru yo); akeru needs someone to do it.
freqNote: 開く read あく #14086 looks low because the tokenizer files much of 開く under ひらく #624; 空く #1498 is the 'free/vacant' aku.
why: The intransitive half of aku/akeru ('the door's open', train doors, shops opening). doa ga shimaru follows the same pattern.

trap: The pairing itself is guessable; the risk is transitivity, mado o akeru (you do it) vs mado ga aiteru (it's open).
why: The transitive half of the aku/akeru pair. It's frequent ('mado akete ii?') but low-trap, so it's mainly here to keep the pair complete.

trap: English 'water' is a verb; Japanese 'gives' water, (hana ni) mizu o yaru, or politely ageru.
freqNote: やる #45 counts every sense (do, give); 水やり #28613 is the noun form.
why: A household chore with a giving-verb no learner would guess. It reuses yaru/ageru from the versatility list in a new sense.

trap: English 'iron' is a verb; Japanese says airon o kakeru, not airon suru.
freqNote: かける #244 counts every sense of kakeru.
why: A strong trap and part of the kakeru family, but ironing comes up less often than the other chores, so it's a reserve.

trap: Not kami o kawaku or fuku: drying it yourself is the transitive kawakasu, while kami ga kawaku means it dries.
freqNote: かみ #1752 is 髪; 紙 #2672 and 神 #1988 are homophones (the existing lists hold kami = paper).
why: A routine after the bath ('kami kawakashite kara neru'). The trap is mainly the kawaku/kawakasu split, so it's a reserve.

trap: English 'taste' is a verb; Japanese says the flavour 'does': ichigo no aji ga suru, not ichigo o ajiwau.
freqNote: Ranks are for the parts only; suru's #15 covers every use of suru. How often the phrase itself comes up is my judgement.
why: The everyday way to describe any flavour (hen na aji suru, nanimo aji shinai); same shape as oto ga suru / nioi ga suru in senses.

trap: Not samuku naru or tsumetaku naru: hot food or drink cooling off is sameru; samui is for weather and people.
freqNote: 冷める #2747 also counts feelings cooling. The verb goes with any hot food or drink (koohii, ocha, ryouri), so gohan is only the headword noun.
why: Heard at nearly every meal (samenai uchi ni douzo, koohii sameta, samechau yo). The transitive samasu (let it cool) is the rarer partner and goes in the notes.

trap: Not ocha o tsukuru: tea and coffee are 'put in' (ireru), not made.
freqNote: #222 is 入れる and counts every sense of ireru (put in, include, switch on). The tea-only spelling 淹れる sits at #19863 because of how it is written, not because the phrase is rare.
why: A daily offer and request (ocha ireru ne, koohii irete). koohii o ireru works the same way. The versatility list's ireru gloss mentions 'make (tea)', and this entry makes the pairing a unit.

trap: Not osake o motenai: low tolerance is 'weak at alcohol' (osake ga/ni yowai).
freqNote: 弱い #970 counts every sense of weak. osake ni yowai is an equally correct variant. How often the phrase itself comes up is my judgement.
why: The standard, face-saving way to turn down drinks (osake yowai n desu). Pair it with osake ga tsuyoi.

trap: Not aji ga yowai or aji ga nai: food short on salt is usui (thin), the same word as weak coffee.
freqNote: 薄い #2547 also counts thin (paper, walls) and pale (colour).
why: The everyday verdict on home and restaurant food (chotto usui ne). Learn it as a pair with aji ga koi.

trap: Not tsuyoi koohii: coffee, tea and flavour are koi (dense) or usui (thin); tsuyoi is for alcohol.
freqNote: The rank is for the kanji 濃い (#3669). The kana こい also matches 来い and 恋, so its rank can't be trusted.
why: The classic 'strong is not tsuyoi' trap. usui koohii is the opposite, and the same koi/usui pair covers koi ocha and koi aji.

trap: Not gohan o ryouri suru or niru: rice has its own verb, taku.
freqNote: 炊く #7563 is used almost only for rice, so its rank roughly tracks this phrase. gohan #1225 also counts the 'meal' sense.
why: A verb nobody could guess, used daily at home (gohan taiteoku, suihanki de taku). Its intransitive half is gohan ga takeru.

trap: English 'smoke' is one verb; Japanese 'inhales' tobacco (tabako o suu). kemuri (smoke) is no help.
freqNote: タバコ #4158 is the most frequent spelling (たばこ #7069, 煙草 #28060). 吸う #1684 also counts breathing in.
why: Asked and answered often (tabako suimasu ka?, sutte mo ii?). The older form tabako o nomu turns up in older speakers' talk.

trap: There is no 'get' to translate: it is the verb you, and the drink takes ni (not o).
freqNote: 酔う #1768 also counts motion sickness (kuruma ni you). The louder synonym 酔っ払う is #3569. In speech the noun is usually dropped (yotta, yotteru).
why: Core nights-out talk (chotto yotta, yotteru desho). The same verb with ni gives kuruma ni you (carsick), and yopparau is the casual partner.

trap: Not suupu o taberu: soup and miso soup are drunk (nomu), even with a spoon.
freqNote: For miso soup: 味噌汁 #9117, みそ汁 #8272. 飲む #229 counts all drinking.
why: English 'eat soup' pushes learners to taberu, and misoshiru o nomu is said at home every day. Thick, chunky soups and stews can take taberu.

trap: English splits grill, roast, bake, toast and fry; Japanese uses yaku for all dry-heat cooking (pan o yaku = make toast).
freqNote: 焼く #1576 also counts burning things.
why: Yakiniku and barbecue talk (niku yaite, yakisugi). The one verb also covers pan o yaku and tamago o yaku. Its intransitive pair is niku ga yakeru.

trap: Not osake o takusan moteru: a heavy drinker is 'strong at alcohol'; with the drink as topic (kono osake wa tsuyoi) it means the drink is strong.
freqNote: 強い #310 counts every sense of strong. How often the phrase itself comes up is my judgement.
why: Said all the time at drinking parties (osake tsuyoi ne!). It also shows that a drink's strength IS tsuyoi, unlike koi koohii.

trap: Not aji ga tsuyoi: heavy salt or sauce flavour is koi.
freqNote: The rank is for the kanji 濃い. The kana こい collides with 来い and 恋.
why: The other half of aji ga usui, and the adjective+noun form koi aji is also common. It largely shares its lesson with koi koohii, so the selector may want only one of the two.

trap: Not shouyu o oku or ireru: sauce poured over food is kakeru (also mayo, dressing, sauce).
freqNote: Ranks are for the kana spellings (しょうゆ #6392, ahead of 醤油 #8743; かける #244). The かける rank counts every sense (call, sit, spend, put on); 掛ける alone is #2742.
why: Table talk (shouyu kakeru?, kakesugi). It uses the same 'cover/hang' kakeru as megane o kakeru, which helps that verb make sense.

trap: Intransitive half: 'the kettle's boiled' is oyu ga waita, not oyu ga wakashita.
freqNote: The kana わく also matches 湧く (#3148, well up), so the rank used is for 沸く (#6780).
why: Completes the pair: oyu waita yo is what you say when the kettle clicks off. ofuro ga waita (home domain) works the same way.

trap: There is no word for 'seconds' or 'refill' to translate; it is the noun okawari, used with suru or on its own (okawari kudasai).
freqNote: お代わり #3640 and the kana おかわり #4023 are counted separately, so the noun is more frequent than either rank shows.
why: A staple at restaurants and at home (okawari jiyuu, okawari suru?). Borderline under the noun+suru rule: the hard part is the noun, and suru is guessable.

trap: Checking the seasoning is aji o miru ('look at the taste') or ajimi suru; ajiwau means savour.
freqNote: The compound most people use, 味見 (ajimi suru), is #5952. How often the phrase itself comes up is my judgement.
why: Kitchen talk (chotto aji mite). Worth more for listening than speaking, because tabete miru is an acceptable fallback.

trap: The rice cooker finishing is gohan ga taketa; gohan ga dekita means the whole meal is ready.
freqNote: 炊ける #16178 is rare as a word, and the phrase is heard almost only at home.
why: The intransitive half of gohan o taku, included so the pair is complete. A reserve.

trap: Meat being cooked through is yakeru ('it got grilled'), not niku ga dekita.
freqNote: 焼ける #3296 also counts burning down and sunburn (hi ni yakeru).
why: The intransitive half of niku o yaku, heard at every yakiniku (mou yaketeru yo). A reserve, included so the pair is complete.

trap: Not ame ga ochiru, and English 'it rains' has no Japanese verb of its own: rain and snow fall with furu.
freqNote: The whole phrase 雨が降る is also listed as a set expression at #5450. Kana あめ also covers 飴 (candy), and ふる covers 振る (wave/dump), so the kanji ranks are used.
why: The core weather sentence (ame futteru, ame furisou). English pushes learners toward both ochiru and a made-up verb 'to rain'.

trap: Not ame ga tomaru or owaru, and not yameru (a person quitting): rain stops with intransitive yamu.
freqNote: Rank is for the kanji 止む. Kana やむ (#3517) is how the word is usually written, but that count mixes in 病む and yamu o enai, so it isn't used.
why: The everyday follow-up to talking about rain (ame yanda?, yamu made matou). Its look-alike yameru (quit) is already in the learner's list, so the two have to be told apart.

trap: Not kirei na tenki or yasashii tenki for 'a beautiful/nice day': good weather is just ii, and bad weather is warui.
freqNote: いい is #24 (the spelling 良い is #1474). The attributive form ii tenki is used just as often.
why: The default small-talk opener (ii tenki da ne). The trap is low, but the learner says it all the time, and tenki ga warui covers bad weather.

trap: English 'windy' is one adjective. Japanese says the wind is strong: kaze ga tsuyoi, not kaze ga ooi.
freqNote: 風 (kaze, wind) is #1532. The homophone 風邪 (kaze, a cold) is a separate entry at #2666. 強風 (strong wind) is #22617 but belongs to news register.
why: A one-word English adjective becomes a Japanese noun phrase. 'Kyou kaze tsuyoi ne' is one of the most common weather remarks.

trap: Not omoi ame: heavy rain is strong rain, ame ga tsuyoi / tsuyoi ame (or ame ga hidoi). Omoi is only for weight.
freqNote: The attributive tsuyoi ame is the same pairing. The single nouns 大雨 (#11181) and 土砂降り/どしゃ降り (#30415–32931) are alternatives, not collocations.
why: English speakers almost always fall into the 'heavy' → omoi trap. 'Ame tsuyoku natte kita' is a staple. Pairs with kaze ga tsuyoi.

trap: Not kasa o tsukau, hiraku or motsu: holding an umbrella over yourself is sasu. Kasa o hiraku only means opening it, and kasa o motsu means carrying it.
freqNote: Rank is for 差す. Kana さす (#3059) mixes 刺す, 指す and the causative -sasu, so it isn't used. Usually written 傘をさす.
why: The verb for a daily action can't be guessed, and it is the umbrella's own verb (kasa sashinasai, kasa sasanakute ii?).

trap: English 'get caught in the rain' points to tsukamaru. Japanese uses the suffering passive of furu with ni: ame ni furareta.
freqNote: The passive 降られる is not a dictionary form, so it isn't in the list. The rank is for the base 降る.
why: The very common way to say you got rained on (kinou ame ni furarechatta). It can't be guessed, and it uses the passive pattern the learner already has.

trap: Not yuki ga ochiru: snow falls with furu, the same verb as rain.
freqNote: Kana ゆき also covers place names and 行き, so the kanji rank is used.
why: Same verb as ame ga furu. Learning the two together ties furu to things falling from the sky. The selector could fold it into the ame entry.

trap: No English verb matches: the day 'closes', hi ga kureru (casually kuraku naru). This kureru is unrelated to kureru 'give me'.
freqNote: The phrase 日が暮れる is listed as a set expression at #7770, which ranks higher than the bare verb 暮れる (#14744). 日 #209 mixes the 'day' and 'sun' senses. Kana くれる (#565) is mostly 'give'.
why: Common in 'hi ga kureru mae ni kaerou'. Nothing in English points to it, and it has to be kept apart from kureru 'give'.

trap: 'Get wet' is the single verb nureru, with no 'get' or naru added. The rain takes ni (ame de nureta is also heard).
freqNote: The kana spelling ぬれる (#5139) is unambiguous and outranks 濡れる (#6660), so it is used. びしょ濡れ (soaked) is about #26971–34709.
why: Needed to say you got soaked (nurechatta, bishonure). Japanese uses one verb where English uses get + adjective.

trap: Not taiyou ga tsuyoi or taiyou ga atsui: strong sun is hizashi (sunlight) ga tsuyoi.
freqNote: 日差し is #16499. The spellings 日ざし (#26917) and 陽射し (#82664) are counted separately, so the real frequency of the noun is higher than the rank shows.
why: A common summer remark. The trap is the noun (sunlight, not sun). Groups with kaze ga tsuyoi and ame ga tsuyoi as the 'tsuyoi' weather set.

trap: English 'it thunders' is one verb. Japanese makes the thunder sound: kaminari ga naru (鳴る 'ring', a homophone of naru 'become').
freqNote: The phrase 雷が鳴る is listed at #42945. Rank is for the kanji 鳴る, because kana なる (#29) is almost all 'become'.
why: The standard way to say it's thundering (kaminari natteru). It separates naru 'sound' from naru 'become'. Same verb as denwa ga naru (media).

trap: Easy to guess once fuku is known. The risk is the homophones: kaze means wind or a cold, and fuku means blow or wipe. Keep it apart from kaze o hiku (catch a cold).
freqNote: Kana ふく is dominated by 服 and 拭く, so the kanji 吹く is used.
why: The pairing is literal, but it anchors the kaze ga fuku / kaze o hiku contrast with the body domain that the plan calls for.

kana: てんきよほうがはずれる
trap: A forecast doesn't machigaeru (that is a person's mistake) or chigau. It misses, hazureru, or hits, ataru.
freqNote: Rank is for the compound 天気予報. 予報 alone is #13931. Its partner 当たる (hit/be right) is #719.
why: A classic weather complaint (yohou hazureta jan), and the verb can't be guessed. Its partner yohou ga ataru belongs in the same entry.

trap: Not ichinichi ga nagai, which means 'it was a long day': daylight hours are hi ga nagai / hi ga mijikai.
freqNote: 日 #209 mixes the 'day' and 'sun' senses. Its partner 短い is #1621. The phrase itself isn't listed.
why: Seasonal small talk (hi ga nagaku natta ne, hi ga mijikaku natta). The catch is which 'day' noun to use.

trap: English 'the weather turns/breaks' points to kawaru or kowareru. Worsening weather 'crumbles': kuzureru.
freqNote: Both parts rank mid-range. Its frequency as a phrase is a judgement call: it sounds forecast-like but is commonly repeated in speech.
why: How people pass on the forecast (gogo kara kuzureru rashii yo). The verb can't be guessed at all, but tenki ga waruku naru also works.

trap: English 'come out/open' points to deru or hiraku. Flowers bloom with saku, and petals fall with chiru, not ochiru.
freqNote: 花 #1169. Kana はな is mixed with 鼻 (nose). 桜 is #3953, and its partner 散る is #5348. 花見 is #10548.
why: Spring talk is dominated by 'sakura saita / mou chitchatta', and saku and chiru are the two verbs it needs. Hana here is the flower, not hana 'nose' (#37 in the noun list).

trap: English 'an earthquake hit/struck' has no matching verb. Say jishin ga okiru (casually jishin ga atta / kita). The shaking itself is yureru.
freqNote: Rank is for the kanji 地震, because kana じしん is dominated by 自信 and 自身. 揺れる (shake) is #3717.
why: Earthquakes are routine conversation in Japan, and okiru 'happen' is already in the versatility list.

trap: English 'the snow is sticking/settling' has no match: snow piles up, tsumoru, not tsuku or nokoru.
freqNote: Ranks are for the parts only. How common the phrase is depends on region (frequent in snowy areas), which is a judgement call.
why: An unguessable verb for snow that stays on the ground. Mostly winter and snow-region talk (sugoi tsumotteru).

trap: English has no verb for it: the rainy season is 'entered', tsuyu ni hairu, and when it ends it 'opens', tsuyu ga akeru.
freqNote: 梅雨 is #22408. The compounds 梅雨入り (#55384) and 梅雨明け (#72305) are listed separately, and 明ける is #6605. Low numbers in drama data, but the phrase is a fixture of June–July small talk.
why: A seasonal fixture in Japan with no English equivalent. Its partner tsuyu ga akeru belongs in the same entry.

trap: English 'there's a rainbow' points to niji ga aru. A rainbow comes out: niji ga deru (or niji ga kakaru).
freqNote: Rank is for the kanji 虹, because kana にじ is dominated by 2時 (two o'clock).
why: A rare topic, but it shows deru for anything appearing in the sky (hi ga deru, tsuki ga deru), so it can stand for that whole pattern.

freqNote: Its partner 下がる (fall) is #1064. Kion sounds like a forecast word; in conversation people mostly say atsuku naru / samuku naru.
why: Guessable (up = agaru) and forecast-flavoured. A weak reserve; kion ga sagaru belongs in the same entry.

trap: Not samui kaze by default: wind you feel on your skin is tsumetai (cold to the touch). Samui describes the air or how you feel.
freqNote: 冷たい #1084 and 寒い #1214 rank close together. The split between them is a judgement call (samui kaze is also heard).
why: Shows the tsumetai vs samui split on wind. The split itself mostly belongs to senses/food (tsumetai mizu), so this is a reserve.

trap: Not kaze o toru or tsukamu: you 'pull' a cold, kaze o hiku (kaze hiichatta).
freqNote: 風邪 #2666 (kana かぜ #1532 is mostly 風 'wind'); 引く #1039. Phrase entries also exist: 風邪ひく #3998, 風邪をひく #10899, 風邪を引く #27734. These are partial counts because the tokenizer usually splits; the particle-dropped form ranking highest supports the casual drop.
why: The textbook unguessable pairing and the everyday excuse: kaze hiita.

trap: Not kusuri o toru: medicine is 'drunk', kusuri o nomu, even pills.
freqNote: 薬 #1283; 飲む #229. No phrase entry.
why: English 'take' leads straight to toru; nomu covers pills, syrup and powder alike.

trap: No 'hungry' adjective: the stomach empties, onaka suita, past tense for the feeling now.
freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758). Verb rank is kana すく #2947, the usual spelling here; it can also be 好く, which is rare in speech. Kanji 空く read すく is #47898. Phrase entries: お腹が空く #22626, お腹がすく #27605.
why: Daily need with no English-shaped route; onaka suita is the only natural 'I'm hungry'.

trap: Not netsu o motteru: a fever 'exists', netsu ga aru (netsu aru mitai).
freqNote: 熱 #1641; ある #21. No phrase entry.
why: The basic sick-day report built on aru, paired with netsu ga deru for the onset.

trap: Not a 'have' sentence: the head hurts, atama ga itai; zutsuu is the written word.
freqNote: 頭 #375; 痛い #336; phrase entry 頭が痛い #8807. That count is partial and includes the figurative 'it's a headache' sense.
why: Body part + ga itai is the pattern for every pain, and head is the most said.

trap: No 'thirsty' adjective: the throat dries, nodo kawaita, past tense for the feeling now.
freqNote: 喉 #3552; 渇く #6159 (its homophone 乾く 'dry' is #6556); phrase entry 喉が渇く #14507.
why: Daily need that mirrors onaka ga suku; teach the two together.

trap: Dictionaries give i for 'stomach', but an everyday tummy ache is onaka ga itai, not i ga itai.
freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758); 痛い #336. No phrase entry.
why: Second most-said pain; reuses the onaka of onaka ga suku.

trap: Not kanjiru: 'I feel sick' has no feel verb; the condition is bad, guai ga warui.
freqNote: 具合 #1423; 悪い #139; phrase entry 具合が悪い #5837, high for a phrase.
why: The general 'I'm not well', and the caring question guai warui no?

trap: Not watashi wa ippai: the stomach is what's full, onaka ippai.
freqNote: おなか #1253; いっぱい #512 counts every sense ('a lot', 'full', 'a cupful'); 一杯 #2892. Ippai is a noun or adverb, not a verb or adjective; it goes in the partner slot. No phrase entry; 満腹 is #18617.
why: The way to turn down more food (mou onaka ippai); it completes the hunger pair with onaka ga suku.

trap: 'Sweat' is a verb in English; Japanese 'scratches out' sweat: ase o kaku, not ase suru.
freqNote: 汗 #2650. Verb rank is kana かく #11889, the spelling used here, which mixes 掻く with kana-written 書く/描く. Kanji 掻く is #51963. Phrase entry 汗をかく #13368.
why: Daily summer and gym talk (ase kaichatta), and the verb can't be guessed.

trap: Not itaku naru or kizutsuku: an injury is 'done', kega o suru, even by accident (kega shita?).
freqNote: けが #3721 (怪我 #7111); する #15. No phrase entry.
why: An unguessable suru pairing that covers any injury; also kega shinai you ni.

trap: 'See a doctor' is byouin ni iku (go to the clinic), not isha ni au; byouin covers any clinic.
freqNote: 病院 #651; 行く #40. No phrase entry.
why: Everyday advice and plans (byouin itta hou ga ii yo); English 'see' and 'hospital' both mislead.

trap: Not netsu o morau or eru: a fever 'comes out', netsu ga deru (netsu deta).
freqNote: 熱 #1641; 出る #81. No phrase entry.
why: The onset partner of netsu ga aru, and the model for seki, hanamizu and chi ga deru.

trap: No 'sore' adjective: the throat hurts, nodo ga itai.
freqNote: 喉 #3552; 痛い #336. No phrase entry.
why: Top cold symptom, and it shares nodo with nodo ga kawaku, so the two sit side by side.

trap: Means physically sick or queasy, not 'grumpy' (that is kigen ga warui); kimochi warui is the casual twin.
freqNote: 気分 #804; 悪い #139; phrase entry 気分が悪い #10247. Compare 気持ち悪い #1740 (one word, also 'gross') and 機嫌 #3757.
why: What you say when you might throw up or faint, and it's easy to misuse as 'in a bad mood'.

trap: English uses the adjective 'stiff'; Japanese uses the verb koru: kata ga kotteru.
freqNote: 肩 #1811; 凝る #6722 (kana こる #4566); phrase entry 肩が凝る #35013; the noun 肩こり is #33119 and 肩凝り #32224.
why: A national complaint in Japan, said constantly, and koru can't be guessed.

trap: Catching it from a person is kaze ga utsuru, not kaze o hiku (utsuru kara chikazukanaide).
freqNote: 風邪 #2666; 移る #2350 (kana うつる #34832; 映る and 写る are separate words). No phrase entry.
why: What the sick person warns and others fear; the intransitive half of the utsuru/utsusu pair.

trap: Not kaze o ageru: you 'transfer' a cold, kaze o utsusu (kaze utsushichatta, gomen).
freqNote: 風邪 #2666; 移す #3371 (kana うつす #12396). No phrase entry.
why: The transitive half of the pair, used in apologies and in 'dareka ni utsusareta'.

trap: 'Cough' is a verb in English; in Japanese the cough comes out, seki ga deru (seki ga tomaranai).
freqNote: 咳 #21022 is the kanji only. Kana せき #11682 probably holds most spoken uses but can't be told apart from kana 席/関, so it is not used. 出る #81; phrase entry 咳が出る #70272.
why: Core cold symptom on the ga deru frame; seki o suru is a near-synonym.

trap: Not hana ga hashiru: 'nose water comes out', hanamizu ga deru.
freqNote: 鼻水 #12653; 出る #81. No phrase entry.
why: Cold and hay-fever symptom on the same ga deru frame as seki and netsu.

trap: Not koeru: the cold itself 'heals', kaze ga naoru (kaze naotta?); you cure it with kaze o naosu.
freqNote: 風邪 #2666; 治る #1604 (transitive 治す #2761; 直る 'be fixed' #4537 is a homophone). No phrase entry.
why: How people ask and answer after an illness; naosu ('hayaku naoshite ne') is the transitive partner.

trap: Not netsu ga oriru or heru: a fever 'drops', netsu ga sagaru (netsu sagatta?).
freqNote: 熱 #1641; 下がる #1064 (上がる #503, for a rising fever). No phrase entry.
why: The recovery check that follows netsu ga deru; agaru/sagaru is the fever's up-down pair.

trap: Not furuku naru (that's for things): people 'take years', toshi o toru (toshi totta naa).
freqNote: 年 read とし #1354 (the reading ねん is #155); 取る #228. Phrase entries 年を取る #5402 and 年取る #8003 rank high for phrases.
why: Common in self-deprecating chat, and furui for people is a classic learner error.

trap: Not kusuri ga hataraku: medicine 'takes effect', kusuri ga kiku, a homophone of kiku 'listen'.
freqNote: 薬 #1283; 効く #1822; phrase entry 薬が効く #19852.
why: Asked after every pill (kusuri kiita?); this kiku has to be kept apart from kiku 'listen'.

trap: Not samui alone: chills 'do', samuke ga suru; samui means the room is cold.
freqNote: 寒気 read さむけ #15754; する #15. No phrase entry.
why: Early fever sign on the sensation + ga suru frame, which English never predicts.

trap: No 'dizzy' adjective: dizziness 'does', memai ga suru.
freqNote: Kana めまい #8617 (kanji 目眩 #67709 is rare); する #15. No phrase entry.
why: Same ga suru frame as samuke and hakike; a set of three learned together.

trap: Not hakike ga aru: nausea 'does', hakike ga suru; in casual talk people say kimochi warui.
freqNote: 吐き気 #12206; する #15; phrase entry 吐き気がする #15877.
why: Completes the ga suru symptom set and is what you'd tell a doctor.

trap: Not netsu o toru: you 'measure' a fever, netsu o hakaru (netsu hakatta?).
freqNote: 熱 #1641; 測る #5009 (計る #10638 is also used for this); phrase entry 熱を測る #89256.
why: Routine at home and at clinics, and English 'take' misleads again.

trap: 'Bleed' is one verb in English; Japanese says blood comes out, chi ga deru (chi deteru yo).
freqNote: 血 #1261; 出る #81. No phrase entry.
why: The only everyday way to say 'bleed'; it joins the ga deru symptom set.

trap: Not warui kaze: a bad cold is hidoi kaze; warui means wrong or at fault.
freqNote: 風邪 #2666; ひどい #444 (酷い #15387). No phrase entry.
why: Adjective + noun trap on the most common illness word (hidoi kaze hiichatta).

trap: No 'stuffy' adjective: the nose clogs, hana ga tsumaru (hana tsumatteru).
freqNote: 鼻 #2627; 詰まる #2789; phrase entry 鼻が詰まる #98306.
why: Cold and hay-fever symptom that sits next to hanamizu ga deru.

trap: Guessable; only the tense trips people: tired eyes now is me ga tsukareta / tsukareteru.
freqNote: 目 #216; 疲れる #714. No phrase entry.
why: Screen-age complaint, near-literal and low trap; a reserve.

trap: Shots are 'hit', chuusha o utsu; as the patient say chuusha utte moratta or utareta.
freqNote: 注射 #6757 (homophone 駐車 'parking' #18495); 打つ #1103; phrase entry 注射を打つ #36338.
why: Clinic and vaccine talk; the patient side needs morau, so it's a reserve.

trap: The ankle isn't named: you sprain the ashi, ashi o kujiku (ashi kujiita), or nenza shita.
freqNote: 足 #707; kana くじく #13346 (挫く #93027). No phrase entry.
why: A common minor injury with an unguessable verb, but narrow; a reserve.

freqNote: 熱 #1641; 高い #421. No phrase entry.
why: Fully guessable from English, and speech more often uses netsu ga takai; keep only as a weak reserve.

trap: Not yobu or iu: phoning someone is denwa o kakeru (or simply denwa suru); yobu is summon, iu is call something a name.
freqNote: verbRank is kana かける, which pools every sense (call, sit, spend, put on); 掛ける alone is #2742.
why: The core phone verb; English 'call' leads to yobu, and casual speech alternates it with denwa suru (ato de kakeru ne / denwa suru ne).

trap: Not kotaeru: picking up the phone is denwa ni deru ('come out to the phone'); kotaeru answers a question.
why: Needed for 'he's not picking up' (denwa ni denai) and 'can you get the phone?' (denwa dete); English 'answer' always points to kotaeru.

trap: Not shinu: the plain way to say a dead phone is juuden kireta ('the charge ran out'); sumaho shinda is only a joke.
freqNote: juuden ranks low overall, but nearly all its uses are this phrase and juuden suru; batterii is #9633.
why: The everyday excuse for a missed call (juuden kirechatta); charging is the plain verb juuden suru, and juuden ga nai covers 'low battery'.

trap: Not asobu: playing music from a speaker is ongaku o kakeru; asobu is play as in have fun, hiku is play an instrument.
freqNote: verbRank is kana かける pooling all senses; 掛ける alone is #2742.
why: 'Can I put some music on?' (ongaku kakete ii?) comes up daily; nagasu is the alternative in shops and at events, and kiku is the listener's side.

freqNote: verbRank is the 撮る spelling (photo/film sense); 取る 'take' is #228.
why: One of the most-said requests (shashin totte moraemasu ka?); guessable from English, but it anchors toreru, douga o toru and shashin o ageru.

trap: Not kakeru (hang): denwa o kakeru makes the call; ending it is kiru ('cut').
why: Every call ends with ja, kiru ne, plus 'she hung up on me' (kirareta); it sounds like kiru 'wear' from the clothes list.

trap: Not eru, and usually not morau: 'I got a message' is meeru kita ('a message came').
why: The message is the subject in every channel: rain kita, denwa ga kita, henji ga konai (no reply yet), renraku ga kuru.

trap: Not hataraku or ugoku: 'the Wi-Fi isn't working' is netto ga tsunagaranai ('doesn't connect').
freqNote: verbRank is kana つながる (繋がる #6342) and also counts people or things being linked.
why: A daily complaint (netto tsunagaranai); the same verb covers a call going through (denwa ga tsunagaranai). This is the intransitive half of the tsunagu pair.

trap: English 'connect' covers both: you tsunagu a device (waifai ni tsunaide), but the net tsunagaru on its own.
freqNote: verbRank is kana つなぐ (繋ぐ #10471) and also counts holding hands (te o tsunagu).
why: The transitive half of the pair, for hooking up a laptop or joining Wi-Fi (waifai ni tsunagu); setsuzoku suru is the formal word.

trap: Not tsukau or asobu: idly being on your phone is sumaho o ijiru ('fiddle with'); tsukau means using it for a task.
freqNote: nounRank is スマホ; keitai (#1458) is the older word and still common. verbRank is kana いじる; 弄る barely appears.
why: Describes what everyone is doing (zutto sumaho ijitteru). Its mild 'idle fiddling' tone lets it double as a complaint.

trap: There is no 'turn up' verb: volume up is oto o ookiku suru ('make the sound big') and down is chiisaku suru; oto o ageru / sageru also work.
freqNote: verbRank is the adjective ookii; suru is not counted. boryuumu is #9893.
why: A household request (oto chotto chiisaku shite) built from known words, since ookii already means 'loud' in the versatility list.

trap: Not deru: 'it came out nice' is kirei ni toreta / yoku toreteru (it got taken well).
freqNote: verbRank is the 撮れる spelling; kana とれる (#3422) mixes in 'come off'.
why: Said over every phone screen after a photo (ii shashin toreta!); the intransitive partner of shashin o toru.

trap: Sounds like naru 'become', but this is 鳴る 'ring': keitai natteru yo = 'your phone's ringing'.
freqNote: verbRank is 鳴る only; kana なる (#29) is almost all 'become'.
why: A short household alert (keitai natteru yo!); the same verb works for alarms and doorbells, which the home list can reuse.

trap: Not terebi ni aru: 'the film is on TV tonight' is konban terebi de yaru ('TV is doing it'); ni deru is for people.
freqNote: verbRank is やる across all senses.
why: For asking or saying what's on (ima terebi de nani yatteru?); it contrasts with terebi ni deru, where a person appears.

trap: Not shingou: phone signal is denpa ('radio waves'); shingou is a traffic light.
why: Explains dropped calls and slow loading (koko denpa warui ne); denpa ga nai or kengai covers no signal at all.

trap: Not just insutooru suru: everyday 'get the app' is apuri o ireru ('put in'); deleting it is kesu.
why: Common when setting up or recommending (kono apuri irete); it reuses ireru from the versatility list, where it already means put in and turn on.

trap: Not okuru: okuru sends to a person; putting a photo up online is ageru ('raise') or appu suru, as in insuta ni ageta.
freqNote: verbRank is 上げる; kana あげる (#668) is mostly 'give'.
why: Social-media talk (sore insuta ni agete ii?); it sounds the same as ageru 'give', so context does the work.

trap: Not terebi ni iru: a person on TV terebi ni deru ('comes out on'); a programme is terebi de yaru.
why: Celebrity and news talk (kinou terebi ni deteta); it uses the same deru as denwa ni deru.

trap: Not kowareru: a cracked screen wareru ('splits'); kowareru means the phone stopped working.
freqNote: kowareru is #1363, for comparison.
why: The common phone mishap (sumaho no gamen wareta); wareru also covers glass and plates, so it carries over to the home list.

freqNote: verbRank 送る also counts seeing someone off and sending parcels.
why: Guessable but constant (ato de meeru okuru ne); casual speech often shortens it to meeru suru or rain suru.

freqNote: verbRank is 聞く (also hear/ask); 聴く is #1930.
why: Fully guessable and very common (ongaku kiki nagara); it earns a place only as the listener's side of ongaku o kakeru.

trap: For a phone or online video the everyday word is douga; bideo suggests a camcorder or tape. The verb is the same toru as for photos.
freqNote: ビデオ is #5141.
why: Phone-camera talk (douga totte!); douga o miru is the watching side (clips, YouTube).

trap: waifai aru? is fine, but natives often ask waifai tonderu? ('is Wi-Fi flying?'), which is opaque if you only know tobu as 'fly'.
freqNote: nounRank is the ＷｉＦｉ spelling (katakana ワイファイ is #78072). Subtitles mostly write it in Latin letters, so the noun is undercounted.
why: Heard in cafes and homes (koko waifai tonderu?). Mainly for listening, since waifai aru? is an acceptable thing to say.

trap: Not shigoto o toru or shigoto ni ikanai: missing work is yasumu ('rest') with o, the same for school (gakkou o yasumu).
freqNote: 仕事 #134, 休む #584. Same frame with gakkou (#661) and kaisha (#474): kyou gakkou yasunda.
why: The everyday way to say you're off sick or skipping work or school. English speakers know yasumu only as 'rest' and wouldn't put it with o.

trap: Not shiken o toru: you 'receive' an exam, ukeru (also tesuto o ukeru, mensetsu o ukeru, and daigaku o ukeru for sitting a university's entrance exam).
freqNote: 試験 #3067, 受ける #356. Everyday school tests are more often tesuto (#2539), with the same verb. 面接 mensetsu (#3050, interview) takes ukeru too.
why: The core exam verb (think JLPT). English 'take' leads straight to toru, which is wrong here; contrast jugyou o toru (take a class), where toru works.

trap: Not shiken o pasu suru: passing is a verb English gives no hint of, ukaru, and the exam takes ni, not o (also daigaku ni ukatta).
freqNote: 受かる #3494 is the spoken verb. 合格 goukaku (#2357) is the formal noun (goukaku suru).
why: Pairs with ochiru as the two outcomes. The verb is unguessable and the particle is counter-intuitive. Learners need it for their own test results.

trap: Not shiken ni shippai suru: failing an exam is 'falling', ochiru with ni (ukatta / ochita).
freqNote: 落ちる #490 counts every 'fall' sense; the exam sense rests on native judgement. Also used for interviews and schools: mensetsu ni ochita.
why: Other half of ukaru. English 'fail' points to shippai, which natives don't use for exams.

trap: Not shigoto o deru or a 'get off' verb: you say the work itself ends, shigoto ga owaru (shigoto owatta? nanji ni owaru?).
freqNote: 仕事 #134, 終わる #190. Same frame: gakkou ga owaru, jugyou ga owaru.
why: A daily question in making plans. English 'get off / finish work' suggests a person-as-subject verb; Japanese makes the work the subject.

trap: 'Something came up at work' is shigoto ga haitchatta (work 'entered' the schedule), not okiru or kuru.
freqNote: 入る #115. The same frame for plans in general (yotei ga hairu) belongs to time-money.
why: The standard reason for cancelling or turning down plans (gomen, kyuu ni shigoto haitchatta). English gives no hint that hairu works here.

trap: 'Work for X' is not X no tame ni hataraku: say X ni tsutometeru (or X de hataraiteru), with ni and almost always in the -te iru form.
freqNote: 会社 #474, 勤める #2170. Homophones 務める (#2501, serve as) and 努める (#8888, strive) are counted separately. 働く hataraku #361 is the general partner (kaisha de hataraku).
why: The self-introduction line about one's job. Neither the verb nor the particle can be guessed from English.

trap: Attending a class is deru with ni. jugyou o deru would mean walking out of it, and shusseki suru is the formal word.
freqNote: 授業 #2326, 出る #81. The deru count covers all its senses; the attend sense rests on judgement.
why: Students say it constantly (kyou jugyou deru?). It shares one ni-deru frame with kaigi ni deru, and the o/ni switch flips the meaning.

trap: Not kaigi o deru (= leave the meeting room) or kaigi ni sanka suru in casual speech: attending is ni deru.
freqNote: 会議 #1612, 出る #81. The other everyday frame is ima kaigi chuu (in a meeting now).
why: The office twin of jugyou ni deru. English 'attend' has no obvious Japanese partner, and deru is the one natives use.

trap: Landing a job is usually intransitive, shigoto ga mitsukatta (a job turned up). English 'I found' pushes toward shigoto o mitsuketa, which sounds less natural.
freqNote: 見つかる #445. shigoto o sagasu (look for a job) is the guessable lead-in.
why: Common news to share or ask about (atarashii shigoto mitsukatta?). It teaches the ga-intransitive habit on a high-need noun.

trap: English 'take' works here. The trap is the contrast: a day off sick is shigoto o yasumu, while a planned break is yasumi o toru.
freqNote: 休み #1322, 取る #228 (撮る, take a photo, is counted separately at #649). At work, 有給 yuukyuu o toru (take paid leave, #13555) uses the same frame.
why: Needed for talking about holidays. It is kept with shigoto o yasumu so the two 'time off' frames don't blur.

trap: Handing in is dasu ('put out'), not ageru or teishutsu suru in speech. When a teacher says it, dasu means 'set homework'.
freqNote: 宿題 #3935, 出す #163. The same verb is used for reports and forms: repooto o dasu, shorui o dasu.
why: Both school senses of dasu (submit / assign) on one noun. The versatility list glosses dasu as 'hand in', so this is the item that carries that sense.

trap: Scores are 'taken', not received: hyakuten totta, ii ten toreta (not ten o morau).
freqNote: 点 #1137 also covers 'point, dot'. It is usually fused with a number (hyakuten, gojutten). 点数 tensuu (#6480) is the noun for 'score'. The same verb scores points in sport.
why: How everyone reports test results. 'Get' tempts morau, and toru is the fixed partner.

trap: Not menkyo o morau: you 'take' a licence by earning it (menkyo totta). The same goes for qualifications: shikaku o toru.
freqNote: 免許 #5824 is mid-frequency, but the pairing is near-fixed. 資格 shikaku (#1671, qualification) takes the same verb and is folded in here.
why: A common life milestone. It covers the whole 'earn a credential = toru' frame (driving licence, certificates).

trap: 'I go to a Japanese school' as a routine is kayotteru, not itteru: iku is one trip, kayou is regular attendance.
freqNote: 学校 #661, 通う #1026. The same frame is used for gyms, classes and hospitals (jimu ni kayotteru).
why: A learner will describe their own language school or classes. English 'go to' hides the iku/kayou split.

trap: Not shukudai o morau: homework 'comes out', shukudai ga deta (we got homework). It is the intransitive half of shukudai o dasu.
freqNote: 宿題 #3935, 出る #81. The deru count covers all its senses; this sense rests on judgement.
why: Completes the dasu/deru pair on the same noun, so the transitive/intransitive split is learned together.

trap: A topic that's on the test 'comes out' in it, kore tesuto ni deru?, not shiken ni aru.
freqNote: Students mostly say tesuto ni deru (テスト #2539). 出る #81 counts all senses.
why: A classic student question. It sits apart from shiken o ukeru and from jugyou ni deru (attend), which share the noun or the verb.

trap: Mostly guessable from yameru = quit. The catch is that you quit the company or the job (kaisha/shigoto o yameru), and 辞める sounds identical to 止める 'stop'.
freqNote: 辞める #604 (resign) is counted apart from kana やめる #117, which mixes both senses.
why: Common life talk. It is low-trap but high-need, and it is built directly on the versatility yameru.

kana: きゅうりょうがはいる
trap: 'I got paid' is the pay 'coming in', kyuuryou haitta (or kyuuryou ga deta), not a passive of harau.
freqNote: 給料 #1927, 入る #115. kyuuryou o morau is also fine and guessable. It borders time-money (money in general).
why: Payday talk (kyuuryou haittara...). It has the same ga-hairu shape as shigoto ga hairu, and English 'get paid' points the wrong way.

trap: English 'notice' has no 'mind' word, so learners say miru or wakaru; and it is ki GA TSUKU, not ki o tsukeru (be careful).
freqNote: Verb rank is 付く; kana つく (#355) mixes several tsuku verbs. The list also holds the whole expression 気が付く #2832 / 気がつく #3139; one-word kizuku 気付く is #1083.
why: Everyday 'I didn't notice' (zenzen ki ga tsukanakatta) and the near-homophone of ki o tsukeru, so the pair must be learned apart.

trap: Not nioi o kagu or nioi da: 'it smells good' is ii nioi ga suru, with suru.
freqNote: nounRank is the kana spelling におい; 匂い #2171, 臭い (bad smell) #7168. Expression 匂いがする #7128.
why: Daily reaction (ii nioi suru!, nanka kusai nioi shinai?) built on the unguessable X ga suru frame shared by oto, koe and aji.

english: hear a sound, there's a noise
trap: Not oto o kiku: you don't 'hear a noise', the noise 'does' it: nanka oto ga shita.
freqNote: Expression 音がする #5813.
why: The normal way to report a sound (nanka hen na oto shinai?); English pushes learners to kiku with the speaker as subject.

trap: Learners say suki for 'I love it!' about something new; natives say ki ni itta, and iru here conjugates godan (itta), not like iru 'be' (ita).
freqNote: 入る read iru (#63142) survives almost only inside this phrase; the whole expression 気に入る is #889.
why: Top-frequency way to say you like a gift, place or purchase (kore ki ni itta); contrasts with ki ni naru and suki.

trap: Not tanoshii or ii kanji for a bath, breeze or massage: physical pleasantness is kimochi ii.
freqNote: Usually said without ga: 気持ちいい #2005 vs 気持ちがいい #13062.
why: Constant spoken reaction (aa, kimochi ii; kaze ga kimochi ii ne) that learners have no word for.

trap: 'Gross/creepy' and 'I feel queasy' are both kimochi warui; learners reach for kirai or byouki.
freqNote: Usually said as one word 気持ち悪い #1740; slang clip kimoi キモい #4580.
why: Very frequent reaction word and the other half of kimochi ii; covers both disgust and nausea.

trap: 'Interested' is not an adjective: X ni kyoumi ga aru. Learners say omoshiroi desu, which means 'it's interesting/funny'.
freqNote: The ga-aru expression has no entry (tokenized apart); 興味ない is #1906 and kyoumi o motsu 興味を持つ #4531.
why: Needed constantly when talking about hobbies and plans (kyoumi aru? / kyoumi nai); English leads to the wrong word class.

trap: 'Can you hear me?' is kikoeru?, not kiku: kiku is deliberate listening, and the thing heard takes ga.
freqNote: No expression entry for 音が聞こえる; noun and verb ranked separately. The same frame takes koe (koe ga kikoenai).
why: Phone and video-call staple (kikoeru? kikoenai); the kiku/kikoeru split is invisible to English speakers.

trap: Not kanjiru for 'it feels like...': the everyday form is ~ kanji ga suru (or ~ tte kanji).
freqNote: Expression 感じがする #3120.
why: Common hedge for impressions (natsukashii kanji ga suru); sits between ki ga suru and tte kanji in the versatility list.

trap: 'I know how you feel' is sono kimochi wakaru, not shitteru: shiru is for knowing facts.
freqNote: No expression entry (tokenized apart); judged from parts.
why: Core empathy line in conversation (wakaru, sono kimochi); English 'know' leads to shiru.

trap: 'I had a scary experience' is kowai omoi o shita, not kowai keiken o motta: the feeling is the object of suru.
freqNote: Expression 思いをする #2427. Noun rank 思い is shared with 'thought'. Always said with an adjective in front (kowai, tsurai, samishii, ii).
why: Native way to recount how something felt (samishii omoi sasete gomen); unguessable suru pairing.

trap: 'I heard someone's voice' is koe ga shita (suru) when it just reaches you, not koe o kiita.
freqNote: Expression 声がする #10808.
why: Completes the X ga suru perception set with oto and nioi (tonari kara koe ga suru).

trap: 'I have a bad feeling about this' is iya na yokan ga suru, not warui kimochi ga aru, which sounds like nausea.
freqNote: No expression entry; noun 予感 #2760, 嫌 #304. Almost always with iya na in front.
why: Fixed chunk heard in drama and daily talk; English 'have a feeling' leads away from yokan and suru.

trap: 'Distracted/distracting' has no adjective in Japanese: ki ga chiru (urusakute ki ga chiru); learners only manage shuuchuu dekinai.
freqNote: Expression 気が散る #11908.
why: The plain way to say you can't focus (borderline rule: IN); useful at home, work and study.

trap: 'Smell this!' is kaide mite: actively smelling is kagu, not nioi o suru or kiku.
freqNote: No expression entry; nounRank is the kana spelling におい (匂い #2171).
why: Active partner to nioi ga suru, so the two smell verbs are learned together. Reserve.

trap: Not meiwaku o suru or tsukuru: you 'hang' trouble on people with kakeru (meiwaku kakete gomen).
freqNote: kakeru: kana かける #244 pools every sense (call, put on, spend); 掛ける #2742 listed separately.
why: The core apology frame; the same kakeru also carries shinpai o kakeru and koe o kakeru, so the set is cheap to learn.

trap: Not uso o hanasu or uso o suru: lies take tsuku (uso tsuite nai yo).
freqNote: uso #1544 (kana うそ #2305 counted separately). tsuku: kana つく #355 pools all kana tsuku senses; 吐く read as つく is only #173635, so no clean rank for this sense.
why: Everyday accusation and denial; the verb cannot be guessed, and the learner already knows uso! as an interjection.

trap: Not tomodachi o tsukuru as the default: friends 'come into being' with ga dekiru (tomodachi dekita).
freqNote: dekiru: kana できる #73 (出来る #1313 separate).
why: A core life-update phrase; the same frame gives kareshi / kanojo ga dekiru.

trap: There is no English equivalent: thanks for someone's help is osewa ni narimashita (you 'became' the one cared for), not sewa o shite kurete arigatou.
freqNote: お世話 #3633 (bare 世話 #2302); naru: kana なる #29.
why: The set thanks to hosts, teachers and colleagues (osewa ni natte imasu). Mostly said in the polite form, and casual osewa ni natta also exists.

trap: English 'go up and talk to' leads to hanasu; approaching someone is koe o kakeru (koe o dasu just means make a sound).
freqNote: kakeru: kana かける #244 pools all senses.
why: Starting contact and 'give me a shout' (nanka attara koe kakete); also used for being approached or hit on. Same kakeru as meiwaku o kakeru.

trap: Not adobaisu o ageru: to listen to someone's problem you 'ride on' it, soudan ni noru (to ask for advice is soudan suru).
freqNote: 乗る #439 (載る #2368 is a different verb).
why: Asking for or offering support between friends (soudan notte kurenai?). It is the plain way to say this, not a metaphor for character.

trap: There is no verb for this: 'we get along' is naka ga ii (the relationship is good). This naka is not naka 'inside'.
freqNote: 仲 #1305; kana なか #4046 mixes in 中 'inside'. ii: kana いい #24.
why: Describes friends, family and coworkers. Its opposite naka ga warui comes free, and it overlaps with the describing domain.

trap: Not kodomo o motte iru or kodomo ga aru: people you 'have' take ga iru (kodomo iru? kyoudai iru? kareshi iru?).
freqNote: 子供 #589 (子ども #2264 separate spelling); iru: kana いる #42 (居る #6802).
why: The get-to-know-you question. H-iru-exist teaches the sense; this item fixes the family and partner slots (kyoudai, kareshi, kanojo).

trap: Not shinpai suru, which means you are the one worrying: worrying someone else is shinpai o kakeru (shinpai kakete gomen).
freqNote: 心配 #210 counts every shinpai use (shinpai da, shinpai suru); kakeru kana #244 pools all senses.
why: A twin of meiwaku o kakeru, set against D-shinpai and shinpai shinaide.

trap: Not ki o tsukeru (be careful): tsukau means fussing over others, as in ki o tsukawanaide (don't go to any trouble).
freqNote: 気 #315; 使う #171 is the general spelling, but this sense is usually written 遣う (#6992).
why: Comes up constantly between hosts and guests. It nearly rhymes with the versatility item ki o tsukeru, so the two must be learned apart.

english: get in touch, stay in contact
trap: Not renraku o morau or tamotsu: making or keeping contact is toru (mada renraku totteru? / renraku ga torenai).
why: Takes the versatility item renraku suru further, to 'still in touch?' and 'can't reach them'. Hearing from someone is renraku ga kuru.

trap: Not naisho o mamoru: 'keep it secret' is ni suru, as in kore naisho ni shite ne (himitsu ni suru is the more neutral twin).
freqNote: 内緒 #2414; kana ないしょ #4442 counted separately; suru #15.
why: A high-use request between friends, and it teaches the X ni suru 'make it X' frame.

trap: Not kareshi o eru or morau: a partner 'comes into being' with ga dekiru (kanojo dekita!).
freqNote: 彼氏 #1230; kanojo (彼女) #273 is inflated by its 'she' sense.
why: Classic catch-up news. It uses the same frame as tomodachi ga dekiru, so kanojo swaps straight into the slot.

trap: Not joudan o tsukuru or suru: a joke is 'said', and joudan da yo means just kidding.
why: A banter staple. joudan desho? and joudan da yo are the most frequent chunks, and both sit next to uso! as replies.

trap: Not onegai o kiku, which means agreeing to a favour: asking one opens with onegai ga aru n da kedo.
freqNote: お願い #258 mostly counts onegai (shimasu) as 'please'; aru #21.
why: The standard opener before a request. It sets the asking side (ga aru) against granting (o kiku); tanomi ga aru is the casual twin.

trap: Not shitsumon o kiku: 'ask a question' is shitsumon (o) suru, and kiku alone means 'ask' without the noun.
why: Comes up in class, at work and everywhere else. It sits near the transparent kango + suru line, but English 'ask' pulls learners toward kiku.

trap: English 'answer' leads to kotae, which is an answer to a question; replying to a person, message or call is henji (o) suru.
why: Covers message replies (henji shite, henji ga konai). The useful lesson is the henji/kotae split; it overlaps with the media domain.

trap: English 'disturb/bother' has no matching verb: it is jama (o) suru, and entering someone's home is the set phrase ojama shimasu.
freqNote: 邪魔 #566 includes jama da (in the way) and ojama shimasu uses.
why: Gives jama shinaide, jama? (am I in the way?) and the unguessable ojama shimasu. Close to noun + suru, but it earns a place through the greeting.

trap: There is no verb for 'thank': you 'say thanks' with orei o iu (orei also means a thank-you gift).
freqNote: お礼 #968; bare 礼 #3119, so the o- form is the spoken headword.
why: For reporting thanks (orei iwanakya) rather than saying arigatou. rei o iu is the stiffer variant.

trap: Not hanasu hitsuyou ga aru: 'I need to talk to you' is chotto hanashi ga aru n da kedo.
freqNote: 話 #96 counts every hanashi use; aru #21.
why: A serious-conversation opener. English 'need to' pushes learners into a grammar construction instead.

trap: Mostly guessable, but 'talk about X' is usually X no hanashi (o suru), shorter than X ni tsuite hanasu.
freqNote: 話 #96 counts every hanashi use; suru #15.
why: Very frequent framing (nan no hanashi? = what are you talking about). Low trap risk, so it is a reserve.

trap: Not ai kontakuto o suru: eyes 'meet' with au 合う (fit), not au 会う (meet a person).
freqNote: 目 #216; 合う #563 (会う 'meet' #110 is a different verb).
why: A literal, storytelling staple (me ga atta). It overlaps with the body and senses domains.

trap: English 'take care of' gives no clue: you 'see to the bother' with mendou o miru. Keep it apart from mendokusai (what a hassle).
freqNote: 面倒 #1114 is mostly the 'hassle' sense; 見る #55.
why: Used for looking after kids, juniors and parents. It competes with sewa o suru, so keep only one if space is short.

trap: There is no verb for 'complain': you 'say complaints', as in monku iwanaide (guchi o iu = grumble, vent).
why: Used daily about people and service. guchi o iu is the venting twin.

trap: Not tatakau, which means battle: a fight or argument between people is kenka suru (kare to kenka shita, with to).
freqNote: kana けんか #5489 and 喧嘩 #6973 are counted separately, so the true noun frequency is higher than either; suru #15.
why: Common in relationship stories. It is a noun + suru, but English 'fight' points to the wrong verb. Pairs with nakanaori.

trap: Not ki o tsukeru: caring for a pet, child or plant is sewa o suru (inu no sewa).
why: The giving side of osewa ni naru; keep the two together or drop both.
