trap: There is no phrasal verb for 'make up': it is nakanaori suru ('mending the relationship'), never tsukuru.
freqNote: 仲直り #3219; suru #15.
why: The second half of kenka o suru, and it shares naka with naka ga ii. This is the weakest reserve.

trap: Not sakkaa o asobu: asobu means playing around, so sports take suru (casually yaru: sakkaa yatteru).
freqNote: suru #15; yaru #45 is the casual partner for sports. tenisu #9450 and yakyuu #3911 take the same verb.
why: Stands for every sport + suru/yaru (tenisu, yakyuu, gorufu). Learners reach for asobu here before anywhere else.

trap: Not geemu o asobu: asobu takes no game object, so a game is done with suru or yaru (geemu yatteta).
freqNote: yaru #45 is the common casual alternative (geemu yaru).
why: Gaming is a top small-talk topic. The same suru slot covers toranpu o suru and janken o suru.

trap: Not piano o suru or asobu: keyboard and string instruments take hiku (piano hiiteru).
freqNote: 弾く (ひく) #5832. The kana ひく #2982 and 引く #1039 are the homophone hiku (pull; kaze o hiku), counted separately.
why: The model for every keyboard or string instrument (gitaa, baiorin). It sounds the same as hiku in kaze o hiku, so it needs a fixed anchor.

trap: Not shiai o katsu: English 'win the game' is transitive, but Japanese wins at it with ni (geemu ni katta).
freqNote: 勝負 (contest) #1203 takes the same ni katsu.
why: Comes up constantly in sport and game talk. The ni carries over to aite ni katsu (beat someone).

trap: Not shiai o nakusu: losing a contest is makeru (losing an object is nakusu), and it takes ni, never o (shiai ni maketa).
why: Pairs with shiai ni katsu. English 'lose' splits in two here, and the same form gives aite ni makeru (lose to someone).

trap: Not gitaa o suru: guitar takes hiku like the piano (gitaa hikeru? = can you play guitar?).
freqNote: バイオリン #12637 takes the same verb.
why: Second anchor for hiku. It shows the verb covers strings as well as keyboards.

trap: Not piano o benkyou suru or ressun o toru: lessons with a teacher are narau (kodomo no koro piano naratteta).
freqNote: 習い事 (lessons taken as a hobby) #15541.
why: Childhood lessons are a standard getting-to-know-you topic. narau is the lessons verb for piano, eigo, karate and ryouri alike, and it is not in the versatility list.

trap: 'Be into / hooked on' has no verb to translate, so learners fall back on suki desu. The native way is X ni hamatteru, with ni.
freqNote: はまる #3789 and ハマる #4047 are one word in two spellings. The subtitles count them separately, so real use is higher than either rank.
why: The everyday way to say what you are into lately (saikin X ni hamatteru), with any hobby noun. It is informal but fine with desu/masu. It is the plain way to say this, not a body-part or character idiom.

trap: Not e o hiku (that is sen o hiku, draw a line) or e o nuru (paint a wall): drawn or painted, a picture takes kaku.
freqNote: 描く is listed under the reading えがく (#1092) and the tokenizer does not split off its かく reading. 書く (かく, write) #233 is the homophone.
why: Covers both drawing and painting. It sounds like kaku (write), so it is best heard as one unit with e.

trap: Not shiai o suru for 'play in the game': taking part is deru (nichiyou shiai deru), and so is taikai ni deru (enter a tournament).
freqNote: 大会 (tournament) #2691 takes the same verb.
why: 'Are you playing Sunday?' is shiai deru no? It is the same deru as terebi ni deru (be on TV), so the 'appear in' sense is worth fixing.

trap: Not taiko o hiku or suru: drums are hit, tataku, and a drum kit works the same way (doramu o tataku).
freqNote: ドラム (drum kit) #14894 takes the same verb. The kana spelling たたく #1900 is counted apart from 叩く, so tataku is commoner than #5024 suggests.
why: Third verb of the instrument set (hiku / fuku / tataku). The selector may prefer doramu as the headword for band talk.

trap: Not chiimu o sanka suru: you 'enter' a team, club or circle with ni hairu (saakuru ni haitta).
freqNote: 部活 (school club) #4867, サークル #5842 and クラブ #3027 take the same verb.
why: 'Join' has no single Japanese verb. For teams, bukatsu and university circles it is ni hairu, building on H-hairu.

trap: Not tsuri o iku or tsuri suru ni iku: an activity noun takes ni iku directly (tsuri ni itta).
freqNote: Also sukii #11454, kyanpu #5473, sanpo #2304 ni iku.
why: Model for English 'go -ing' with activity nouns (sukii, kyanpu, sanpo, karaoke ni iku). It is the noun twin of the versatility pattern -ni iku.

trap: Not fue o hiku or suru: wind instruments are blown with fuku, the verb of kaze ga fuku (the wind blows).
freqNote: フルート #31008 and トランペット #33519 take the same verb. The 吹く rank #2962 includes the wind sense.
why: Completes the instrument set, and also covers toranpetto/sakkusu o fuku and kuchibue o fuku (whistle).

trap: Not shumi o motsu in speech: having a hobby is ga aru (nanka shumi aru?), like jikan ga aru.
why: The opener for hobby talk, alongside shumi wa nan desu ka. Its trap is mild, since shumi o motsu exists in writing.
Guessable (sing = utau) and usually said as utau alone (karaoke de utau). It is kept only because the domain brief named it, so the selector can rule on it.

trap: Not 'kare wa takai' or 'nagai': height is se ga takai, and takai alone sounds like 'expensive'.
freqNote: 背 (せ) #5388, plus 背 (せい) #39147 for the sei ga takai variant. The bare noun ranks low because se almost only occurs inside this phrase.
why: The most-used way to describe someone. English 'tall' has no one-word Japanese equivalent.

trap: Not se ga mijikai: short in height is hikui (low). Mijikai is only for length.
freqNote: 背 (せ) #5388; 低い #1747. Casual speech also uses chiisai for a short person.
why: The other half of se ga takai, and the textbook trap for 'short' (hikui, not mijikai).

trap: Not sumaato (that means slim and stylish): 'smart' is atama ga ii. Kashikoi exists but is less everyday.
freqNote: 頭 #375; いい #24 (良い #1474, よい #120). Its opposite, atama ga warui, is common in casual self-deprecation but rude about others.
why: The everyday word for 'smart', used constantly about kids, colleagues and friends.

trap: Not kanashii or daun: 'you seem down' is genki nai ne. Genki ja nai sounds more like 'not healthy'.
why: The stock way to notice someone seems low ('genki nai ne, doushita no?'). It treats genki as a noun, not the versatility adjective.

kana: うんどうしんけいがいい
trap: There is no adjective for 'athletic': say undou shinkei ga ii ('motor nerves are good'), not supootsu ga jouzu.
freqNote: 運動神経 #12050 as a whole compound. It occurs almost only in this phrase and in undou shinkei ga nai/warui, so the phrase is commoner than the rank suggests.
why: The everyday way to call someone sporty or coordinated. English gives no route to it.

trap: Not me ga yowai or 'warui me ga aru': poor eyesight is me ga warui (shiryoku is the formal word).
freqNote: 目 #216; 悪い #139. The opposite, me ga ii, is rarer and can also mean 'has a good eye' (taste).
why: The standard way to explain glasses or contacts, or why you can't read something.

trap: Not koe ga takai, which means high-pitched, and not just urusai: a loud voice is ookii (big).
freqNote: 声 #327; 大きい #536. Koe ga chiisai (quiet voice) is the everyday opposite.
why: A frequent remark about people, and the ookii/takai split for voices is a real confusion.

trap: Not popyuraa da: 'popular' is ninki ga aru ('has popularity'), and ninki nai for unpopular.
freqNote: 人気 #1303; ある #21. Ninkimono (#5320, 'a popular person') is a related noun, noted only.
why: The everyday 'popular' for people, shops and shows. The noun + aru shape is not guessable.

trap: False friend: sutairu ga ii means a good figure (slim, well-proportioned), not good fashion sense. Fashion is oshare.
freqNote: スタイル #3954 covers both senses of the loanword, so it is not a count of this phrase.
why: A very common compliment, and an English speaker will misread or misuse it.

trap: Not 'nagai kami ga aru' for 'she has long hair': say kanojo wa kami ga nagai.
freqNote: 髪 #1752; 長い #467. The kana かみ is shared with 神 #1988 and 紙 #2672.
why: Basic appearance description. It drills the 'person wa X ga ADJ' frame instead of English 'has'.

trap: Not kami ga hikui: hair length is mijikai. Hikui is only for height (se ga hikui).
why: Completes the hair pair and is the direct contrast to se ga hikui (two kinds of 'short').

trap: Not 'hayai rannaa': a fast runner is ashi ga hayai ('legs are fast'). Ashi ga osoi is slow.
freqNote: 足 #707; 速い #2346 (speed). 早い #396 is 'early' and shares the kana はやい #396, so the kana rank overstates this sense.
why: Common about kids, school sports and friends. It frames speed through the legs, not 'runner'.

trap: Not 'sugu byouki ni naru hito' as the default: 'gets sick a lot' is karada ga yowai. Karada ga joubu is the sturdy opposite.
freqNote: 体 (からだ) #371, separate from 体 (たい) #47884; 弱い #970. Joubu #6353 for the opposite.
why: The plain way to describe a delicate constitution in yourself, kids or parents. It is the opposite of genki.

trap: Not se ga sodatsu: 'you've grown!' is se nobita ne (or ookiku natta ne).
why: The stock remark to kids, nieces and nephews. Nobiru also feeds kami ga nobiru.

trap: Not kami ga sodatsu: hair grows = nobiru. 'Your hair's grown' is kami nobita ne.
why: The intransitive half of the nobiru/nobasu pair on the same noun. A common catch-up remark.

trap: Not kami o sodateru: growing your hair out is nobasu ('lengthen'), e.g. ima kami nobashiteru.
why: The transitive half of the pair. Learners need it to talk about their own look ('nobashiteru tochuu').

trap: Not 'shiroi hito', which reads as 'a white person': fair skin is iro ga shiroi ('colour is white'). Iro ga kuroi means tanned.
freqNote: 色 #1136; 白い #1914. The compound irojiro #17583 says the same thing as one word.
why: A common appearance remark and compliment in Japan. The shape cannot be guessed and the literal alternative misfires.

trap: Not petto ga aru or petto o motsu: you keep an animal with kau (飼う), which sounds exactly like kau, 'buy'.
freqNote: 飼う #2759 is the kanji entry. Kana かう is dominated by 買う 'buy' (#238).
why: 'Do you have any pets?' (petto katteru?) is a staple of small talk. English 'have' pushes learners to aru or motsu, and the right verb sounds like 'buy'.
gap: Checking 'have' and 'keep': the pool has kodomo ga iru but no pet item, and the 飼う/買う homophone trap appears nowhere.

trap: English 'clean your room' leads to souji suru, which means scrubbing and vacuuming. Putting things away is katazukeru.
freqNote: The 片づける spelling is #2251 and 片付ける is #2543; the higher one is recorded.
why: It's the most common household nag (heya katazukenasai) and the everyday word for tidying up. 'Clean' sends learners to the wrong verb.
gap: Checking 'clean': the pool has soujiki o kakeru (vacuum) but no item for tidying, which comes up far more often.

english: lay out the futon (make up the bed)
trap: Not futon o tsukuru or futon o oku: you spread bedding out with shiku. Putting it away is futon o tatamu (fold) or shimau.
why: A daily routine in Japanese homes, ryokan and with host families. Nothing in English points to shiku.
gap: Checking 'make (the bed)': the home domain has no bedding item, and shiku appears nowhere in the pool.

trap: English 'it's locked' has no noun in it, so learners can't guess kagi ga kakatteru. It's the intransitive partner of kagi o kakeru.
freqNote: かかる #385 is the kana entry, shared with jikan ga kakaru and okane ga kakaru. Kanji 掛かる alone is #5316.
why: 'Is it locked?' (kagi kakatteru?) is the half of the lock pair that you hear and have to answer. It also keeps kakaru, 'take time / cost', apart from the lock sense.
gap: The pool has kagi o kakeru but not its intransitive half, and the brief counts the other half of a pair as a new item.

trap: Not mezamashi ga deru or ga iku: alarms, phones and bells ring with naru (鳴る), which sounds like naru, 'become'.
freqNote: 目覚まし #15035 counts only the short form; mezamashi tokei is a separate compound. 鳴る #2069 is a different entry from なる 'become' (#29).
why: 'My alarm didn't go off' (mezamashi naranakatta) is the classic excuse for being late. It pairs with mezamashi o kakeru.
gap: The pool has mezamashi o kakeru (set the alarm) but not the event itself. Checking 'go off' and 'go out' turned up only denki ga kieru.

trap: Not mizu o kesu: kesu is for lights, the TV and fire. Water and gas are stopped with tomeru. To turn the tap on: mizu o dasu.
freqNote: 止める #545. Kana とめる is a separate entry and also covers 泊める.
why: The pool teaches denki o kesu, so learners will carry kesu over to taps. This is the needed contrast.
gap: Checking 'turn off': the pool's tsukeru/kesu pairs cover lights, the TV and the air conditioner, with nothing for taps, where kesu is wrong.

trap: Nothing in English 'run a bath' points to wakasu: Japanese heats the bath, the same verb as oyu o wakasu. When it's ready: ofuro waita yo. Ofuro o ireru is also heard.
why: A nightly household exchange in Japan (ofuro waita yo, the bath is ready). The pool can't express it at the moment.
gap: The pool has ofuro ni hairu and oyu o wakasu but no way to say the bath is being run or is ready.

english: sleep lightly, be a light sleeper
trap: Not karui nemuri: sleep is 'shallow', asai. Deep sleep is nemuri ga fukai.
why: Sleep complaints are common in conversation. English 'light' and 'heavy' push learners to karui and omoi, which are wrong here.
gap: Checking 'light / heavy / deep': the pool has no sleep-quality item, and asai appears nowhere.

trap: Not hana o fuku: fuku is for blowing air, wind or a flute. You blow your nose with kamu, which sounds like kamu, 'bite'.
freqNote: かむ #4775 is the kana entry, which mixes 擤む 'blow (nose)' with 噛む 'bite' (#6347). 擤む itself is not in the list.
why: The pool's kaze ga fuku and fue o fuku actively push learners toward hana o fuku. The cold cluster also needs this action.
gap: Checking 'blow': hanamizu ga deru and hana ga tsumaru are in the pool, but blowing your nose isn't.

trap: Not ka ni kamareru: mosquitoes and bees 'sting' with sasu, used in the passive. Kamu is for dogs and snakes.
freqNote: The rank is for the dictionary form 刺す. The passive 刺される has no entry of its own.
why: A summer staple (ka ni sasareta, kayui). English 'bite' gives the wrong verb.
gap: Checking 'get' and 'bite': the pool has no insect item at all.

trap: Not te ga yakeru or moeru: burning your skin is the noun yakedo + suru, like kega o suru.
freqNote: Kana やけど is #5364 and kanji 火傷 is #20901; the higher one is recorded.
why: The kitchen counterpart of kega o suru. The brief allows noun + suru when the pairing can't be guessed, and here 'burn' leads to yakeru or moeru.
gap: The pool has kega o suru but not the other common household injury.

english: get an upset stomach, get diarrhoea
trap: English 'have an upset stomach' gives no usable verb. Japanese 'breaks' the stomach with kowasu, transitive, with the speaker as subject: onaka kowashita.
freqNote: Kana おなか is #1253 and お腹 is #4758; the higher one is recorded.
why: One of the most common reasons for calling in sick or skipping food. It's the polite everyday stand-in for diarrhoea.
gap: Checking 'have': the pool has onaka ga itai, suku and ippai, but nothing for a stomach bug.

trap: Not senaka ga itai: 'bad back' pain sits in the koshi (lower back and hips). Senaka is the upper back.
why: Probably the most common adult aches-and-pains line. Here the noun is the trap, not the adjective.
gap: The pool has atama, onaka and nodo ga itai but not the back. English 'back' would produce senaka.

trap: Not ashi ga neru or nemuru: a numb, tingling foot is shibireru.
freqNote: Kana しびれる is #6477 and 痺れる is #37594; the higher one is recorded.
why: Sitting on the floor and in seiza makes this frequent in Japan, and the English image of 'asleep' is wrong.
gap: Checking 'fall': nothing in the pool covers a numb limb.

trap: There's no separate verb for 'tan' or 'burn': the skin is 'grilled by the sun', hi ni yakeru, the same yakeru as niku ga yakeru.
freqNote: 日 #209 counts every 'day / sun' use. The compound noun hiyake 日焼け is #11984.
why: Summer small talk (yaketa ne!). It links to the pool's niku ga yakeru and hizashi ga tsuyoi.
gap: Checking 'get': the pool has hizashi ga tsuyoi (the cause) but not the result on the skin.

trap: English 'lie down' has no Japanese verb a learner could guess: it's 'become sideways', yoko ni naru. It has nothing to do with the 'lie' of uso o tsuku.
why: Needed whenever you feel unwell (chotto yoko ni naru) and at the doctor's. Learners can't build it from what they know.
gap: Checking 'lie': the pool has only uso o tsuku, and nothing for resting or lying down.

trap: Not me o shimeru: shimeru is for doors and windows. Eyes take tsuburu (casual) or tojiru (neutral).
freqNote: Kana つぶる is #8069 and つむる is #42175. 閉じる #3880 also covers books and apps. The phrase also has a figurative 'turn a blind eye' sense, but the literal one comes first.
why: Me tsubutte ('close your eyes') is everyday: surprises, eye drops, photos. The pool's open/close items all teach shimeru.
gap: Checking 'close': the pool's only open/close items are doors and windows.

english: make sense; get what something means
trap: There's no 'make sense' verb: 'that makes no sense' is imi ga wakaranai (imi wakannai), 'the meaning can't be grasped'.
why: Imi wakannai is one of the commonest casual reactions. English 'make sense' gives the learner nothing to translate.
gap: Checking 'make': the pool has no item for 'make sense / doesn't make sense'.

trap: Not kibun ga warui, which means feeling sick: a bad mood is kigen ga warui. A good mood is kigen ga ii or gokigen.
freqNote: Same sound as kigen 期限 'deadline' (see kigen ga kireru).
why: It's what learners mean when they say kibun ga warui and get misread as feeling ill. The pool already has kibun ga warui, so the two should be taught as a pair.
gap: The pool has kibun ga warui (feel sick) but not the mood phrase it gets confused with.

trap: Not torihada o morau or ga deru: goosebumps 'stand up' with tatsu, and the noun is the subject. It covers cold, fear and being moved.
freqNote: 鳥肌 is only #19017 in drama scripts. Calling it more common in real talk (torihada tatta! after a song or a scary story) is a judgement, not data.
why: It's the literal, plain word for goosebumps (not an idiom), and a frequent reaction phrase. English 'get' gives the wrong verb.
gap: Checking 'get' in senses and feelings: no physical-reaction item beyond samuke ga suru.

trap: Not okane o tsukuru: 'make money' is kasegu, 'earn'. Okane o tsukuru sounds like printing it or raising funds.
why: Jobs, side work and part-time work (baito de kasegu) are core small-talk topics. 'Make' gives exactly the wrong verb.
gap: Checking 'make': the pool has okane o tsukau, tameru, kariru, kasu, kaesu and orosu, but no verb for earning.

trap: Not okane o kowasu or waru: breaking a note into change is kuzusu, 'crumble'. For example, ichiman en kuzushite moraemasu ka.
why: Needed at shops, ticket machines and buses that need coins. 'Break' would give kowasu.
gap: Checking 'break': the pool has yakusoku o yaburu and gamen ga wareru, but nothing for money.

trap: Not kanjou o wakeru: splitting the bill is the noun warikan + ni suru, literally 'make it warikan'. Warikan de ii? is the usual question.
freqNote: 割り勘 is low in drama scripts (#12038). Calling it common whenever friends eat out is a judgement, not data.
why: Comes up almost every time you eat out with friends. English 'split' gives the wrong verb.
gap: Checking 'pay' and 'split': the pool has no item for paying or splitting a bill.

english: have something to do, have an errand
trap: Learners say suru koto ga aru or just isogashii. The standard vague excuse is chotto youji ga atte.
why: The default polite way to turn down an invitation or leave early. Learners need it ready to say.
gap: Checking 'have': the pool has yotei ga aru and yakusoku ga aru but not youji ga aru, the stock excuse.

trap: Not takarakuji ni katsu: you don't beat a lottery. The ticket 'hits' with ataru, and the lottery is the subject. The same goes for raffles and prize draws (kuji ga ataru).
why: 'What would you do if you won the lottery?' (takarakuji atattara nani suru?) is a classic small-talk question. It's the luck-based counterpart to shiai ni katsu.
gap: Checking 'win': the pool has only shiai ni katsu, and ataru appears nowhere.

english: a shop opens (for the day), is open
trap: Not mise ga akeru or hiraku: 'is it open?' is aiteru? or nanji made aiteru?. Mise o hiraku means opening a new shop.
freqNote: 開く read as aku shows #14086, but the tokenizer probably files most 開いてる under 開く read as hiraku (#624), so the real spoken rank of aku 'open' is higher. 空く #1498 is a different word.
why: Opening hours (nanji made aiteru?) are one of the most common shopping and plan-making questions.
gap: Checking 'open': the pool covers doors and windows (doa ga aku, mado o akeru) but has no item for opening hours.

trap: Not mise ga tojiru: closing time is shimaru, as in mou shimatteru ('it's already closed'). Mise o shimeru is the owner closing up, and mise o tatamu is closing down for good.
why: The other side of mise ga aku. 'It's closed already' and 'it closes at 9' are needed constantly.
gap: Checking 'close': the pool has no shimaru item at all, not even doa ga shimaru.

trap: There's no adjective for 'picky': it's 'many likes and dislikes', sukikirai ga ooi (or ga hageshii). Not picky at all: sukikirai nai.
why: Hosts and new friends ask sukikirai aru? when sharing food. It's built entirely from words the learner already knows.
gap: Checking 'picky' and 'fussy': the food domain has no item about food preferences.

english: expire, go past the use-by date
trap: There's no verb for 'expire': the deadline 'snaps' with kireru. For food, people say shoumi kigen ga kireteru. Passports and cards just say kigen ga kireta.
freqNote: 賞味期限 'best-before' is #12993. Kigen 期限 sounds the same as kigen 機嫌 'mood'.
why: Fridge talk and expired cards or passports. It uses the same kireru as the pool's juuden ga kireru.
gap: Checking 'run out' and 'expire': the pool has juuden ga kireru but no date or food item.

trap: Learners reach for hagu or toru. Peeling the skin off fruit or vegetables is muku, as in mikan no kawa o muku.
freqNote: 剥く #30971 is the kanji entry. The kana むく entry is #6799 but is shared with 向く written in kana.
why: Everyday kitchen and fruit-sharing talk (ringo muite ageru). The verb can't be guessed.
gap: Checking 'peel' and 'cut': the pool's cooking verbs are taku, yaku and wakasu, with nothing for preparing fruit.

trap: Not tamago o wakasu: wakasu is for boiling water. Cooking food in boiling water (eggs, pasta, noodles) is yuderu.
freqNote: Kana ゆでる is #9809 and 茹でる is #25651; the higher one is recorded.
why: Completes the 'boil' set with oyu o wakasu and oyu ga waku. Otherwise English 'boil' sends eggs and pasta to wakasu.
gap: Checking 'boil': the pool's only boiling item is oyu o wakasu, which teaches the wrong verb for food.

trap: Not sumaho ga kooru: kooru is ice. A frozen screen 'hardens' with katamaru. Furiizu suru is also heard.
freqNote: 固まる #4448 also counts 'harden / set / freeze up (a person)'. The device sense is one use among several.
why: A daily tech complaint. English 'freeze' leads straight to kooru.
gap: Checking 'freeze' and 'crash': the pool's device problems are gamen ga wareru and juuden ga kireru, with nothing for a phone that hangs.

trap: Not kopii o tsukuru: copies are 'taken' with toru. Kopii suru is also used.
why: A routine office and school request. It joins the pool's toru set (shashin, menkyo, ten, yasumi o toru).
gap: Checking 'make': the work-school domain has no office-task item.

english: have a baby (a child is born)
trap: Not kodomo o motsu or kodomo ga aru: 'we had a baby' is kodomo ga umareta (or akachan ga umareta), with the child as subject.
freqNote: 赤ちゃん #2204 is the common alternative noun.
why: Core life news. English 'have' gives aru or motsu. It pairs with the pool's kodomo ga iru.
gap: Checking 'have': the pool has kodomo ga iru (have kids) but not the birth itself.

trap: Not kao o tsukuru: wearing an expression is kao o suru, as in hen na kao shiteru or sonna kao shinaide.
why: The 'X kao o suru' pattern (kanashii, kowai, hen na kao) is how people describe someone's expression, and English 'make' gives the wrong verb.
gap: The brief names iya na kao o suru as a valid noun + suru case, but the pool has no 'kao o suru' item.

trap: Not te o motsu: holding hands is 'linking' them with tsunagu, the same verb as netto ni tsunagu.
freqNote: Kana つなぐ is #1886 and 繋ぐ is #10471; the higher one is recorded.
why: Comes up with children, couples and crowds. English 'hold' gives motsu.
gap: Checking 'hold': the pool's only 'hold' items are kasa o sasu and soudan ni noru, with nothing for hands.

trap: Not hirou or toru: you pick a person up by going 'to meet' them, mukae ni iku. When they come for you: mukae ni kuru.
freqNote: 迎え #8575 is the noun on its own. Calling it common is a judgement: pick-ups are daily family and friend logistics (eki made mukae ni iku ne).
why: Learners need to say this constantly, and the pool's takushii o hirou will teach them hirou for 'pick up'.
gap: Checking 'pick up': the only pick-up item in the pool is takushii o hirou, which is wrong for people.

trap: Not raido o ageru: giving a lift uses noseru ('put on board'), the transitive of noru. To ask for one: nosete kureru?
why: Asking for or offering a ride is common. It's the transitive half of the pool's densha ni noru.
gap: The pool has densha ni noru but not its transitive partner noseru, and the brief counts the other half of a pair as a new item.

trap: Not seki o mamoru or tameru: saving a seat is 'taking' it, seki o toru. Totte oku means keeping it for later.
why: Comes up in cafés, trains and events (seki totte oku ne). 'Save' and 'keep' give the wrong verbs.
gap: Checking 'save' and 'keep': the pool has seki ga aku and seki o yuzuru but nothing for saving a seat.

trap: Not konbini ni tomaru, which means staying the night there: dropping in on the way is yoru.
why: A daily plan-making line (chotto konbini yotte iku). The pool's densha ga tomaru and hoteru ni tomaru make tomaru the likely mistake.
gap: Checking 'stop': the pool has two tomaru items and no yoru item.

english: pollen is in the air (hay-fever season)
trap: English 'the pollen count is high' has nothing to translate. Japanese pollen 'flies' with tobu: kafun tonderu ne.
freqNote: 花粉 is #16753 in drama scripts. Calling it common in real spring talk is a judgement, not data.
why: Spring small talk in Japan centres on hay fever. It's the same tobu as the pool's waifai ga tobu.
gap: The weather domain has nothing seasonal beyond tsuyu ni hairu, and no hay-fever item.

english: get a haircut, cut one's hair
trap: Not kami o kitte morau or a 'haircut' noun: Japanese says kami kitta even when a hairdresser did the cutting.
freqNote: 10-list-nouns #14 kami means 'paper' (a homophone), so it isn't cross-referenced.
why: Kami kitta? is the standard way to notice someone's new look, and English 'get a haircut' pushes learners to the -te morau form.
gap: The pool has kami o nobasu, musubu and kawakasu, and kami ga nagai and mijikai, but not the haircut itself.

english: have good taste / a good eye (style)
trap: English 'good taste' leads to aji (flavour). Taste in clothes, music or gifts is sensu ga ii; shumi ga ii is also used.
why: Sensu ii ne is a stock compliment. The pool's aji ga suru and aji o miru train learners toward aji.
gap: Checking 'taste': the pool's 'taste' items are all about flavour, with no compliment on style.

trap: Not kao ga aoi or kao ga shiroi: 'you look pale' is kaoiro ga warui (your complexion is bad).
freqNote: Phrase entry 顔色が悪い is in the drama list at #13422.
why: Said to anyone who looks ill (kaoiro warui yo, daijoubu?). Going through 'pale' gives aoi or shiroi, which sound wrong here.
gap: Noun sweep: 顔色 (#2897) is not a pool noun. The pool's guai ga warui and kibun ga warui cover feeling ill, not how someone looks.

trap: English gives no hint of kuzusu ('crumble'). Learners say byouki ni naru, which sounds like a real illness rather than being run down.
freqNote: Phrase entry 体調を崩す at #9388.
why: The standard way to say you got run down or caught something minor (taichou kuzushichatte). It comes up all the time in work and school excuses.
gap: 体調 (#1944) is not a pool noun, yet the drama list has 体調を崩す as its own entry (#9388).

trap: Not tsukare ga naoru: tiredness 'comes off' (toreru). It isn't cured.
freqNote: 取れる #631 counts all its senses (come off, can get, be taken). 疲れを取る is a phrase entry at #62068.
why: Comes up in everyday talk about sleep, baths and holidays (nete mo tsukare torenai), and the verb can't be guessed.
gap: 疲れ (#3920) is not a pool noun. The pool covers tiredness only through me ga tsukareru.

english: be off, not feel right; (a machine) act up
trap: Not just genki ja nai: choushi ga warui covers being off form, a bad stomach, or a phone or PC that's acting up.
freqNote: Phrase entries 調子が悪い #8863 and 調子がいい #16780.
why: One phrase for 'something's off' with your body, your form or a device (pasokon no choushi ga warui). Choushi ga ii is the positive. It is broader than the pool's guai ga warui.
gap: 調子 (#1124) is one of the highest-ranked nouns missing from the pool. Choushi ni noru (get carried away) is an idiom and stays out.

english: see a doctor, get checked by a doctor
trap: Not isha o miru, which means you look at the doctor. The doctor looks at you: isha ni mite morau.
freqNote: verbRank is the dictionary form 診る. 医者にかかる is a phrase entry at #47992.
why: A classic reversal: 'see a doctor' translated word for word gives the wrong sentence. The pool's byouin ni iku names the place and avoids the verb.
gap: 医者 (#1501) is not a pool noun, and byouin ni iku sidesteps this trap.

trap: Not shujutsu o suru, which is what the surgeon does. The patient 'receives' it: shujutsu o ukeru.
freqNote: Phrase entry 手術を受ける at #9903.
why: Comes up constantly in talk about family health. The same ukeru frame gives kensa o ukeru (get a checkup).
gap: 手術 (#2050) is not a pool noun, and the drama list has 手術を受ける as its own entry.

trap: Not hone ga kowareru: bones, sticks and umbrellas 'snap' (oreru). Kowareru is for machines.
freqNote: Phrase entry 骨が折れる at #17817. That count includes the figurative sense 'be hard work'.
why: The literal injury phrase (ashi no hone ga oreta). The transitive hone o oru is mostly the idiom 'take pains', which is out of scope.
gap: 骨 (#2934) and 折れる (#2860) are both in the top 3,000 with no pool item. Kega o suru covers injury only in general.

trap: There's no English verb to translate: breath 'runs out' (kireru), the same verb as juuden ga kireru.
freqNote: Phrase entry 息が切れる at #37126. 息をする (breathe) is at #11944.
why: Said after stairs, running or sport (iki kireta). Paired with the pool's juuden ga kireru, it shows that kireru means 'run out'.
gap: 息 (#2382) is not a pool noun, and nothing in the pool covers breathing.

trap: 'Healthy' sends learners to kenkou. For food and habits Japanese says karada ni ii ('good for the body'), and karada ni warui for the opposite.
freqNote: Phrase entries 体にいい #11815 and 体に悪い #13606.
why: Part of daily talk about food, sleep and smoking, and it brings karada ni warui with it.
gap: 体 appears in the pool only as karada ga yowai. The drama phrase entries 体にいい and 体に悪い have no item.

trap: Not byouki o toru or byouki ga dekiru: illness is something you 'become' (ni naru).
freqNote: Phrase entry 病気になる at #4880.
why: The general frame for getting ill. The pool has only specific illnesses and symptoms.
gap: The drama phrase entry 病気になる (#4880) is one of the most frequent collocation entries and has no pool item.

trap: Not inu o motsu or inu ga aru: pets are 'kept' (kau, which sounds like 'buy'). You can also say inu ga iru.
why: One of the first questions about someone's life (petto katteru?). The verb sounds the same as 'buy', so learners need to hear the two apart.
gap: 飼う (#2759) turned up in the sweep. The pool has sewa o suru for pets but no way to say you have one.

trap: There's no single verb for 'feed': you give the food (esa o yaru or ageru), with the same yaru as mizu o yaru.
freqNote: やる #45 is mostly the 'do' sense. This 'give' sense is a small share of it.
why: Comes up with pets and kids, and pairs with the pool's mizu o yaru. Many speakers now say esa o ageru.
gap: 餌 (#3627) is not a pool noun. The pool has mizu o yaru but not its pet counterpart.

trap: Not heya ga kitanai for clutter: messy is chirakatteru, and kitanai means dirty.
freqNote: The transitive 部屋を散らかす is a phrase entry at #118129.
why: Hosts say it whenever a guest comes in (chirakatte te gomen). It needs to be kept apart from kitanai (dirty).
gap: 部屋 (#353) is the highest-ranked home noun with no pool item.

trap: Not kabi ni naru: mould 'grows' the way hair does (haeru).
freqNote: Phrase entry カビが生える at #39241. カビ ranks low in dramas but is a fixture of rainy-season home talk.
why: Comes up with bread, bathrooms and the rainy season (pan ni kabi haeteru). Haeru also gives hige ga haeru.
gap: Found among the drama phrase entries. Neither カビ nor 生える appears in the pool.

trap: Not oto o tsukuru: 'make a noise' is oto o tateru ('raise' a sound).
freqNote: Phrase entry 音を立てる at #18077.
why: Oto tatenaide (don't make noise) comes up in shared homes, at night and with kids.
gap: 音 is in the pool only for hearing sounds (oto ga suru, oto ga kikoeru), not for making them.

trap: Not tamago o kowasu: eggs, glasses and plates 'split' (waru).
why: Basic cooking. Waru is the transitive partner of the pool's gamen ga wareru.
gap: 卵 (#2385) and 割る (#2974) are both in the top 3,000. The pool has wareru but not waru.

trap: Not just mise ga ippai or hito ga ooi: busy restaurants and trains are konderu, and the opposite is suiteru.
why: Used when deciding where to eat (ima konderu kara ato de). The pool's michi ga komu is the traffic use. This is the much more frequent use for places and trains, and it pairs with suku.
gap: 店 (#440) is the highest-ranked everyday noun missing from the pool, and komu appears only with roads.

trap: Not denwa o morau: an incoming call 'hangs' on you (denwa ga kakatte kuru). It is the intransitive of denwa o kakeru.
freqNote: Phrase entries 電話がかかる #10203 and 電話がかかってくる #32857.
why: As in sakki haha kara denwa kakatte kita. It is the other half of the pool's denwa o kakeru.
gap: The pool has denwa o kakeru but not its intransitive pair, which the drama list carries as a phrase entry.

trap: Not sumaho o kesu: devices are powered off with dengen o kiru ('cut the power'). Kesu is for lights and TVs.
freqNote: Phrase entry 電源を切る at #16226.
why: Heard in announcements at cinemas, on planes and in exams, and used when restarting a phone (ichido dengen kitte mite).
gap: 電源 (#4712) is not a pool noun. The pool's on/off items cover only lights, the TV and the air conditioner.

trap: Not tsuku: a dead phone that 'won't turn on' is dengen ga hairanai.
freqNote: Phrase entry 電源が入る at #9986.
why: Used when troubleshooting (sumaho no dengen ga hairanai). Pairs with dengen o kiru and dengen o ireru.
gap: The drama phrase entry 電源が入る (#9986) has no pool item.

trap: There's no verb for 'scratch': a scratch 'attaches' (kizu ga tsuku).
freqNote: Phrase entries 傷がつく #8777 and 傷が付く #17905. verbRank is 付く.
why: Said of phones, cars and floors (sumaho ni kizu tsuita). Pairs with the pool's gamen ga wareru.
gap: 傷 (#1248) is not a pool noun, and the drama phrase entry 傷がつく ranks #8777.

trap: Not wasuremono o oku: leaving something behind is wasuremono o suru, or just wasureta.
why: Comes up on trains, in taxis and in classrooms (wasuremono shinai you ni). A classic noun + suru that can't be guessed.
gap: 忘れ物 (#2580) is not a pool noun.

trap: Not only nakusu: losing a wallet or phone while out is usually otosu ('drop'), and the police ask where you dropped it.
why: The standard way to report a lost item (saifu otoshichatta). Otosu is also what lost-and-found staff will say back.
gap: 財布 (#2377) and 落とす (#923) both rank high, and the pool has nothing for losing things.

trap: Not kyanseru sareru for events: rained-off matches and cancelled events chuushi ni naru. Postponed is enki ni naru.
freqNote: 延期 (postponement) is #6376, and 延期になる is a phrase entry at #20128.
why: Comes up in talk about weather and plans (ame de chuushi ni natta). Enki ni naru uses the same frame.
gap: 中止 (#2024) is not a pool noun. The pool covers making and keeping plans but not their being called off.

english: have no time, money or room to spare
trap: There's no verb for 'afford': 'I can't afford it' and 'I'm swamped' are both yoyuu ga nai (no margin).
why: Covers money, time and mental bandwidth. Yoyuu (de) is also slang for 'easy'.
gap: 余裕 (#1340) is one of the highest-ranked nouns missing from the pool.

english: wait and see, keep an eye on it
trap: Not matsu: 'let's wait and see' is yousu o miru ('watch how things look').
freqNote: Phrase entry 様子を見る at #3061.
why: Used by doctors and parents and in plans (ni-san-nichi yousu mimashou).
gap: 様子 (#815) and the phrase entry 様子を見る (#3061) both rank high, and there is no pool item.

trap: Not kekka o morau: results 'come out' (kekka ga deru). Getting good results yourself is kekka o dasu.
freqNote: 結果を出す (produce results) is a phrase entry at #8074.
why: Used for exams, medical tests and job applications (kensa no kekka ga deta).
gap: 結果 (#626) is the highest-ranked noun of its kind missing from the pool.

trap: Not hazukashii ni naru: making a fool of yourself is haji o kaku, with the same kaku as ase o kaku and ibiki o kaku.
freqNote: verbRank is hiragana かく, the form used for sweat, snoring and shame. Phrase entry 恥をかく at #6752.
why: The action that goes with hazukashii (minna no mae de haji kaita).
gap: The drama phrase entry 恥をかく (#6752) has no pool item, though the pool already teaches kaku through ase and ibiki.

trap: Not namae o ageru: you 'attach' a name (namae o tsukeru).
freqNote: Phrase entries 名前を付ける #14728 and 名前をつける #20826. verbRank is 付ける.
why: Used for babies, pets and files (neko ni nan te namae tsuketa?).
gap: 名前 (#256) is the second-highest-ranked noun not in the pool.

english: be expecting a baby, get pregnant
trap: Not akachan o motsu: 'we're having a baby' is akachan ga dekita (a baby 'came into being').
why: Big life news. It contrasts with the pool's kodomo ga iru (have children) and teaches dekiru as 'come into being'.
gap: 赤ちゃん (#2204) is not a pool noun. The pool has kodomo ga iru but not the event itself.

trap: There's no verb for 'cheer up': you say genki dashite ('put out your energy').
freqNote: Phrase entries 元気が出る #8964 and 元気を出す #13529.
why: The standard thing to say to comfort someone. Genki ga deru (feel better, get a lift) is its intransitive partner, and the pool already has genki ga nai.
gap: The pool has genki ga nai but neither of the drama phrase entries 元気が出る (#8964) and 元気を出す (#13529).

trap: Not just renraku dekinai: 'I can't reach him' is renraku ga torenai (or renraku ga tsukanai).
freqNote: Phrase entries 連絡が取れる #4561 and 連絡がつく #7918. 取れる #631 counts all senses.
why: Used when worrying about someone or chasing a reply (zenzen renraku torenai). It is the intransitive partner of the pool's renraku o toru.
gap: The pool has renraku o toru, but its intransitive partners are frequent drama phrase entries (#4561, #7918) with no item.

english: visit someone in hospital, visit a sick person
trap: Not byouin o tazuneru or houmon suru: visiting a sick person is omimai ni iku.
freqNote: The bare form 見舞い is #5796.
why: Part of family and work life. English uses one verb where Japanese needs this noun phrase.
gap: お見舞い (#3293) is not a pool noun.

trap: Not chiketto o morau: securing tickets is chiketto o toru, and toreta! means 'I got them'.
why: Used for concerts, flights and trains (raibu no chiketto toreta!). Same toru as the pool's yoyaku o toru.
gap: チケット (#3553) is not a pool noun.

english: get some exercise, move your body
trap: Not only undou suru: the casual 'I need some exercise' is karada o ugokasu.
freqNote: Phrase entry 体を動かす at #13082.
why: How people actually talk about exercise (tamani wa karada ugokasanai to).
gap: The drama phrase entry 体を動かす (#13082) has no pool item, and the pool's sport items all name specific sports.

trap: Not yume ga hontou ni naru: dreams are 'granted' (kanau).
freqNote: verbRank is 叶う. Hiragana かなう (#935) also counts kanawanai ('no match for').
why: Common in talk about goals, weddings and travel. The pool's yume o miru is the sleeping sense.
gap: 夢 (#351) appears in the pool only as yume o miru.

trap: There's no adjective for 'motivated': motivation 'comes out' (yaruki ga deru, or yaruki ga denai).
why: Yaruki denai is one of the most common everyday complaints. Yaruki ga aru (be keen) is the stative version.
gap: やる気 (#1776) is not a pool noun.

trap: Not sutoresu ni naru: stress 'piles up' (tamaru).
freqNote: verbRank is hiragana たまる, the usual spelling (溜まる is #16850).
why: Comes up in talk about work and life (sutoresu tamatteru). Same tamaru as the pool's okane ga tamaru.
gap: ストレス (#2415) is not a pool noun.

trap: False friend: tenshon means excitement or energy, not stress. 'I'm excited' is tenshon agaru, and tenshon takai means hyper.
freqNote: Phrase entry テンションが上がる at #30223. The tokenizer usually splits it.
why: Constant in casual speech, especially among younger speakers, and the English word 'tension' points the opposite way.
gap: テンション (#3506) is not a pool noun.

trap: No 'addictive' adjective is used for snacks: you say kuse ni naru ('it becomes a habit').
freqNote: Phrase entries 癖になる #14210 and クセになる #22463.
why: Common when reacting to food and music (kono aji kuse ni naru). It also has the plain meaning 'become a habit'.
gap: 癖 (#3237) is not a pool noun.

trap: Not benri for people and advice: 'useful' or 'helpful' is yaku ni tatsu. Benri means convenient.
freqNote: Phrase entry 役に立つ at #1516, the highest-ranked collocation entry missing from the pool. 役に立たない is #6939.
why: Used in thanks and self-deprecation (yaku ni tatte yokatta; yaku ni tatanakute gomen).
gap: The drama list ranks 役に立つ as a phrase at #1516, above every pool collocation except the ki phrases already in the versatility list.

trap: You don't need a word for 'handwriting': say ji ga kirei or ji ga kitanai (the characters are neat or messy).
freqNote: verbRank is hiragana きれい, the usual spelling.
why: A common compliment and self-description. Ji ga heta is also used.
gap: 字 (#2167) is not a pool noun.

trap: There's no adjective for 'fit': stamina is something you have or lack (tairyoku aru, tairyoku nai).
why: Comes up in talk about ageing, sport and work. Mou tairyoku nai is the most common form.
gap: 体力 (#3077) is not a pool noun.

trap: 'Lucky' is an adjective in English, but Japanese says un ga ii (your luck is good), or rakkii. Unlucky is un ga warui.
freqNote: Phrase entries 運が悪い #10068 and 運がいい #11653.
why: An everyday reaction (un yokatta ne) that pairs naturally with un ga warui.
gap: 運 (#4015) is at the edge of the top 4,000, and its phrase entries outrank many pool items.

trap: English has no verb to translate: a hole 'opens' (ana ga aku). Making one is ana o akeru.
freqNote: Phrase entries 穴が開く #9696 and 穴があく #24499. verbRank is 空く; 開く read as aku is #14086.
why: Said of socks, clothes and walls (kutsushita ni ana aiteru).
gap: 穴 (#2765) is not a pool noun, and the drama phrase entry 穴が開く ranks #9696.

kana: でんわがかかってくる
trap: Not denwa o morau: a call comes in, so it's denwa ga kakatte kita (casually just denwa kita).
freqNote: verbRank is kana かかる, all senses together.
why: The receiving half of denwa o kakeru: 'okaasan kara denwa kakatte kita'.
gap: Kakaru sweep: the pool has denwa o kakeru, denwa ni deru and denwa ga naru, but nothing for 'I got a call'.

trap: Not isha o miru (that means looking at the doctor): to see a doctor is isha ni kakaru, or isha ni mite morau.
freqNote: verbRank is kana かかる, all senses together.
why: Common advice, 'isha ni kakatta hou ga ii yo', and English 'see' leads straight to miru.
gap: Kakaru sweep: the pool only has byouin ni iku for this.

trap: Not okane o tsukau when you mean putting money into something: fuku ni okane o kakeru. It's the transitive half of okane ga kakaru.
freqNote: verbRank is kana かける (#244), all senses; 掛ける alone is #2742.
why: For talking about where money goes: hobbies, looks, travel.
gap: Kakeru sweep: the pool has okane ga kakaru and jikan o kakeru but not okane o kakeru.

english: the call drops, get cut off
trap: Not denwa ga ochiru: a dropped call is denwa ga kireta, the intransitive half of denwa o kiru.
why: Everyday phone trouble: 'gomen, denwa kireta'.
gap: Kiru/kireru sweep: the pool has denwa o kiru and juuden ga kireru but not the dropped call.

trap: Lights and the TV take tsukeru, but powering up a phone or PC is dengen o ireru ('put the power in').
why: Device trouble talk: 'dengen ireta?' The negative dengen ga hairanai means 'it won't turn on'.
gap: Ireru sweep: the pool's ireru items are ocha, kontakuto, apuri and yotei. Nothing for powering a device on.

trap: Not denpa o morau: having signal is denpa ga hairu, and 'no signal' is denpa hairanai.
why: 'Koko denpa hairanai' is said more often than denpa ga warui and is harder to guess.
gap: Hairu sweep: the pool has denpa ga warui but not the hairu pairing natives actually use.

english: get through (on the phone), reach someone
trap: 'I can't reach him' isn't todokanai or aenai: it's denwa ga tsunagaranai.
freqNote: verbRank is kana つながる (#902); 繋がる is #6342.
why: Common when someone isn't answering: 'zenzen tsunagaranai'.
gap: The pool has tsunagaru only for the internet (netto ga tsunagaru), not for reaching a person.

trap: Not sakujo suru in speech: 'delete that photo!' is sono shashin keshite. Kesu means erase as well as switch off.
why: Constant in casual phone talk. The same verb covers deleting messages and apps.
gap: Kesu sweep: the pool uses kesu only for lights (denki o kesu).

trap: Not sumaho o kowashita, unless you broke it: 'my phone broke' is intransitive, sumaho kowareta.
why: English 'my phone broke' hides the transitive/intransitive choice. The same frame works for pasokon and terebi.
gap: Kowareru sweep: the pool has gamen ga wareru but no kowareru item.

trap: Not tsumoru (that's for snow): work, chores and laundry pile up with tamaru.
freqNote: verbRank is kana たまる.
why: A common reason to be busy: 'shigoto tamatteru'. The same frame works for sentakumono.
gap: Tamaru sweep: the pool has nothing for a backlog of work.

trap: 'Tear up' has no verb to copy: tears come out, so namida deta. Naku is crying outright.
why: Movies, onions, yawning and laughing: 'waraisugite namida deta'.
gap: Deru sweep: the pool has seki, hanamizu and chi with deru, but not tears.

english: speak up; say it out loud
trap: English 'speak up' pushes toward hanasu. Japanese 'puts out the voice': motto koe dashite.
why: Classes, karaoke and sport. Also an audio-first learner's own practice instruction ('say it out loud').
gap: Dasu sweep: the pool has koe o kakeru and koe ga ookii but not koe o dasu.

trap: Not only harau: offering to pay or chip in is watashi ga dasu yo ('I'll put the money out').
why: Splitting and treating are everyday social moves: 'kyou wa watashi ga dasu ne'.
gap: Dasu sweep: the pool has orosu, kasu, kaesu, tsukau and tameru with okane, but not paying up.

english: drive (someone), offer to take the car
trap: Not unten suru when offering a lift: 'I'll drive' is kuruma dasu yo ('take the car out').
why: How lifts get offered and arranged among friends and family.
gap: Dasu sweep: the pool has kuruma o tomeru and kuruma ni you, but not offering to drive.

trap: Okuru isn't the default here: posting a letter or card is tegami o dasu ('put it out'); the same goes for nengajou.
why: Fewer letters now, but the pairing carries over to cards, forms and parcels at the post office.
gap: Dasu sweep: the pool's dasu items are gomi and shukudai. The post-office use is missing.

trap: English 'graduate' leads to sotsugyou suru (fine but stiff). In conversation people say daigaku deta ('left university').
why: Self-introductions and background chat: 'daigaku dete kara...'
gap: Deru sweep: the pool has uchi o deru but nothing for finishing school.

trap: Not gohan ga junbi da: 'dinner's ready!' is gohan dekita yo (dekiru = come into being).
freqNote: verbRank is kana できる (#73); 出来る is #1313.
why: Called out in every household. The pool's gohan ga takeru covers only the rice cooker.
gap: Dekiru sweep: the pool has no dekiru item with food.

trap: Not nikibi o morau: spots, rashes and blisters 'form', so nikibi dekichatta.
freqNote: ニキビ (katakana) #28682; hiragana にきび #69135.
why: The model for every skin complaint (mame, kuma and aza all take dekiru).
gap: Dekiru sweep: the body set has no 'something formed on me' pairing.

trap: Not mise ga aku (that's opening for the day): a shop that has just opened is atarashii mise ga dekita.
why: Neighbourhood small talk: 'eki no mae ni atarashii kafe dekita yo'.
gap: Dekiru sweep: no item in the pool talks about places in town appearing or opening.

trap: Not youji ga kuru: 'something came up' is kyuu ni youji ga dekita. Youji ga aru means 'I have things to do'.
why: The standard polite excuse for cancelling plans.
gap: Dekiru sweep: the pool has yotei ga hairu but not this more common excuse.

english: be expecting, have a baby on the way
trap: Not kodomo o motsu: 'we're having a baby' is kodomo ga dekita. Kodomo ga iru means you already have children.
why: Life news among friends, and the clearest contrast with the pool's kodomo ga iru.
gap: Dekiru sweep: the pool has tomodachi and kareshi with dekiru, and kodomo only with iru.

trap: 'Confident' is an adjective in English, but Japanese has confidence: jishin aru / jishin nai. (Jishin is also 'earthquake', as in jishin ga okiru.)
freqNote: 自信 #839 is its own entry, separate from 地震 #7156.
why: 'Jishin nai' is constant before tests, interviews and dates.
gap: Aru sweep: the pool has kyoumi, shumi and ninki with aru, but not confidence.

trap: Dipping is tsukeru, pouring over is kakeru: sushi ni shouyu tsukeru, but toufu ni shouyu kakeru.
freqNote: Noun is kana しょうゆ (#6392); 醤油 is #8743. Verb is kana つける (#393), all senses; 付ける is #1452.
why: Teach it with the pool's shouyu o kakeru: the two are a classic table-manners mix-up.
gap: Tsukeru sweep: the pool has shouyu o kakeru but not the dipping verb it gets confused with.

ja: シートベルトを締める
kana: シートベルトをしめる
trap: Not tsukeru or kiru: belts and ties are shimeru ('tighten'). Casually, shiitoberuto shite.
freqNote: 締める #4630; kana しめる (#1764) is mostly 閉める 'close'.
why: Said every time you get in a car or taxi.
gap: Shimeru sweep: shimeru appears only in nekutai o shimeru; travel has no in-car phrase.

trap: English 'get out' pushes toward deru. Families say ofuro agatta? ('came up out of the bath').
why: The other half of ofuro ni hairu, used every evening at home.
gap: Agaru sweep: the pool's only agaru item is kion ga agaru.

trap: Not uchi ni hairu: you step up into a home, so 'come on in' is douzo agatte.
freqNote: Noun is kana うち (#113), which also counts 'within'; 家 read いえ is #152.
why: Hosting and visiting: 'agatte agatte' and 'ojama shimasu'.
gap: Agaru sweep: the pool has nothing for entering someone's home.

trap: Not hi o morau: sunlight 'hits', so a sunny room is hi ga ataru heya.
freqNote: 日 #209 also counts 'day'.
why: Housing talk, plants and laundry: 'kono heya, hi ga ataranai'.
gap: Ataru sweep: the pool has no ataru item; the weather set has hizashi ga tsuyoi but nothing about where the sun reaches.

trap: Not takarakuji ni katsu: you don't beat a lottery, it hits you. 'Takarakuji atattara...' (also ga ataru).
why: A favourite 'what if' topic, and the same verb covers prize draws and raffles.
gap: Ataru sweep: the pool has shiai ni katsu, which this contrasts with, but no ataru.

english: take, walk or drive someone home
trap: Not tsurete iku: seeing someone home is okuru ('send'), so okutte iku yo, or eki made okuru.
freqNote: Noun is kana うち, which also counts 'within'.
why: After every evening out: 'okutte iku yo' / 'okutte kurete arigatou'.
gap: Okuru sweep: the pool uses okuru only for sending email.

trap: 'Punctual' is an adjective in English, but Japanese 'protects the time': jikan mamotte ne.
why: Workplace and friend expectations. The same mamoru is used with ruuru and shimekiri.
gap: Mamoru sweep: yakusoku o mamoru is the pool's only mamoru item.

trap: English 'skip' pushes toward tobasu. Meals are 'pulled out': asagohan nuita (any meal works).
freqNote: 朝ご飯 #5780; 朝ごはん is #6629.
why: Common in health and diet chat: 'hiru nuite shimatta'.
gap: Nuku sweep: the pool has no nuku item.

trap: On the stove you 'put out the fire' (hi keshita?), not gasu o shimeru. Turning it on is hi o tsukeru.
why: Cooking and leaving the house: 'hi keshita kke?'
gap: Kesu sweep: the pool's kitchen items have no way to turn the heat off.

english: a stain or dirt comes out
trap: Not yogore ga deru: stains 'fall off', so kono shimi ochinai. Removing them is yogore o otosu.
why: Laundry and cleaning talk. It's the intransitive model behind the pool's keshou o otosu.
gap: Ochiru sweep: the pool uses ochiru only for exams (shiken ni ochiru).

trap: Not shimi o morau: a stain 'attaches', so shimi tsuichatta. Getting it out uses ochiru.
freqNote: Noun is katakana シミ (#9793); 染み is #13129. Verb is kana つく (#355), which also counts 'arrive'; 付く is #1570.
why: Spilled coffee and curry on clothes. The frame also covers nioi ga tsuku and kizu ga tsuku.
gap: Tsuku sweep: the pool has neguse ga tsuku and denki ga tsuku, but no stain.

trap: Not megusuri o ireru or nomu: eye drops take sasu, the same verb as kasa o sasu.
freqNote: 差す #7696; kana さす (#3059) mixes several sasu verbs.
why: Hay-fever season and screen strain. A doctor or pharmacist will say it to you.
gap: Sasu sweep: the pool's medicine items cover only kusuri o nomu and chuusha o utsu.

trap: Not gohan o oku: leaving food on your plate is nokosu, as in nokoshite ii? or nokosanaide.
why: Table manners and full-up talk: 'gomen, chotto nokoshichatta'.
gap: Nokosu sweep: the pool has no nokosu/nokoru item.

trap: Not kakkou o kiru: 'dressed like that' is sonna kakkou shite. Kakkou means outfit or look.
why: Comments on outfits: 'sono kakkou de iku no?', 'kawaii kakkou shiteru'.
gap: Suru sweep: every clothes item in the pool is a single garment. Nothing describes a whole outfit.

trap: Not koe o nakusu: a hoarse voice 'withers', as in karaoke de koe kareta.
freqNote: verbRank is 枯れる (#6468), which also covers withering plants; 嗄れる is only listed with the reading しゃがれる.
why: After karaoke, cheering or a cold.
gap: Body sweep: the pool has nodo ga itai but nothing for losing your voice.

trap: Not nimotsu ga tsuku: deliveries 'reach' you, so nimotsu todoita. Tsuku is for people and vehicles arriving.
why: Online orders arrive daily. Messages and letters use the same verb.
gap: Todoku sweep: the pool has nimotsu o azukeru and eki ni tsuku but nothing arriving at the door.

trap: 'Flush' has no Japanese verb of its own: you make the water flow, as in toire no mizu nagashite.
why: Household and kids' talk, plus signs in toilets.
gap: Nagasu sweep: the pool has toire o kariru but nothing for using the toilet itself.

trap: Not kiru or tsukeru: creams and lotions are spread on, so nuru (the paint verb).
why: Summer routine. Nuru also covers ointment, butter and lip balm.
gap: Nuru sweep: the clothes set has the 'put on' verbs, but none for anything spread on skin.

trap: Not atsui ga dame: 'I can't take heat (or cold)' is atsusa ni yowai / samusa ni yowai. It's the osake ga yowai idea with ni.
why: Weather small talk about yourself. The pool's osake ga yowai gives the model.
gap: Weather sweep: the pool describes the weather but never how a person copes with it.

english: be pleasant, nice (a person or place)
trap: For a pleasant manner or vibe, not yasashii: kanji ga ii, as in kanji no ii hito / kanji warui.
why: The everyday verdict on staff, new acquaintances and shops.
gap: Describing sweep: the pool has kanji ga suru (seem) but not this common verdict on people.

trap: Not atama o tataku (that's hitting on purpose): banging your head into something is butsukeru, as in tana ni atama butsuketa.
why: A common small injury. The same verb works for knees, toes and cars.
gap: Utsu sweep: the pool has kega o suru and ashi o kujiku but no bump.

trap: Not tsuyu ga owaru: the rainy season 'opens out' (akeru), the same akeru as yo ga akeru (day breaks).
freqNote: 梅雨 is seasonal, so its drama rank understates how much it comes up in June and July.
why: The second half of the tsuyu ni hairu / tsuyu ga akeru pair that frames every early-summer weather chat. The verb can't be guessed.
gap: The pool has tsuyu ni hairu (it starts) but not the end. Scene: July weather talk ('mou tsuyu aketa?').

trap: English has a verb, but in Japanese a sneeze 'comes out' (kushami ga deru); kushami o suru also works.
why: Completes the cold and hay-fever set with seki ga deru and hanamizu ga deru. English offers no noun to start from.
gap: Scene: hay fever or a cold. The pool has seki and hanamizu ga deru but not kushami. akubi ga deru (yawn) uses the same frame and can go in the notes.

english: get a cramp in one's leg
trap: Not ashi ni kuranpu ga aru: a cramping leg 'tsuru' (pulls tight). It's usually said in the past: ashi tsutta!
freqNote: 攣る is nearly always written in kana, and kana つる (#2909) is shared with 釣る and 吊る, so the kanji row (#151338) understates it.
why: Used for cramps in sport, swimming and at night. Nothing in English leads to tsuru.
gap: Scene: sport or swimming ('ashi tsutta!'). The pool has ashi o kujiku but no cramp.

trap: Not kusuri o nomu or tsukeru: creams, ointment and sunscreen are 'spread' on (nuru); nomu is only for swallowing.
why: Contrasts directly with kusuri o nomu (in the pool) on the same noun. It also covers hiyakedome o nuru (sunscreen).
gap: Scene: an insect bite, burn or sunburn. The pool has kusuri o nomu and kusuri ga kiku but nothing for creams.

trap: Not bansoukou o kiru or kakeru: anything stuck on flat (plasters, compresses, stickers, posters) is haru.
freqNote: nounRank is the kana spelling (#19099); 絆創膏 is #23672. Regional brand-names (kizuban, sabio, bando-eido) vary.
why: The small-injury follow-up to kega o suru. The same haru covers shippu (compresses).
gap: Scene: cutting a finger while cooking. The pool has kega o suru and chi ga deru but not the fix.

trap: Not tebukuro o kiru: gloves 'fit on' (hameru), like rings; tebukuro o suru is also everyday.
freqNote: verbRank is the kana spelling はめる (#2952), the usual one.
why: Gloves are the commonest hameru item in daily life, more so than rings.
gap: Scene: dressing for the cold. The pool has mafuraa o suru and yubiwa o hameru but no gloves.

trap: Not just atatakai fuku o kiru: 'wrap up warm' is one noun, atsugi ('thick wearing'), plus suru.
freqNote: atsugi is seasonal and rare in drama subtitles; commonness is judged from winter talk.
why: Parents and friends say it every winter, and the suru pairing on a native noun can't be guessed.
gap: Scene: getting dressed for cold ('kyou samui kara atsugi shite itte ne'). Not in the pool.

trap: Not kami o migaku: teeth are brushed with migaku, hair with tokasu.
freqNote: 梳かす is almost always written in kana, and kana とかす (#46719) also covers 溶かす (melt), so the kanji row is a floor, not a real count.
why: English 'brush' gives the wrong verb, and it fits between ha o migaku and kami o kawakasu.
gap: Scene: getting ready in the morning. The pool has ha o migaku and kami o kawakasu but not this one. (10-list-nouns #14 kami is paper, so it isn't linked.)

trap: English 'shave' needs no object, but Japanese names what comes off: hige o soru (face), ashi no ke o soru (legs).
freqNote: nounRank is the katakana spelling ヒゲ (#9045); ひげ is #10683 and 髭 #35748.
why: A daily grooming action that pairs with hige o hayasu (grow a beard).
gap: Scene: getting ready in the morning ('hige sotte nai'). Not in the pool.

english: turn on the tap / the water
trap: Not mizu o tsukeru: tsukeru is for lights and power, while water is 'let out' (dasu).
why: The water half of the on/off set. English 'turn on' leads to tsukeru, which is wrong here.
gap: Scene: kitchen and washing up. The pool's on/off items cover lights, the TV and the aircon, but not water.

trap: Japanese has no word for 'flush': you make the toilet 'flow' (nagasu), as in toire nagashite or mizu o nagasu.
why: Everyone needs it, and nothing in English points to nagasu.
gap: Scene: home routine, reminding a kid. The pool has only toire o kariru.

kana: せんたくものをとりこむ
trap: Not sentakumono o ireru or motte kuru: laundry is 'taken in' (torikomu). Example: ame futte kita, sentakumono torikonde!
why: The other half of sentakumono o hosu (in the pool), and a daily rush whenever rain starts.
gap: The pool has sentakumono o hosu but not bringing it in. Scene: rain starts while the washing is out.

trap: Switches are 'put in' (ireru) to turn on and 'cut' (kiru) to turn off, not tsukeru and kesu.
why: Covers heaters, kotatsu, rice cookers and PCs. dengen o ireru / kiru (power) uses the same frame.
gap: Scene: kotatsu, heater, rice cooker. The pool's on/off items use only tsukeru and kesu.

trap: Not osake o ireru: ireru is for making tea and coffee, while pouring into someone's glass is tsugu.
freqNote: 注ぐ is listed only under the reading sosogu (#4243), and kana つぐ (#10827) is mixed with 継ぐ and 次ぐ, so there's no clean rank for tsugu.
why: Pouring for others is central to drinking etiquette, and it contrasts with ocha o ireru in the pool.
gap: Scene: drinking with friends or colleagues ('tsugimasu yo'). The pool has osake ni you but no pouring.

trap: Japanese has no verb for 'sober up': being drunk 'wears off' (sameru), the same verb as me ga sameru.
freqNote: Also written 醒める (#51825); 覚める is the commoner spelling.
why: Completes the drinking set (osake ni you, osake ga tsuyoi) and links the three sameru items in the pool.
gap: Scene: drinking with friends and the walk home ('yoi sameta'). Not in the pool.

english: have time or money to spare; be relaxed about it
trap: English 'can afford' or 'have time to spare' has no single verb here; Japanese uses yoyuu ga aru / nai for time, money and calm.
why: A high-frequency noun with one fixed partner, and it covers 'afford', 'spare' and 'composure'.
gap: Scene: making plans and money talk ('ima okane no yoyuu nai'). Not in the pool.

trap: Not just yotei ga ippai: a full schedule is 'stuffed' (tsumaru), like a blocked nose. Example: raishuu wa yotei ga tsumatteru.
why: Used to decline or reschedule, and it links to hana ga tsumaru in the pool.
gap: Scene: making and breaking plans. The pool has yotei ga aru and yotei ga hairu but not 'fully booked'.

english: can make it, can fit it in
trap: Not tsugou ga dekiru: an arrangement 'attaches' (tsuku). Example: tsugou tsuitara renraku shite.
why: The other everyday tsugou pairing besides tsugou ga ii. tsugou ga tsukanai is the soft way to decline.
gap: Scene: arranging to meet. The pool has only tsugou ga ii.

trap: Not jugyou o nuku or tobasu: skipping class or work is saboru (from 'sabotage'), while skipping a meal is nuku.
freqNote: verbRank is the katakana spelling サボる (#3137), the usual one.
why: Very common in school and uni talk, and it splits English 'skip' from asagohan o nuku.
gap: Scene: school and uni small talk. The pool has jugyou ni deru but not missing class.

trap: Keep it apart from shigoto o sagasu (look for one) and shigoto ga mitsukaru (one turns up): mitsukeru is the transitive 'find'.
why: The transitive half of a pair the pool has only one side of.
gap: Transitive partner of shigoto ga mitsukaru, which is in the pool.

trap: Not tomodachi o tsukuru: 'make friends with X' is X to tomodachi ni naru, while tomodachi ga dekiru means gaining friends in general.
why: The only one of the two that takes a person, and it's very frequent.
gap: Scene: meeting new people ('tomodachi ni naroo yo'). The pool has tomodachi ga dekiru, which can't take a person.

trap: Japanese has no verb for 'dump': you get 'shaken off' (furu, passive furareru), as in kanojo ni furareta. Don't confuse it with ame ni furareru.
freqNote: The passive 振られる has its own row (#23700).
why: A staple of relationship talk. It works the same with kareshi, and it forms a confusable pair with ame ni furareru.
gap: Scene: a falling-out or break-up gossip. The pool has kareshi ga dekiru but not the end.

trap: Not uso ga mitsukaru: lies and secrets 'come out' with bareru (casual), as in uso bareta.
freqNote: nounRank is katakana ウソ (#1168); 嘘 is #1544. verbRank is katakana バレる.
why: Pairs with uso o tsuku in the pool. bareru is very frequent in speech.
gap: The pool has uso o tsuku but not the lie being found out. Scene: a falling-out ('bareta?').

english: the conversation gets lively, have a great chat
trap: No English verb fits: talk and parties 'swell up' (moriagaru), as in sugoi moriagatta ne.
why: The usual way to say a chat, party or event went well. The verb is frequent and can't be guessed.
gap: Scene: drinking with friends or meeting new people. Not in the pool.

trap: Japanese has no verb for 'look forward': you 'make it a pleasure', as in tanoshimi ni shiteru (ne).
why: The versatility list has tanoshimi da, but only the ni suru frame takes an object ('X o tanoshimi ni shiteru'), and it's the closing line of most plans.
gap: Scene: making plans ('raishuu tanoshimi ni shiteru ne'). Not in the pool, and the versatility list lacks this frame.

trap: Like kami o kiru, you say you dyed your hair even when the salon did it. kinpatsu ni someru = go blond.
why: A common appearance change to describe, and it goes with kami o kiru.
gap: Scene: describing someone ('kami someta?'). Not in the pool.

trap: Not hige o sodateru or nobasu: facial hair is 'made to sprout' (hayasu), the transitive of haeru. hige haeteru hito = a man with a beard.
freqNote: nounRank is the katakana spelling ヒゲ (#9045).
why: The standard way to describe facial hair. It pairs with kabi ga haeru and hige o soru.
gap: Scene: describing someone to a friend. The pool has kami o nobasu but nothing for beards.

english: be a good person, have a nice personality
trap: 'He's nice' is usually seikaku ga ii or yasashii; seikaku ga warui means mean or nasty.
why: The literal personality description (not a metaphor), used constantly when describing people.
gap: Scene: describing someone to a friend. The pool covers looks and ability but not personality.

trap: Not mimi ga kikoenai: the plain, polite way is 'far ears' (mimi ga tooi), the mirror of me ga warui.
why: The plain, literal description of hearing ability, a sibling of me ga warui. It's often said about grandparents.
gap: Scene: describing a grandparent. The pool has me ga warui but nothing for hearing.

trap: Not furui (things only) or ookii: 'older than me' is watashi yori toshi ga ue (toshiue), and younger is toshishita.
freqNote: ue is a noun, not an adjective. The compound 年上 toshiue is #3068.
why: Age comparison comes up when meeting anyone in Japan, and English 'older' leads to furui.
gap: Scene: meeting new people, describing a partner ('kare, mittsu ue nan da'). The pool has toshi o toru only.

english: take / drop someone to the station, see someone off
trap: Not just eki made tsurete iku: walking or driving someone somewhere is okuru (the 'send' verb), as in okutte iku yo.
why: The end of most evenings. okuru (escort) and mukae (pick-up) form a pair.
gap: Scene: the end of an evening ('eki made okuru yo'). Not in the pool.

trap: Not juutai de tomaru: you 'fall into' traffic (hamaru), the same verb as geemu ni hamaru (get hooked).
freqNote: verbRank is kana はまる (#3789), which also counts the 'get hooked' sense.
why: The standard excuse for being late, and it pairs with geemu ni hamaru in the pool.
gap: Scene: the commute and explaining lateness ('juutai ni hamatchatte'). The pool has michi ga komu (a state) but not being stuck in it.

english: get hit / run over by a car
trap: Not kuruma ni utareru: being run over is hikareru, the passive of hiku, which sounds the same as the hiku in kaze o hiku.
freqNote: 轢く is often written in kana, and kana ひく (#2982) mixes 引く and 弾く.
why: Shouted as a warning and used in near-miss stories ('hikaresou ni natta').
gap: Scene: crossing the road ('abunai! hikareru yo'). The pool has jiko ni au but nothing more specific.

trap: Not gasorin o kau or morau: fuel is 'put in' (ireru), as in gasorin irete kara iku.
why: A routine driving line, and English 'get' leads to the wrong verb.
gap: Scene: a road trip. The pool's car items stop at parking.

trap: Not just yoku kikoenai: the set phrase is 'the phone is far', as in chotto denwa ga tooi n desu ga.
why: The fixed polite phrase for a bad line. It mirrors mimi ga tooi.
gap: Scene: a phone call with bad sound. The pool has denpa ga warui (signal) but not this.

english: be in a photo, appear in a picture
trap: Not shashin ni iru or haitte iru: appearing in a photo is utsuru, as in kono shashin ni utsutteru no dare?
why: Common when looking through photos together. English 'be in' leads to iru.
gap: Scene: looking through photos. The pool has shashin o toru and shashin ga toreru but not being in one.

trap: 'Silent mode' is the made-in-Japan manaa moodo ('manner mode') with ni suru, not sairento ni oku.
freqNote: Rare in drama subtitles but heard daily in train and venue announcements; commonness is judged.
why: A Japan-made loanword with a fixed frame, needed in cinemas, on trains and in meetings.
gap: Scene: a cinema, train or meeting ('sumaho, manaa moodo ni shite'). The pool's phone set lacks it.

trap: English 'turn off' leads to kesu; a ringing alarm is stopped: tomeru.
freqNote: 目覚まし #15035 (めざまし same entry); アラーム #12854 is the loanword alternative; 止める #545 covers every 'stop' sense.
why: Part of every morning, and the step the alarm set is missing: you set it (kakeru), it goes off (naru), you stop it (tomeru).
gap: tomeru sweep: the pool has kuruma o tomeru, mizu o tomeru, mezamashi o kakeru and mezamashi ga naru, but nothing for switching the alarm off.

english: get worn out, tiredness builds up
trap: English 'worn out' gives only tsukareta; built-up tiredness is a noun that tamaru (piles up), like sutoresu ga tamaru.
freqNote: 疲れ #3920; 1650 is kana たまる, which mixes 溜まる and 貯まる (溜まる alone #16850).
why: Very common way to say you're run down (tsukare tamatteru), and the opposite of tsukare ga toreru, which is already in the pool.
gap: tamaru sweep: the pool has okane, sutoresu and shigoto ga tamaru, and tsukare ga toreru, but not tiredness building up.

english: light the stove or a fire; light a cigarette
trap: English 'light' has no obvious verb; it is tsukeru, the same verb as for lights, and hi o tsukete sounds like ki o tsukete (be careful).
freqNote: 火 #1743 (kana ひ is shared with 日 #209). 393 is kana つける, the usual spelling, which mixes all senses; 付ける #1452, 点ける #52228.
why: The opposite of hi o kesu, which is already in the pool; used for cooking and for cigarettes.
gap: tsukeru sweep: the pool has hi o kesu but not its opposite. 10-list-nouns leaves out hi and says it should come in through collocation cards.

trap: English 'yawn' is one verb; Japanese is a noun that deru (comes out), or akubi o suru.
freqNote: Kana あくび #14579 (the kanji 欠伸 is not in the list); 出る #81.
why: An everyday body reflex. It follows the same deru pattern as seki and kushami, so it fits in the same group.
gap: deru sweep for body reflexes: the pool has seki, kushami, hanamizu and namida ga deru, but no yawn.

trap: Not shakkuri ga aru: hiccups deru, and 'I can't stop hiccupping' is shakkuri ga tomaranai.
freqNote: Kana しゃっくり #28750, a low rank, so commonness is set at 2; 出る #81.
why: An everyday reflex with an unguessable verb. It is one of the weaker additions and can be cut if space is tight.
gap: Same deru sweep as akubi ga deru; the pool has no hiccups.

trap: The stomach rings: naru (鳴る), the verb for a phone or alarm, not the naru that means 'become'.
freqNote: Kana おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758); 2069 is 鳴る. Kana なる #29 is almost all 'become'.
why: Common and slightly embarrassing moment (onaka natchatta). It links the ringing naru of denwa ga naru to the body.
gap: Sweep of naru (ring): the pool has denwa, mezamashi and kaminari ga naru, and four onaka items, but not this one.

english: get a belly, have a paunch
trap: English 'get a gut' or 'put on weight' gives no clue: the belly deru (sticks out), usually onaka dete kita.
why: The everyday way to talk about middle-age weight, about yourself or someone else.
gap: deru sweep: the describing domain covers height, hair and build (sutairu ga ii) but has no belly.

trap: The candidate ukeru (receives) the interview, like shiken o ukeru; mensetsu o suru means you are the one interviewing.
why: Job hunting and part-time job interviews are common talk, and English 'have' leads the wrong way.
gap: ukeru sweep: the pool has shiken o ukeru and shujutsu o ukeru, but not the interview, the other common thing a learner 'has'.

trap: English 'take' leads to motte iku; natives say dasu (send out), the same pattern as shuuri ni dasu.
freqNote: クリーニング #7486; 出す #163.
why: A routine errand (suutsu o kuriiningu ni dasu). It teaches dasu as 'send out for a service'.
gap: dasu sweep: the pool has gomi, shukudai, tegami and okane o dasu, but not the 'send out for a service' sense.

english: send (something) for repair, get it fixed
trap: English 'get it fixed' has no verb to translate; Japanese sends it out: sumaho o shuuri ni dasu.
why: The follow-up to the pool's broken-device items: a learner needs to say they're getting the phone fixed.
gap: The pool has sumaho ga kowareru and gamen ga wareru, but no way to say you're getting it repaired.

trap: Not kasa o shimeru: an umbrella is folded, tatamu; opening it is sasu (or hiraku).
why: The opposite of kasa o sasu, which is in the pool. English 'close' leads straight to shimeru.
gap: The pool has kasa o sasu but not its opposite; tatamu appears nowhere in the pool.

kana: せんたくものをたたむ
trap: Not oru: oru is for folding paper (origami) or breaking things; clothes and laundry are tatamu.
why: A daily chore whose verb English sends to the wrong word (fold → oru).
gap: The pool covers the laundry cycle (sentakuki o mawasu, hosu, torikomu) but stops before folding.

trap: Not botan o shimeru or kakeru: buttons are tomeru (fasten); undoing them is hazusu.
freqNote: ボタン #3688 also counts push-buttons. 10553 is 留める; kana とめる #9778 and 止める #545 are the same sound, often written that way.
why: The only fastening item for clothes, with an unguessable verb. It is one of the weaker additions.
gap: The clothes domain has a wear and take-off verb for each garment but nothing for fastening; botan is already #127 in 10-list-nouns.

english: get dirt or a stain off, clean it off
trap: English 'get off' or 'remove' suggests toru; the usual verb is otosu (drop), as in keshou o otosu.
why: The transitive half you use when you are the one cleaning (kono yogore otosenai).
gap: otosu/ochiru sweep: the pool has yogore ga ochiru and keshou o otosu, but not the transitive half for dirt.

trap: Not butsukaru: a crashing app ochiru (falls); a frozen one katamaru.
why: An everyday phone problem, and English 'crash' leads straight to the wrong verb.
gap: ochiru sweep: the pool has shiken ni ochiru, yogore ga ochiru and sumaho ga katamaru (freeze), but no crash.

english: ruin one's health, make oneself ill (from overwork)
trap: English 'ruin your health' gives no verb; Japanese breaks the body: muri suru to karada kowasu yo.
why: The everyday warning and explanation (karada kowashite yameta). The pool's taichou o kuzusu is the formal version.
gap: kowasu sweep: the pool has onaka o kowasu and taichou o kuzusu, but not the common casual karada o kowasu.

trap: English 'unplug' is one verb; Japanese pulls out the konsento (plug/socket). Plugging in is konsento ni sasu.
freqNote: コンセント #20298, a low rank for a word used daily, because it is a household word rather than drama dialogue; 抜く #1432.
why: Household instruction (konsento nuite) with a loanword that is a false friend and a verb English never suggests.
gap: nuku and sasu sweep: the pool has dengen o ireru/kiru and suicchi o ireru but no plugging in or unplugging.

english: be good at one's job, be capable
trap: Not shigoto ga jouzu: being good at your job is dekiru, usually shigoto ga dekiru hito.
why: The most common praise for a coworker. English 'good at' leads to jouzu, which is wrong here.
gap: dekiru sweep: describing has atama ga ii and undou shinkei ga ii, but nothing for competence at work.

trap: Not shokuyoku o motte inai: an appetite ga aru or ga nai.
freqNote: 食欲 #3504; ない #43 also counts the negative ending.
why: Doctors and friends ask about it whenever you're ill, and a learner has to answer.
gap: aru sweep: the sickness set (netsu ga aru, guai ga warui, kibun ga warui) has no appetite line.

english: the AC is working (cooling or heating properly)
trap: Not ugoku: for an AC that is running but not cooling, Japanese says it doesn't kiku (take effect), as in kusuri ga kiku. Usually eakon kiitenai.
freqNote: エアコン #9318; 効く #1822 (homophone 聞く #67).
why: A daily complaint in summer and winter. It reuses the 'take effect' kiku from kusuri ga kiku.
gap: kiku sweep: the pool has kusuri ga kiku only; eakon o tsukeru is there but nothing for whether it is cooling.

trap: Not ofuro ga dekiru: a bath that is ready waku (heats up). The bath panel announces ofuro ga wakimashita.
why: Heard every evening (ofuro waita yo), and the intransitive half of ofuro o wakasu.
gap: The pool has ofuro o wakasu and oyu ga waku, but not the intransitive half for the bath itself.

english: get dark circles under one's eyes
trap: Dark circles are a noun, kuma, and they dekiru (form), like nikibi ga dekiru.
freqNote: 68268 is 隈. Subtitles usually write クマ (#6292) or くま (#14871), but both are mostly 'bear', so the true rank is unknown and higher than 68268. Commonness rests on judgement.
why: The standard remark about someone who looks exhausted (kuma sugoi yo).
gap: dekiru sweep for skin marks: the pool has nikibi ga dekiru only.

trap: A bruise dekiru (forms), not tsuku; usually aza dekichatta.
freqNote: Kana あざ #10267 may include the clipped slang あざっす (thanks); アザ #11029, 痣 #34510.
why: A common minor injury. It joins kega o suru, yakedo o suru and hone ga oreru.
gap: dekiru sweep: the pool has injuries (kega, yakedo, atama o butsukeru, hone ga oreru) but no bruise.

english: a cockroach shows up, there's a cockroach
trap: Not gokiburi ga iru for one that has just appeared: pests (and ghosts) deru. The usual cry is gokiburi deta!
why: A classic summer moment at home. It teaches the 'appear' sense of deru, which English 'there is' hides.
gap: deru sweep for 'appear': the pool has only niji ga deru.

trap: English 'unlock' is one verb; Japanese 'opens the key', kagi o akeru, the opposite of kagi o kakeru.
why: Needed every day (kagi akete), and the missing half of the pool's lock items.
gap: The pool has kagi o kakeru and kagi ga kakaru but nothing for unlocking.

trap: English 'wave' is one verb; Japanese shakes the hand, te o furu.
freqNote: 手 #259; 振る #1638 (homophone 降る #2179, as in ame ga furu).
