why: A plain, literal everyday action with no single-verb equivalent. It sounds the same as the furu of ame ga furu.
gap: Found while checking body part + verb pairs outside the lens verbs: the people domain has te o tsunagu but no wave.

trap: English 'get food poisoning' gives no verb; Japanese is 'hit by' the food: kaki ni atatta.
freqNote: 食べ物 #2103; 当たる #719. In real speech the specific food usually replaces tabemono (kaki ni atatta).
why: A high-trap idiom-free phrase for a common travel and eating mishap. It is one of the weaker additions by frequency.
gap: ataru sweep: the pool has hi ga ataru and takarakuji ni ataru, but not the food-poisoning sense.

english: be online, be posted on the internet
trap: Not netto ni aru: being posted or listed is noru (載る), the same sound as getting on a train. Usually netto ni notteru.
why: Common when pointing someone to information (netto ni notteta yo). The same verb covers 'it's on the menu' (menyuu ni notteru).
gap: noru sweep: the pool has only the ride sense (densha ni noru) and soudan ni noru.

trap: A smell clinging to clothes tsuku (sticks), like shimi ga tsuku: yakiniku no nioi ga fuku ni tsuita.
freqNote: Kana におい #1940 (匂い #2171, 臭い as におい #7168); 1570 is 付く (kana つく #355 mixes in 着く 'arrive').
why: Comes up after every yakiniku, smoky bar or cooking session. It sounds the same as tsuku 'arrive'.
gap: tsuku sweep: the pool has shimi ga tsuku and kizu ga tsuku, but not smells.

english: get a bonus (a bonus is paid out)
trap: The usual line is that the bonus deru (comes out): boonasu deta? Boonasu o morau is also fine.
why: A standard Japanese work topic twice a year. It pairs with the pool's kyuuryou ga hairu.
gap: deru sweep: the pool has kyuuryou ga hairu but no bonus line. It is a weaker addition.

trap: Not kinniku o tsukuru: muscle tsuku (attaches); building it on purpose is kinniku o tsukeru.
freqNote: 筋肉 #4421; 1570 is 付く (kana つく #355 is mixed).
why: The usual way to talk about the result of gym or sport, with a verb English never suggests.
gap: tsuku sweep: hobbies and sport has karada o ugokasu but nothing for the result of training.

english: be informative; learn a lot (from it)
trap: Not benkyou shita: 'that's really useful to know' is benkyou ni naru (benkyou ni narimashita), and nobody is studying.
freqNote: The whole phrase 勉強になる has its own entry in the drama list at #4175.
why: One of the most common polite reactions when someone explains something. Learners reach for wakarimashita or benkyou shimashita instead.
gap: Work scene where someone explains something: the reaction benkyou ni narimashita is in neither the pool nor the versatility list, which has only benkyou suru.

english: make yourself understood; speak the same language
trap: Not wakaru: being understood in a language is tsuujiru, usually with the language as the subject (eigo tsuujiru?, nihongo ga tsuujita).
why: This is the learner's own situation: asking whether English works and saying they got through. It also gives hanashi ga tsuujinai (we're not on the same page).
gap: Travel and meeting-people scenes: nothing in the pool lets the learner say whether a language gets through (eigo tsuujiru?).

trap: Not infuru o hiku (hiku goes with kaze only): named illnesses take ni kakaru (infuru ni kakatta, korona ni kakatta).
freqNote: Short form インフル is #38273 and full インフルエンザ is #15539. かかる #385 is the kana spelling shared by every sense (take time, cost, hang); the illness kanji 罹る is #126444.
why: After kaze o hiku, this is the next illness phrase learners need, and the verb changes. Byouki ni kakaru uses the same frame, and infuru ni natta is a casual alternative.
gap: Feeling-sick scene: the pool has kaze o hiku, byouki ni naru and isha ni kakaru (see a doctor), but no frame for catching a named illness.

trap: Not shigoto ga hima ni naru or shizuka ni naru: a busy stretch 'settles' (ochitsuku), the same verb as calming yourself down.
why: The usual polite way to put off plans: shigoto ga ochitsuitara nomi ni ikou. It connects work talk to making plans.
gap: Making and breaking plans: no pool item covers 'once things calm down', the most common way to put something off.

trap: English 'swamped' or 'snowed under' gives no verb: Japanese says you're 'chased by work' (owareru, the passive of ou).
freqNote: The passive 追われる has no entry of its own (lemmatised), so verbRank is the base verb 追う (#1006).
why: A small-talk and excuse staple (saikin shigoto ni owaretete). It says more than isogashii and is the natural way to put it.
gap: Workday and excuse scenes: the pool has shigoto ga tamaru and shigoto ga hairu but not being swamped.

english: how much it comes to (in total)
trap: A total isn't 'is' but 'becomes': zenbu de ikura ni naru? asks the total, and every cashier says sen-en ni narimasu.
why: Shopping and paying: asking for the total and understanding the till's X-en ni narimasu, heard at every purchase. It contrasts with ikura suru, which asks one item's price.
gap: Paying in a shop or splitting a bill: the pool has ikura suru (an item's price) but not the 'total comes to' frame.

english: turn out fine, clear up (the weather)
trap: Not 'become weather': here tenki alone means fine weather (ashita tenki ni naru kana = hope it's nice tomorrow).
why: Small talk about tomorrow's plans and the forecast, and the meaning can't be worked out from the parts. Learn it beside ame ni naru (turn to rain) and tenki ga kuzureru.
gap: Weather small talk ('will it be nice tomorrow?'): the pool has tenki ga ii and tenki ga kuzureru but not this forecast-style phrase.

trap: Not ireru or tsunagu: plugs go in with sasu and come out with konsento o nuku. Konsento is the wall socket, not 'consent'.
freqNote: Both 差す (#7696) and 挿す (#17730) are written for plugs; the kana さす (#3059) mixes several verbs.
why: Charging your phone at a friend's place or a hotel (juudenki sashite ii?). It's the third sasu after kasa o sasu and megusuri o sasu.
gap: Phone and home scenes: the pool has juuden ga kireru and dengen o ireru but no way to plug in, the fix for a dead battery.

trap: Not hanashi ga kawaru or hanareru: a conversation that drifts 'veers off' (soreru), and hanashi o modosu brings it back.
freqNote: verbRank uses the kana spelling それる (#17987); the kanji 逸れる is #64636.
why: Managing a conversation: hanashi soreta kedo... or gomen, hanashi sorechatta. Useful for a learner keeping a chat going.
gap: Chatting with friends: the pool has hanashi ga aru, hanashi o suru and hanashi ga moriagaru but nothing for drifting off topic.

trap: There's no fog word: glasses 'cloud over' with the same verb as the sky (kumoru).
why: A winter and mask complaint in Japan (masuku suru to megane ga kumoru). It belongs in the glasses set with kakeru and hazusu.
gap: Coming in from the cold or wearing a mask: the pool has megane o kakeru/hazusu and masuku o suru, but not this.

english: have the same tastes, share interests
trap: English 'we share hobbies' points to a sharing verb, but Japanese says your tastes 'match' (au), as in saizu ga au.
why: Meeting people and saying why you get on (shumi ga au hito ga ii). It's a literal way to say it, unlike the idiom ki ga au, which is out of scope.
gap: Meeting new people and dating talk: the pool has shumi ga aru and naka ga ii but no way to say your tastes match.

trap: English 'it says read' has no noun: on LINE the read mark 'attaches' (kidoku ga tsuku), and reading without replying is kidoku suruu.
freqNote: kidoku suruu (既読スルー, read and ignored) has its own entry at #25718.
why: Messaging in Japan runs on LINE, and kidoku tsuita kedo henji konai is an everyday complaint.
gap: Calls and messages: the pool has meeru ga kuru, meeru o okuru and henji o suru but nothing about read receipts.

english: air out a room, let fresh air in
trap: English 'air out' has no Japanese match: you 'swap the air' (irekaeru), usually after opening a window.
why: Home routine and cooking smells (mado akete kuuki irekaeyou). Airing rooms became a daily habit after the pandemic.
gap: Evening at home and after cooking: the pool has mado o akeru but not why you open it.

trap: Not hana ga ochiru: scattering petals (above all sakura) chiru (sakura mou chitchatta).
freqNote: hana here is flower (#1169), not the nose homophone in 10-list-nouns #37; sakura (#3953) is the usual subject.
why: Spring sakura talk and timing hanami before the petals go. It pairs with hana ga saku, already in the pool.
gap: Spring and hanami small talk: the pool has hana ga saku but nothing for when the blossoms go.

trap: Not just takai: 'pricey but worth it' is ne ga haru, built from ne (price) and haru (stretch), words a learner won't connect.
freqNote: 値 read 'ne' has no single-word entry (only あたい and ち readings); the whole phrase 値が張る has its own entry at #38507. 値段 (nedan) is #2953.
why: Recommending a shop or restaurant (chotto ne ga haru kedo oishii). It's softer than takai when the price is worth it.
gap: Café and restaurant recommendations: the only price phrases in the pool are ikura suru and okane ga kakaru.

english: be worthwhile, do you good (advice, a book, an experience)
trap: Not yaku ni tatsu for advice or experiences: a tool is yaku ni tatsu, but something that does you good is tame ni naru.
freqNote: ため at #203 is mostly the grammar word (tame ni). The phrase ためになる is its own row at #4007.
why: Used to praise a talk, book or piece of advice. Kept apart from yaku ni tatsu and from the grammar pattern tame ni (in order to).
gap: In the sweep, ためになる is its own row at #4007. The pool has yaku ni tatsu but nothing for 'it did me good'.

english: not be in the mood, not feel like it
trap: Nothing in 'I don't feel like it' leads to noru (ride). The plain way to say it is ki ga noranai.
freqNote: 気が乗らない is not a phrase row in the list. The positive ki ga noru is rare, so the headword keeps the negative, like genki ga nai.
why: A soft way to turn down plans (ima ki ga noranai). Without it, learners say yaritakunai, which sounds blunter.
gap: The pool has five literal ki phrases (ki ga tsuku, ki ga chiru, ki ga kawaru, ki o tsukau, ki ni iru) but not this one. Found while checking 乗る at #439.

english: feel heavy and run-down, feel sluggish
trap: Not just tsukareta: the heavy, achy feeling of a cold coming on is karada ga darui.
why: One of the first things you say at the doctor's or when calling in sick.
gap: The pool's body set has fever, headache, chills and nausea but no general malaise. 体 (#371) appears only in karada ni ii, karada ga yowai and karada o ugokasu.

trap: Not suibun o nomu: you 'take in' fluids, suibun o toru, just as you say eiyou o toru for nutrition.
why: What everyone says to someone who is ill, or in summer heat: chanto suibun totte ne.
gap: The sweep found 水分 (#7438) with no pool entry. Nothing in the pool covers drinking enough when ill or in the heat.

trap: 'Sigh' is a verb in English. Japanese uses a noun with tsuku, the same verb as uso o tsuku.
freqNote: つく at #355 lumps all its kana senses together. The 吐く (つく) reading alone is #173635.
why: Tameiki tsukanai de and tameiki bakkari are everyday remarks. Learners have no other way to say 'sigh'.
gap: The sweep found ため息 (#5484) with no pool entry.

english: work a shift, be on the rota
trap: Not shifuto o suru: you 'enter' a shift, shifuto ni hairu (ashita shifuto haitteru).
why: Part-time and shift workers say this every week to explain why they can't come.
gap: The sweep found シフト (#5797) with no pool entry. The pool has no part-time-job talk beyond shigoto ga hairu.

english: get the hang of it, get the knack
trap: The set phrase is kotsu o tsukamu ('grab the knack'). Kotsu ga wakaru is also heard, but kotsu o toru is not.
why: How you talk about improving at any skill, sport or job (yatto kotsu tsukanda).
gap: The sweep found コツ (#4861) with no pool entry. The hobbies set has no way to talk about getting better.

english: work up the courage, be brave
trap: Not yuuki o motsu or mitsukeru: you 'put out' courage, yuuki o dasu (yuuki dashite itta), as in genki o dasu.
why: Used for confessing, asking someone out or speaking up. It pairs with genki o dasu, which is already in the pool.
gap: The sweep found 勇気 (#1550) with no pool entry. The pool has genki o dasu but nothing for courage.

english: be perceptive, quick to catch on, have good instincts
trap: English 'sharp' leads to atama ga ii, which means clever. Picking up on things is kan ga ii.
why: A frequent remark when someone guesses right (kan ii ne!). It is literal (intuition is good), not a character idiom.
gap: The sweep found 勘 (#2843) with no pool entry. The describing set has atama ga ii but nothing for intuition.

english: be compatible, go well together (people, also food pairings)
trap: 'We're compatible' has no Japanese verb to copy. You say the match is good, aishou ga ii (also wain to chiizu wa aishou ga ii).
why: Everyday talk about couples, friends, coworkers and food pairings. It is the plain, literal word, not the idiom ki ga au.
gap: The sweep found 相性 (#4593) with no pool entry. Naka ga ii covers being close, not being a good match.

english: have things to talk about, click in conversation
trap: Here au means 'fit', not 'meet'. People whose conversation fits are hanashi ga au; ki ga au is the separate idiom.
why: The literal way to say you get on with someone (kare to wa hanashi ga au). Its link to H-au-meet keeps the two meanings of au apart.
gap: The pool has three hanashi entries (aru, suru, moriagaru) but not this one. Found while checking 合う at #563.

trap: Not demae o chuumon suru or kau: you 'take' delivery, demae o toru. Younger people also say uubaa tanomu.
why: The standard way to say you're getting food delivered instead of cooking.
gap: The sweep found 出前 (#6403) with no pool entry. The food set covers cooking and drinking but not delivery.

english: a queue forms, there's a line
trap: Not gyouretsu ga aru: a queue 'comes into being', gyouretsu ga dekiteru. Joining it is narabu.
why: Used for popular ramen shops, sales and attractions (itsumo gyouretsu ga dekiteru mise).
gap: The sweep found 行列 (#6839) with no pool entry. Mise ga komu covers crowding inside, not the line outside.

english: put something off, deal with it later
trap: 'Put off' has no Japanese verb to copy. You turn the task into 'later', atomawashi ni suru.
why: Used for chores, homework and replies you keep putting off (sore wa atomawashi ni shiyou).
gap: The sweep found 後回し (#7247) with no pool entry. The plans set has nothing for putting off your own tasks.

english: a bug turns up (in the house)
trap: Not mushi ga iru for the moment of seeing it: pests (and ghosts) 'come out', gokiburi ga deta!
why: Gokiburi deta! is the classic household cry. Deru for things appearing is not obvious.
gap: The sweep found 虫 (#3256). The pool has only ka ni sasareru for insects.

english: be a small eater, not eat much
trap: Not taberu no ga sukunai or chiisai: a small eater's eating is 'thin', shoku ga hosoi.
why: Common when refusing more food or describing kids and older people. It is the plain expression, not a body-part metaphor.
gap: The sweep found 食 (#4108). The food and describing sets have sukikirai ga ooi but nothing for how much someone eats.

english: get tested, have a (medical) check or test
trap: Not kensa o suru, which is what the doctor does: the patient 'receives' a test, kensa o ukeru, as in shujutsu o ukeru.
why: Blood tests, check-ups and screenings come up constantly. Kenshin o ukeru (annual health check) works the same way.
gap: The sweep found 検査 (#2053) with no pool entry. The pool has shujutsu o ukeru and chuusha o utsu but no tests or check-ups.

english: do someone a favour (agree to a request)
trap: Not onegai o suru, which means making the request. Doing the favour is onegai o kiku (chotto onegai kiite kureru?).
freqNote: お願い #258 includes the onegai (shimasu) phrase; 聞く #67 counts all listen/hear/ask uses
why: This is the usual way to ask "can you do me a favour?" and to agree to one. English "do" leads to suru, which reverses who is asking.
gap: The pool has onegai ga aru (have a favour to ask) but nothing for agreeing to a favour, so the do → suru trap was not covered.

trap: Not oru, which is for paper or snapping something. Clothes, laundry, futons and umbrellas are tatamu.
freqNote: 服 #1051; 畳む #6592 (kana たたむ #20410 counted separately)
why: Folding laundry is a daily chore, and learners can't guess the verb. The same verb closes an umbrella (kasa o tatamu) and puts the futon away (futon o tatamu), both next to pool items.
gap: The pool has sentakumono o hosu / torikomu, kasa o sasu and futon o shiku but no folding step, so the fold → oru trap was missing.

english: hear from someone (they get in touch)
trap: Not X kara kiku, which means you heard some news from X. "Did he get in touch?" is renraku kita?
freqNote: 連絡 #326; 来る #52 counts all coming
why: Comes up constantly when making plans or dating (mada renraku konai, renraku kitara oshiete). It is the receiving side of renraku suru in the versatility list.
gap: The pool has renraku o toru and renraku ga toreru (reaching someone) but not hearing from them. meeru ga kuru covers only an arriving email or message.

english: run a shop, bar or restaurant
trap: Not hashiru or motsu. Running a shop is yaru (oya ga izakaya yatteru); keiei suru is formal.
freqNote: 店 #440 (みせ reading; てん #3482 counted separately); やる #45 counts every casual 'do'
why: Comes up when talking about family and jobs (jikka de pan'ya yatteru). English "run" gives no route to yaru.
gap: The pool covers shops opening, closing and appearing (mise ga aku / shimaru / dekiru) but not who runs them. The run → hashiru trap was missing.

trap: Not tsukau, which treats time as a resource you use up. Spending time with people, or spending a weekend, is sugosu (shuumatsu dou sugoshita?).
why: Used in small talk about holidays and weekends, and for "had a good time" (tanoshii jikan o sugoshita). English "spend" leads to tsukau.
gap: The pool has jikan o kakeru (spend time on a task) and okane o tsukau, but nothing for spending time with people or a holiday.

trap: Plugging something in is sasu (insert), and the socket takes ni: konsento ni sasu. Unplugging is nuku.
freqNote: Both parts are rare in dramas: 充電器 #21014, 差す #7696 (挿す #17730; kana さす #3059 mixes several meanings). Commonness is judgement.
why: Comes up whenever phones need charging (juudenki sashite oite, konsento ni sasu). English "plug in" has no Japanese verb a learner could guess.
gap: The media pool has juuden ga kireru and dengen o ireru but no way to say plug in or unplug.

trap: Not tsukuru for "make a mess". Making a mess is the one verb chirakasu, the transitive partner of chirakaru.
why: The transitive half of heya ga chirakaru, which is in the pool. People say it to kids and roommates (chirakasanaide, mata chirakashita).
gap: The pool has only the intransitive heya ga chirakaru; the transitive partner, for whoever made the mess, was missing.

english: make a hole; get (one's ears) pierced
trap: Not ana o tsukuru. Making a hole is akeru, and getting your ears pierced is piasu (no ana) o akeru.
freqNote: 穴 #2765; 開ける #480 (空ける #3596 is another spelling of the same verb); ピアス #13111
why: The transitive half of ana ga aku, which is in the pool. Its everyday use is piercings (piasu aketa, mimi ni ana aketai).
gap: The pool has only the intransitive ana ga aku; its transitive partner and the piercing phrase were missing.

english: step away (from one's desk or the table)
trap: Not seki o deru. Stepping away for a moment is hazusu ('remove'), as in the phone line tadaima seki o hazushite orimasu.
why: The standard way to excuse yourself from a meeting or table (chotto seki hazushimasu), and what you hear when you phone an office.
gap: The pool has seki ga aku, seki o yuzuru and seki o toru but not stepping away; megane o hazusu is the pool's only hazusu.

trap: Not omoi. Heavy makeup is koi (thick, dense) and light makeup is usui; meiku ga koi works the same way.
why: A common comment on appearance (kyou meiku koi ne). It uses the same koi / usui split the pool teaches for coffee and seasoning.
gap: The pool has keshou o suru / otosu and aji ga koi but not heavy versus light makeup, so the heavy → omoi trap was missing.

kana: きゅうきゅうしゃをよぶ
trap: English 'call' pushes to denwa o kakeru; you yobu (summon) an ambulance, as in the shout kyuukyuusha yonde!
freqNote: Both ranks are real lookups. Dramas inflate emergencies, so commonness is judged lower than the noun rank suggests, while speakNeed stays high.
why: This is the one emergency phrase a learner must be able to produce. It also teaches that yobu (summon) applies to services, not only to people, alongside takushii o yobu.
gap: 救急車 ranks #1854, inside the top 2000 drama words, but no pool item uses it. The only yobu item in the pool is takushii o yobu.

trap: No English pairing to copy. 'Do you like the food here?' is asked as nihon no tabemono, kuchi ni au? Here au means 'fit', not 'meet'.
why: This is the stock question put to foreigners (kuchi ni au?) and the polite hedge when serving food (okuchi ni au ka wakaranai kedo). Natives hear it as the plain, literal way to say 'suits my palate', not as a character metaphor, so it passes the borderline rule.
gap: 口 ranks #556 and is item #36 on 10-list-nouns, but no pool item pairs it with a verb.

trap: English 'not a morning person' has no calque (asa no hito ja nai is wrong). Say asa ga yowai, and asa ga hayai for an early start or an early riser.
why: People use it all the time to describe their own daily routine. It is the same yowai as osake ga yowai and atsusa ni yowai already in the pool, and it is worth contrasting with asa ga hayai ('I have an early start tomorrow').
gap: 朝 is in the top 500 (#453), yet the pool has no collocation built on asa.

trap: Not waruguchi o hanasu. Badmouthing takes iu, like monku o iu and joudan o iu.
why: It comes up constantly in talk about friends, coworkers and family (hito no waruguchi iwanai de). It belongs in the pool's iu set next to monku o iu, joudan o iu and orei o iu.
gap: 悪口 ranks #3248. The pool's speech-act items cover complaints, jokes, thanks and lies but not badmouthing.

english: skin gets rough or irritated, break out
trap: English 'my skin is dry / bad' pushes to hada ga kawaku or warui. Skin that flares up from stress, cold or lack of sleep areru (hada areta).
why: This is everyday self-care talk (nebusoku de hada areta, fuyu wa hada ga areru). The partner verb cannot be guessed from English, and the pool's skin item, nikibi ga dekiru, does not cover it.
gap: 肌 ranks #2768 and its partner 荒れる #3701, both inside the top-4000 sweep. The pool has no hada collocation.

trap: Not himitsu o motsu or tamotsu. You keep a secret with mamoru (protect), the same verb as yakusoku o mamoru.
why: Typical uses are himitsu mamotte ne and zettai mamoru kara. It complements naisho ni suru (make something a secret) in the pool: this one is keeping it, that one is creating it.
gap: 秘密 ranks #1003, close to the top 1000. The pool has naisho ni suru but no himitsu item, and nothing for 'keep a secret'.

english: get over a cold (actively), shake off a cold
trap: English 'get well' has no object, but Japanese makes you naosu the cold: hayaku kaze naoshite ne (get well soon).
why: Hayaku (kaze) naoshite ne is the everyday get-well wish. This is the transitive half of kaze ga naoru, which is already in the pool; the two are learned as a pair.
gap: The pool has kaze ga naoru (intransitive) but not its transitive half. The pair rule makes the other half a new item.

trap: English 'rest up / recover' has no noun. Japanese 'takes off' the tiredness: onsen de tsukare o toru, yukkuri yasunde tsukare totte ne.
why: This is the transitive half of tsukare ga toreru, which is in the pool. You hear it in caring phrases and in talk about baths and holidays.
gap: The pool has tsukare ga toreru and tsukare ga tamaru but not the transitive tsukare o toru.

english: make one's dream come true, achieve a dream
trap: English 'achieve / realise a dream' pushes to tassei suru or jitsugen suru. The everyday verb is kanaeru, the transitive half of yume ga kanau.
freqNote: verbRank is for the kana spelling かなえる (#2619). The kanji spelling 叶える ranks #6190 separately, because subtitles split the spellings.
why: You hear it when people talk about goals and ambitions (yume o kanaeru tame ni ganbaru). It completes the transitive/intransitive pair with yume ga kanau.
gap: The pool has yume ga kanau but not its transitive partner. 夢 is a top-400 noun (#351).

trap: Not kinniku o tsukuru. Muscle is 'attached' with tsukeru, the transitive half of kinniku ga tsuku.
freqNote: verbRank is for 付ける. The kana つける (#393) lumps every sense together (turn on, attach, wear), so it is not used here.
why: It is common in gym and fitness talk (kinniku tsuketai) and is said about yourself, which is where speakNeed comes from. It completes the transitive/intransitive pair with kinniku ga tsuku.
gap: The pool has kinniku ga tsuku only. 筋肉 ranks #4421, just past the 4000 cut, and turned up while checking the pool's pair halves.

english: a typhoon is coming, a typhoon hits
trap: English 'a typhoon hits' pushes to ataru or utsu. Japanese says the typhoon comes: ashita taifuu kuru rashii yo.
freqNote: 台風 ranks #8171 because drama subtitles under-count weather talk. In a Japanese late summer it is daily small talk, so commonness is a judgement.
why: From August to October this is daily small talk and planning ('will the trains run?'). The weather set should not leave it out.
gap: The weather pool covers rain, snow, wind, thunder, earthquakes, the rainy season and pollen, but not typhoons. 台風 is already in the vocab-trainer weather-terms set.

english: join a company, start working at a company
trap: English 'join a company' pushes to sanka suru (take part). Joining a firm, school or club is hairu: kaisha ni haitte sannen.
why: This is a self-introduction staple (kono kaisha ni haitte go-nen desu). The same pattern gives daigaku ni hairu (get into university), so the item also covers school entry.
gap: The pool has kaisha ni tsutomeru and kaisha o yameru but no item for starting at a company. Its only 'hairu = join' item is chiimu ni hairu. 会社 ranks #474.

kana: けっこんしきをあげる
english: have a wedding, hold the ceremony
trap: English 'have a wedding' pushes to motsu or aru. A ceremony is held with ageru (shiki o ageru). Casual speech also says kekkonshiki yaru.
why: It is standard in adult talk about friends and family (shiki wa itsu ageru no?). It sounds the same as the stage-2 verb ageru (give) but is a different verb, which a learner must keep apart.
gap: 結婚式 ranks #2115. The people pool covers dating, break-ups and babies but has no wedding item.

trap: Not futsukayoi ga aru. You become hungover (futsukayoi ni natta), or simply say futsukayoi da.
why: It is the natural follow-on to the drinking set already in the pool (osake ni you, yoi ga sameru, osake ga tsuyoi/yowai), and a frequent Monday-morning line.
gap: The pool has drinking and sobering up but nothing for the morning after. 二日酔い ranks #6633.

english: have a meal now, make it mealtime
trap: English 'let's eat' pushes to gohan o tabeyou. At home people say sorosoro gohan ni shiyou (let's switch to the meal), and ofuro ni suru? gohan ni suru? asks which comes first.
why: This is a constant household phrase. The same frame gives ohiru ni suru (let's have lunch). It fits next to warikan ni suru, naisho ni suru and manaa moodo ni suru in the pool.
gap: ご飯 ranks #1225. The pool's gohan items are about cooking and serving (taku, takeru, sameru, dekiru, nokosu), not deciding to eat now.

trap: Not junbi desu or redi: 'Are you ready?' is junbi dekita?, where ready means the preparation has come into being.
freqNote: できる #73 is the kana form; 出来る #1313.
why: The everyday 'Ready?' / 'I'm ready' before going out, eating or starting something, as in junbi dekitara oshiete.
gap: No pool item for 'be ready'. Dekiru's 'ready' sense only appears as gohan ga dekiru (the meal is ready).

english: be treated (to a meal), let someone pay
trap: Not a passive like gochisou sareru: being treated is gochisou ni naru, like osewa ni naru. The person paying says gochisou suru or ogoru.
freqNote: ごちそう #2702 (kana) also counts gochisousama; ご馳走 #15229.
why: Said every time someone pays for your meal or drinks. The set thanks gochisou ni narimashita goes with gochisousama.
gap: The pool's naru family has osewa ni naru but not its meal-specific twin, and nothing for being treated.

english: run a fever, come down with a fever (of a person, often a child)
trap: Not netsu o morau: with the person as subject it is netsu o dashita (musuko ga netsu dashite). Netsu ga deta is the same event from the fever's side.
why: The standard way to say someone came down with a fever, the commonest reason for cancelling plans or missing work.
gap: The pool has netsu ga deru, netsu ga aru and netsu ga sagaru, but not the transitive half netsu o dasu.

trap: Not pointo o morau as the default: points build up, so tamaru. Pointo o tameru is collecting them and pointo o tsukau is spending them.
freqNote: ポイント #2464 also counts 'point' as in key point. 貯まる #24870 is the money/points spelling. Kana たまる #1650 mostly counts tamaranai ('unbearable'), so it is not used.
why: Every checkout in Japan asks about point cards. Pointo tamatteru and tamaru kara kocchi de kau are everyday shopping talk.
gap: The pool's tamaru family covers okane, sutoresu, shigoto and tsukare, but not points, the commonest partner in daily shopping.

english: music is playing (in a shop, at a party, on the radio)
trap: Not ongaku ga hiku or ongaku ga suru: a song that's on is kakatteru (or nagareteru), the intransitive of ongaku o kakeru.
freqNote: かかる #385 pools all senses (take time, cost, be locked); 掛かる alone is #5316.
why: How you say a song was on in a shop, at a party or on the radio (kono kyoku, mise de kakatteta).
gap: The pool has ongaku o kakeru but not its intransitive half. The kakaru family is otherwise covered (jikan, okane, kagi, denwa, isha).

trap: Not iyahon o kiru: earphones take suru (or tsukeru), like a watch or a mask, as in iyahon shiteta kara kikoenakatta. Taking them out is hazusu.
freqNote: イヤホン #13621; the variant spelling イヤフォン is #123250.
why: A daily excuse and request: earphones in on the train, so I didn't hear you; iyahon hazushite.
gap: The pool's suru-for-wearing items are tokei, masuku and mafuraa. Earphones, worn every day, are missing.

english: stick in one's mind, be memorable
trap: Not oboeyasui or kioku suru: 'the most memorable part was…' is ichiban inshou ni nokotta no wa…
why: The stock way to say what stood out about a trip, film or person, asked and answered constantly (nani ga ichiban inshou ni nokotta?).
gap: The pool's nokoru/nokosu family has only gohan o nokosu, so there is no way to say 'memorable'.

trap: Not ruuru ni tsuite iku: following rules is mamoru ('protect'), like promises and time. Ruuru ni shitagau is stiffer.
why: Comes up with kids, sharehouses, rubbish sorting, sport and work. Kimari o mamoru is the same pairing.
gap: The pool's mamoru family has only yakusoku o mamoru and jikan o mamoru. Rules, the next most common partner, are missing.

trap: Not koe ga fukai: a deep voice is low, hikui. A high-pitched one is koe ga takai.
why: How people describe a voice (on the phone, a singer, someone they like). Koe ga takai is its pair, and koe ga ookii (loud) is already in the pool.
gap: The pool's only voice item is koe ga ookii (loud). Pitch, the trap pair where deep = hikui, is missing.

trap: Not kaze ga mawaru: an illness going around is 'in fashion', hayatteru. Infuru ga hayatteru is just as common.
freqNote: 流行る #7728. Kana はやる #3176 is probably mostly this verb but also counts 逸る, so it is not used.
why: Standard winter small talk and warning (ima kaze hayatteru kara ki o tsukete). Hayaru also covers trends.
gap: The pool's illness items (kaze o hiku, kaze ga utsuru, infuru ni kakaru) have no way to say something is going around.

trap: Not kami ga ochiru: hair coming out (in the shower, from stress, with age) is nukeru. Ochiteru is only for a hair lying on the floor.
freqNote: かみ is ambiguous (神 #1988, 紙 #2672), so 髪 #1752 is used.
why: Common talk about stress, ageing, pets shedding and the shower drain. English 'fall out' pushes learners to ochiru.
gap: The pool has kami ga nagai/mijikai/nobiru and kami o kiru/someru/nobasu, but nothing for losing hair. The nukeru family is absent apart from konsento o nuku and asagohan o nuku.

english: come with a drink (a set includes it)
trap: Not dorinku to kuru: 'comes with' is tsuku (kore, saarada tsuku?). Tsuku 'arrive' is a different verb.
freqNote: 付く #1570; kana つく #355 pools arrive / turn on / stick.
why: Ordering sets and lunch menus (dorinku tsukimasu ka; setto ni suupu ga tsuku). The noun swaps freely (saarada, suupu, omake).
gap: The pool's tsuku family covers stains, scratches, muscle, light and read receipts, but not 'comes with', its restaurant use.

english: be shocked, be hurt (by news, a remark)
trap: Not shokku suru: you receive a shock, so shokku uketa. Shokku datta is the other natural way.
why: Reacting to bad news, a breakup or a harsh comment.
gap: The pool's ukeru family is only exams, interviews, operations and tests. Its one common emotional partner is missing.

kana: きゅうりょうがあがる
trap: Not kyuuryou o morau, which is just 'get paid': a raise is the salary going up, kyuuryou agatta.
freqNote: 上がる #503; kana あがる #3514 is listed separately.
why: A staple of work small talk and complaints about prices. It pairs with kyuuryou ga hairu in the pool.
gap: The pool's agaru family covers kion, tenshon, ofuro kara and uchi ni, but not pay going up.

trap: Not mushiba o motsu: cavities, like pimples and bruises, 'come into being', so dekiru.
freqNote: できる #73 is the kana form.
why: The dentist sentence. The pool has the dekiru-for-body set (nikibi, kuma, aza), and teeth are its commonest case.
gap: The pool's dekiru body items are nikibi, kuma and aza, with nothing for teeth or the dentist.

trap: Not deeta o nakusu: files and photos disappear, kieru (shashin zenbu kiechatta). Kesu is deleting them yourself.
why: The phone-disaster sentence after a reset or a broken phone. It is the intransitive partner of shashin o kesu.
gap: The pool's kesu/kieru family pairs only denki. Shashin o kesu has no intransitive half for losing data or photos.

trap: Not kaminari ga utsu: lightning falls (ochita). Kaminari ga naru is the thunder you hear.
why: Summer storm talk (ima ochita!, chikaku ni ochita). It pairs with kaminari ga naru in the pool, and English 'strike' sends learners to utsu.
gap: The pool has only kaminari ga naru. Its ochiru items cover exams, dirt and apps, but not lightning.

trap: Not shio o kakeru: salt is shaken on, furu (same sound as ame ga furu). Kakeru is for liquids like shouyu.
freqNote: 振る #1638 also counts 'wave' and 'dump (a partner)'.
why: Cooking together and at the table (shio futta?). It is the third seasoning verb beside shouyu o kakeru and shouyu o tsukeru.
gap: The pool's seasoning verbs are kakeru and tsukeru, both with soy sauce. There is no verb for dry seasoning.

english: hot water comes out / runs (tap, shower)
trap: 'There's no hot water' is oyu ga denai, not oyu ga nai. This is the intransitive of mizu o dasu / oyu o dasu.
why: What you tell a landlord or hotel front desk (shawaa no oyu ga denai). It is the other half of mizu o dasu in the pool.
gap: The pool has mizu o dasu and mizu o tomeru (transitive) but no intransitive half for water or hot water running.

english: make fun of, look down on
trap: Not warau or anything with tsukuru: 'make fun of' is baka ni suru, literally 'treat as a fool'.
freqNote: nounRank is the katakana spelling バカ (#433). ばか is #2695 and 馬鹿 #6994. There is no phrase count.
why: A stock line in teasing and complaints ('baka ni shinaide yo', 'baka ni sareta'), and the passive is as common as the active. English 'make fun of / mock' gives no route to it, and warau ('laugh at') covers only part of the meaning. It is the plain literal phrase, not a metaphor idiom.
gap: In the 'make' sweep, the pool covers make a call, tea, friends, a plan, noise and a face, but has no 'make fun of'. No entry anywhere in the pool uses baka.

english: blame (someone else), pin it on someone
trap: Not semeru, which means 'criticise, attack'. To pin the blame on someone is X no sei ni suru.
freqNote: せい #400 is the hiragana 'fault' noun. That count also includes X no sei de ('because of X'). There is no phrase count.
why: 'Hito no sei ni suru na' and 'ore no sei ni shinaide' are stock lines in any argument, and X no sei da ('it's X's fault') comes with them. The dictionary verb for 'blame' (semeru) is too strong, and a learner has no way to guess the noun + ni suru shape.
gap: Found in the 'put (it on someone)' and 'blame' part of the sweep. The pool has no entry with sei, and the versatility list has neither sei nor okage.

trap: Not iiwake o tsukuru: you 'do' an excuse, iiwake (o) suru.
why: The noun is high-frequency (#1512) and shows up in arguments and apologies: 'iiwake shinaide', 'iiwake ja nai kedo...' ('I'm not making excuses, but...'). It works the same way as kenka o suru and henji o suru, which are already in the pool, where English 'make' pulls a learner toward tsukuru.
gap: In the 'make' sweep, the pool has nothing for 'make an excuse'.

trap: Not chigai o iu or oshieru: here 'tell' is wakaru, and the difference is the subject. It is usually heard as chigai ga wakaranai.
why: It comes up when tasting, shopping and comparing ('zenzen chigai ga wakannai'). English 'tell' pushes a learner toward iu or oshieru. It is a third everyday X ga wakaru, next to imi ga wakaru and kimochi ga wakaru in the pool.
gap: In the 'tell' sweep, the pool has uso o tsuku, michi o oshieru and joudan o iu, but no 'tell the difference'.

trap: There is no single verb for 'waste': Japanese says muda ni suru ('make it useless'), and 'a waste of time' is jikan no muda.
freqNote: verbRank is 無駄 (muda), the content word of muda ni suru. suru is #15, and ムダ is #5230.
why: 'Jikan no muda da' and 'jikan o muda ni shita' are everyday complaints, and muda ni suru works the same with okane and tabemono. English 'waste' has no single verb a learner could find.
gap: In the 'waste' sweep, the pool's time items are jikan o tsubusu, jikan o kakeru and jikan o sugosu. None covers wasting time or money.

trap: Not inu o aruku, because aruku can't take the dog as its object. You go on the dog's walk: inu no sanpo ni iku, or inu o sanpo ni tsureteku.
why: A daily routine for any dog owner and a standard small-talk line. The pool has inu o kau and esa o yaru for pets, but not the walk. English 'walk' is transitive here and Japanese aruku is not.
gap: In the 'walk' sweep, the pool has no entry with sanpo and no 'walk the dog'.

english: invite someone over (to your place), have people over
trap: Not shoutai suru, which is for formal invitations such as weddings. Having friends over uses yobu, 'call': tomodachi o uchi ni yobu.
freqNote: nounRank is the kana form うち (#113). That count includes uchi meaning 'we/our' and -uchi ni ('while'), so it overstates the 'home' sense. 家 read as いえ is #152.
why: This is the everyday way to say you're having people over ('kondo uchi ni yobu ne', 'tomodachi yonde paatii shita'). Dictionaries give shoutai suru for 'invite', which sounds formal. The pool's takushii o yobu teaches yobu only as 'call'. The guest's side is asobi ni kuru, which the versatility pattern -ni kuru already covers.
gap: In the 'call/invite' sweep, the pool uses yobu only in takushii o yobu and has nothing for having someone over.

english: be reliable, dependable (someone you can count on)
trap: There is no plain adjective for 'reliable': a dependable person 'becomes a support', tayori ni naru. Tayori ni suru means 'rely on someone'.
freqNote: 頼り #4701 is the 'reliance' word. The homophone 便り ('news, letter') is counted separately (#11999).
why: Common praise for friends, partners and colleagues ('tayori ni naru ne', 'tayori ni shiteru yo'). English 'reliable' or 'count on' leads a learner to shinrai or kazoeru. It is literal, not a body-part or metaphor idiom, like seikaku ga ii in the pool.
gap: In the 'count on / rely' sweep, the pool's describing set has atama ga ii, seikaku ga ii and kanji ga ii, but nothing for 'dependable'.

trap: Not taijuu o tsukeru or eru: weight is the subject and it increases, taijuu ga fueru. To lose weight is taijuu ga heru, or simply yaseru.
why: It comes up in health, diet and holiday-eating talk ('shougatsu de taijuu fuechatta'). English 'put on / gain' leads to tsukeru or eru. The single verbs futoru and yaseru are more common, so this item earns its place as the 'put on' trap rather than on frequency.
gap: In the 'put on' sweep, the pool covers clothes, makeup, cream, plasters and music, but not weight.

trap: Not nikki o motsu or tamotsu: keeping a diary or any record is tsukeru, as in kakeibo o tsukeru (keep household accounts).
freqNote: つける #393 covers every sense of tsukeru (turn on, attach, keep a record). 付ける alone is #1452.
why: This is the textbook 'keep' trap: English 'keep' leads to motsu or tamotsu. It is also the only record-keeping sense of tsukeru, which elsewhere in the pool means 'turn on' or 'wear'. It is lower frequency in speech, so include it for trap value only if there is room.
gap: In the 'keep' sweep, the pool has yakusoku o mamoru, petto o kau and naisho ni suru, but nothing for keeping a record.

trap: Not paama o suru or morau: a perm takes kakeru, like an iron (airon o kakeru). At the salon it is paama o kakete morau.
freqNote: The noun is rare in dramas (#16625), so commonness rests on judgement of hair-salon and appearance talk.
why: It completes the hair set already in the pool (kami o kiru, kami o someru, kami o nobasu). Of these, it is the only one whose verb can't be guessed: English 'get' gives morau or toru. Include it if the hair set goes in as a group.
gap: In the 'get' sweep, the pool's hair items cover cutting, dyeing and growing hair, but not perms.

trap: English 'my legs are sore' leads to ashi ga itai. Next-day exercise ache is one noun, kinnikutsuu, with ni naru.
freqNote: The list has no phrase counts. nounRank is 筋肉痛 and verbRank is なる.
why: Said after any gym session, hike or moving day (kinou hashitte kinnikutsuu ni natta). It fits the same 'illness noun + ni naru' shape as byouki ni naru, but the noun can't be guessed.
gap: Hobbies/sport scene, the day after: the pool has kinniku ga tsuku, karada o ugokasu and ase o kaku, but nothing for being sore afterwards.

kana: ねっちゅうしょうになる
trap: Not netchuushou o toru / morau: you 'become' heatstroke, ni naru, usually in the warning netchuushou ni naranai you ni.
freqNote: The list has no phrase counts. nounRank is 熱中症 and verbRank is なる. The drama corpus undercounts it; it is a staple of summer news and everyday warnings.
why: Every Japanese summer, people say this to each other as a 'stay safe' line (mizu nonde ne, netchuushou ni naranai you ni).
gap: Hot-day small talk: the pool has atsusa ni yowai, hizashi ga tsuyoi and suibun o toru, but not the illness that all of these warn about.

english: be wide awake (and can't get to sleep)
trap: Not me ga sameru, which means waking up. Lying in bed wide awake is me ga saeru (koohii nonda kara me ga saete nerarenai).
freqNote: verbRank is the kana entry さえる (#13581); kanji 冴える is #18380.
why: The usual way to explain a sleepless night. It must be learned alongside me ga sameru (in the pool) and okiru.
gap: Evening-at-home and dream scenes: the pool has me ga sameru, nemuri ga asai and ibiki o kaku, but nothing for being unable to fall asleep.

english: appear in a dream; dream about (someone)
trap: English 'I dreamt about you' leads to translating 'about'. Japanese says the person came out in the dream: yume ni kimi ga dete kita.
freqNote: nounRank is 夢 and verbRank is 出る. The list has no phrase counts.
why: Telling someone about last night's dream nearly always uses this (kinou yume ni dete kita yo). It uses the 'appear' sense of deru, like terebi ni deru.
gap: Dream scene: the pool has yume o miru and yume ga kanau, but nothing for saying who or what was in the dream.

trap: English 'is it cooked / done?' leads to yaketa? or ryouri sareta. Asking whether meat is cooked through is mou hi tootteru?
freqNote: nounRank is 火 (fire), not 日 (#209). verbRank is 通る.
why: Said at every yakiniku, BBQ and home cooking session. The transitive form is hi o toosu (chanto hi toshite ne).
gap: Cooking and drinking-with-friends (yakiniku) scenes: the pool has niku o yaku and niku ga yakeru, but nothing for 'cooked through', which is the actual question people ask.

english: (a dish) makes you eat more rice; goes great with rice
trap: English has no matching phrase. Praising a dish as moreish with rice is gohan ga susumu, 'the rice moves forward', also sake ga susumu.
freqNote: nounRank is ご飯 and verbRank is 進む. The list has no phrase counts.
why: One of the most common ways to compliment home food or a side dish (kore gohan susumu ne). A learner could never build it from English.
gap: Café/restaurant and cooking scenes: the pool has taste words (aji ga koi/usui, aji ga suru, kuse ni naru), but not this stock compliment for a dish.

trap: Not gohan o ireru / dasu: dishing rice or soup into a bowl is yosou (gohan yosotte kureru?).
freqNote: verbRank is the kana entry よそう (#18376). 予想 (yosou, 'prediction', #2712) is a different word, as is 装う (よそおう).
why: Said at every family dinner and when dishing up for others. The verb has no other everyday use, so the pairing is the only way to learn it.
gap: Cooking dinner, lines at the table ('can you dish up the rice?'): the pool has gohan o taku, gohan ga takeru and okawari o suru, but not serving.

english: the flavour has soaked in (simmered food)
trap: Not aji ga hairu: flavour soaking into simmered food is shimiru (kono daikon, aji ga shimite oishii).
freqNote: verbRank is kanji 染みる (#10142). The kana しみる (#7498) also counts the 'sting' sense, so it isn't used here.
why: A standard compliment for oden, nimono and curry the next day. It belongs in the same set as the pool's aji ga koi / aji ga usui.
gap: Cooking and eating scenes: the pool's aji- set (koi, usui, suru, miru) has no way to praise how a dish has soaked up flavour.

english: the alcohol kicks in; start to feel drunk
trap: English 'it's hitting me' has no verb a learner could map. Feeling the drink kick in is yoi ga mawaru, also osake ga mawaru.
freqNote: nounRank is 酔い and verbRank is 回る. The list has no phrase counts.
why: Common at nomikai (kyou wa mawaru no hayai na). It contrasts with yoi ga sameru (sobering up), which is already in the pool.
gap: Drinking-with-friends scene: the pool has osake ni you, osake ga tsuyoi/yowai and yoi ga sameru, but not the point where the drink starts to hit.

english: black out; one's memory goes blank (from drinking)
trap: Not kioku o nakusu (amnesia, formal): blacking out from drink is kioku ga tobu (nomisugite kioku tonda).
freqNote: nounRank is 記憶 and verbRank is 飛ぶ. The list has no phrase counts.
why: The usual casual way to say you can't remember last night. It must be kept apart from plain oboete nai.
gap: Drinking-with-friends scene, the morning after: the pool has no way to say 'I don't remember anything after the second bar'.

kana: しんごうにひっかかる
english: get caught at a red light
trap: Not shingou de tomaru / matsu alone: getting stopped by lights is hikkakaru, 'get snagged' (shingou zenbu hikkakatta).
freqNote: verbRank is 引っ掛かる (#3595); the 引っかかる spelling is #3643.
why: The stock excuse for running a bit late (gomen, shingou ni hikkakatte). It goes with okureru.
gap: Commute and being-late scenes: the pool has michi ga komu, juutai ni hamaru and densha ga okureru, but nothing for red lights.

trap: Not pakku suru or nimotsu o ireru: packing a bag is tsumeru, 'cram in' (mou nimotsu tsumeta?). nimotsu o matomeru means 'get your stuff together'.
freqNote: nounRank is 荷物 and verbRank is 詰める.
why: Every trip starts with this. The same verb is used for bentou o tsumeru.
gap: Trip scene, the night before: the pool has nimotsu o azukeru and nimotsu ga todoku, but nothing for packing.

kana: くつのひもがほどける
trap: Not himo ga hazureru / aku: a knot coming loose is hodokeru (himo hodoketeru yo). Tying it is himo o musubu.
freqNote: nounRank is kanji 紐. The kana ひも (#9283) is inflated by the slang 'kept man' sense. verbRank is the kana entry ほどける, because the 解ける kanji entries are dominated by the とける reading.
why: A line you say to someone else. hodokeru has no other common use, so the pairing is the only way in.
gap: Getting-dressed and walking scenes: the pool's clothes set covers putting on and taking off, but not something coming undone.

english: be offended, take it the wrong way
trap: Not okoru or kizutsuku: 'don't take this the wrong way / no offence' is ki o waruku shinaide (ne).
freqNote: The list has no entry for 悪くする. verbRank is the adjective 悪い (warui). nounRank is 気.
why: Used to soften frank remarks and in apologies (ki o waruku shitara gomen). It is the plain, literal way to say 'be offended', not a character idiom, so it passes the borderline rule. Keep apart from ki ni shinaide.
gap: Falling-out and making-up scene: the pool has kenka o suru, nakanaori o suru and monku o iu, but no way to say 'no offence' or 'did I upset you?'

english: reply to a message or email
trap: Not meeru ni kotaeru: replying to a text is kaesu, 'send back' (LINE kaeshite, henji kaesu). kotaeru is for answering questions.
freqNote: nounRank is メール and verbRank is 返す. The same verb goes with LINE / henji.
why: The most common messaging verb after okuru (gomen, kaesu no wasureteta). The pool's henji o suru is the general 'reply' and doesn't give the messaging verb. Keep apart from kaeru (go home).
gap: Phone-and-messages scene: the pool has meeru o okuru, meeru ga kuru, kidoku ga tsuku and renraku ga kuru, but not the verb for replying to a message.

english: look up (a word) in the dictionary
trap: Not jisho o miru / sagasu: consulting a dictionary is hiku, 'pull' (jisho de hiite mita).
freqNote: nounRank is 辞書 and verbRank is 引く (pull). 弾く (play an instrument) is a separate entry.
why: A learner talks about looking up words more than most people do. It is the third common use of hiku after kaze o hiku and piano o hiku, which are both in the pool.
gap: School/studying scene ('I looked it up but it wasn't there'): the pool has no way to say look something up.
